title: Comment from Van blarigan , Amber
printtext:
I support returning grizzly bear management to the State of Montana once recovery goals have been met and the population is shown to be healthy and sustainable. I believe grizzly bears are an important part of Montana’s wildlife, and I want to see them remain on the landscape for future generations. At the same time, I also believe that good conservation includes active management.
I spend a lot of time outdoors in Montana, and I’ve seen firsthand how much wildlife populations and predator numbers have changed over the years. From my perspective, state wildlife managers are better equipped to respond to local conditions, monitor populations, and make adjustments when needed than a one-size-fits-all federal approach.
I am concerned about the overall balance of our wildlife populations. In many areas of Montana, hunters, landowners, and people who spend time outside have noticed declines in elk, deer, and especially moose. I understand that predators are only one factor, and that habitat, weather, disease, and other issues also affect these populations. However, I believe predator management should remain an important tool, especially as populations of wolves, mountain lions, and grizzly bears continue to overlap with important big game habitat.
Montana has experienced tremendous success in recovering grizzly bears. I believe that success should now be followed by responsible, science-based state management that keeps grizzly populations healthy while also protecting people, livestock, and balanced wildlife populations.
Thank you for considering my comments.

title: Comment from Israel, Will
printtext:
Strong Support for the Revised Grizzly Bear 4(d) Rule

Dear U.S. Fish & Wildlife Service, I am writing in strong support of the revised proposed 4(d) rule for grizzly bear management in the Northern Rockies. This proposal represents a responsible and science-based approach to grizzly bear conservation. It properly recognizes that grizzly populations in the Greater Yellowstone and Northern Continental Divide Ecosystems have met or exceeded federal recovery benchmarks, while keeping the species listed as threatened under the Endangered Species Act. The rule wisely grants state wildlife agencies greater flexibility to manage conflicts, protect public safety, and address livestock depredation without delisting the species.

States like Montana, Wyoming, and Idaho have demonstrated they have the expertise, resources, and commitment to manage grizzly bears effectively. Giving them enhanced tools for proactive management — especially lethal removal in legitimate conflict situations — will reduce human-bear conflicts, improve public tolerance for grizzlies, and ultimately support long-term conservation of the species.

I urge the Service to finalize this revised 4(d) rule without further delay.

Thank you for considering my comments.

Sincerely,

William Israel
Helena, MT
director@mogamt.org

title: Comment from Anonymous
printtext:
Docket ID: FWS-R6-ES-2024-0186
RIN: 1018-BI14
Agency: U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (FWS)
Action: Revised Proposed Section 4(d) Rule for Grizzly Bear DPS
COMMENT IN OPPOSITION TO THE REVISED SECTION 4(d) PROTECTIVE REGULATIONS
I. Introduction & Statement of Interest
The commenter strongly opposes the FWS's Supplemental Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (SNPRM) altering the protective regulations under Section 4(d) of the Endangered Species Act (ESA) (16 U.S.C. § 1533(d)) for the grizzly bear (Ursus arctos horribilis) Distinct Population Segment (DPS). As an individual invested in native apex predator conservation and public land ecosystems, the commenter’s interest is directly harmed by policies that increase human-caused mortality and degrade subpopulation connectivity. The proposed expansion of lethal "take" allowances and state subdelegation violates the ESA and constitutes an "arbitrary and capricious" action under the Administrative Procedure Act (APA) (5 U.S.C. § 706(2)(A)).
II. Statutory Overreach Under Section 4(d): Failure to Conserve
Section 4(d) mandates that the Service issue regulations deemed "necessary and advisable to provide for the conservation of such species." 16 U.S.C. § 1533(d). "Conservation" requires using all methods necessary to bring a species to the point where ESA protections are no longer needed. 16 U.S.C. § 1532(3).
The proposal expands exceptions for human-caused take, allowing state agencies and private operators to execute lethal measures during livestock conflicts on public and private lands without federal oversight. Broadening lethal take parameters does not biologically advance conservation. Following Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo, 144 S. Ct. (2024), courts will not defer to an agency’s expansive readings of its own powers. The text of Section 4(d) strictly binds the agency to conservation-promoting rules; relaxing protections for localized economic convenience exceeds this explicit boundary.
III. Unlawful Subdelegation of Core Federal Authority
The rule establishes mechanisms where critical verification and lethal enforcement discretion are handed over to state departments and private actors. Under administrative law, an agency cannot subdelegate its statutory duties to non-federal entities without clear congressional authorization. By removing strict federal oversight and formal FWS verification before a bear is lethally removed, FWS abdicates its role as the primary trustee of listed species, risking fragmented and inconsistent management.
IV. Disregard for the Best Available Science & Biological Connectivity
The ESA commands that protective frameworks be grounded in the "best scientific and commercial data available." 16 U.S.C. § 1533(b)(1)(A). The Service's Species Status Assessment identifies human-caused mortality and geographic isolation as primary threats to lower-48 grizzly bears.
Biologically, for an apex predator with low reproductive rates, "genetic connectivity" between isolated zones (e.g., the Greater Yellowstone and Northern Continental Divide Ecosystems) is vital to avoid long-term population collapse.
Layman's Terms: When wildlife groups are cut off from one another by farms or roads, they face inbreeding. Inbreeding makes them weaker, less healthy, and less able to survive environmental shifts. To survive long-term, bears must safely travel across regions to maintain healthy breeding populations.
By introducing state-authorized lethal takes in key transit corridors, the Service increases human-caused mortality in the exact pathways needed to solve isolation. This internal contradiction renders the rule arbitrary and capricious under Motor Vehicle Mfrs. Ass'n v. State Farm, 463 U.S. 29 (1983).
V. Failure to Analyze Non-Lethal Alternatives
Under the APA, an agency must show a rational connection between the facts found and the choices made. FWS has failed to explain why it rejected mandatory non-lethal conflict-mitigation tools—such as range riders, carcass removal, electric fencing, and livestock guard dogs—which empirical data demonstrates protect both livestock and predators. Skipping this analytical step is a fatal procedural omission.
VI. Conclusion
FWS must withdraw the proposed revisions. The rule exceeds Section 4(d) limits, violates the post-Chevron standard of statutory adherence, unlawfully subdelegates federal duty, and ignores the best available science regarding connectivity.

title: Comment from Anonymous
printtext:
I respectfully urge the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to retain federal management protections for grizzly bears and not transfer primary management authority to the states at this time.
While grizzly bear populations have recovered in some ecosystems, recovery is not complete across their historic range. Long-term conservation depends not only on maintaining current population numbers but also on ensuring genetic connectivity between ecosystems, preserving suitable habitat, and minimizing human-caused mortality. These goals require consistent, science-based management that extends beyond state boundaries.
State wildlife agencies often have multiple management objectives, including maximizing hunting opportunities and responding to local conflicts. These priorities may not always align with the long-term recovery goals established under the Endangered Species Act. Once federal protections are removed, management decisions can change over time due to political, economic, or social pressures, creating uncertainty for the species' future.
You know grizzly bears reproduce slowly, have low reproductive rates, and are particularly vulnerable to increases in adult female mortality. You also know even relatively small increases in human-caused deaths can have significant effects on population growth. Given ongoing habitat fragmentation, increasing human development, road expansion, and the impacts of climate change on food resources, continued federal oversight provides an important safeguard.
Federal management also ensures that conservation decisions are coordinated across state lines. Grizzly bears do not recognize political boundaries, and maintaining connected populations is essential for preserving genetic diversity and long-term resilience.
It can not be overstated that grizzly bear recovery should not be determined solely by population numbers. Recovery should also consider genetic diversity, habitat connectivity, ecosystem health, and the species' long-term viability.
I support management decisions that are based on the best available scientific evidence and that prioritize sustained recovery over short-term management objectives. Until the Service can demonstrate that recovered populations are secure, genetically connected, resilient to changing environmental conditions, and unlikely to require relisting in the future, transferring primary management authority to the states would be premature.
Thank you for considering my comments and for your continued commitment to conserving grizzly bears for future generations.

title: Comment from Phelps, Dollynda
printtext:
Public Comment Open: Stop the Expansion of State Control Over Grizzly Bears.
Grizzlies Are Not Recovered.

Grizzly bears still occupy only a small fraction of their historic range in the lower 48 states. True recovery depends on reconnecting isolated populations, protecting secure habitat, and investing in coexistence—not expanding state authority to lethally manage bears before recovery is complete.

As climate change alters food availability, wildfire patterns, drought, and habitat conditions across the West, explorer bears will become increasingly important as they seek new territory and food resources. These bears are essential for maintaining healthy, genetically connected populations that can adapt to a changing landscape.

The Tetonia mother grizzly and her cubs should have been a wake-up call. Instead of strengthening federal oversight after that tragedy, this proposal would give states broader authority to lethally manage federally protected grizzly bears while reducing federal review of those decisions. We should be investing in proven conflict prevention measures not making it easier to kill bears that remain protected under the Endangered Species Act.
Grizzly Bears Are Not Recovered
Grizzly bears still occupy only a small fraction of their historic range in the lower 48 states. Recovery is not complete.

Recovery Depends on Connectivity
Explorer bears are essential for reconnecting Yellowstone, the Northern Continental Divide, the Bitterroot, the Selkirks, the Cabinet-Yaak, and future recovery areas.

As climate change changes food availability and habitat conditions, these bears will become even more important for helping grizzly populations adapt and remain genetically connected. They should be protected not placed at greater risk.

Climate Change Makes Connectivity More Important
Climate change is changing the landscapes grizzly bears depend on. Federal management should protect habitat connectivity that allows bears to naturally move into suitable new areas instead of increasing the likelihood of lethal removal.

Prioritize Conflict Prevention
Conflict prevention should always come before lethal removal. The Fish and Wildlife Service should require proven nonlethal measures before authorizing the killing of federally protected grizzly bears.

Keep Strong Federal Oversight
While grizzly bears remain protected under the Endangered Species Act, the federal government should retain strong oversight of lethal management decisions rather than shifting greater authority to the states.

Learn From the Tetonia Tragedy
The Tetonia mother grizzly and her cubs demonstrated why stronger accountability is needed not less. The Service should strengthen federal oversight and emphasize prevention instead of expanding state authority over lethal management.

Support Bear Smart Communities
Invest in Bear Smart Communities by expanding the use of bear-resistant trash containers, secure food storage, attractant management, community education, and other proven measures that prevent conflicts before they occur.

Promote Bear Spray
Encourage hunters, outfitters, anglers, hikers, and all backcountry recreationists traveling through grizzly habitat to carry and know how to use bear spray. Bear spray is one of the most effective tools for preventing serious injuries to both people and bears.

Invest in Coexistence
Expand funding for electric fencing, bear-resistant trash containers, carcass removal, range riders, livestock conflict prevention, food storage requirements, and public education. Preventing conflicts protects both people and grizzly bears.

Include Tribal Leadership

Complete Recovery Before Expanding State Authority

Keep strong federal oversight of grizzly bear management.

title: Comment from Christensen , Michele
printtext:
To Whom It May Concern,

I am a Colorado resident who deeply values wildlife conservation and healthy ecosystems, and I respectfully urge the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to maintain strong federal protections for grizzly bears.

Grizzly bears are an iconic native species that have inhabited the American West for thousands of years. They were driven to the brink of extinction largely due to human persecution, habitat loss, and intolerance. Their recovery under the Endangered Species Act represents one of our nation’s great conservation achievements, but that recovery is not yet complete.

True recovery cannot be measured solely by population numbers in a few isolated regions. Long-term success requires secure habitat, genetic diversity, and connectivity between populations so that grizzly bears remain resilient and self-sustaining into the future. Fragmented populations remain vulnerable to increasing development, habitat loss, and human-caused mortality.

I am concerned that shifting greater management authority to states could lead to increased lethal management and potentially future hunting seasons before full recovery objectives have been achieved. History has shown that large carnivores often become political targets, and fear-based narratives can overshadow long-term conservation needs.

The lessons learned from the management of wolves and other large carnivores demonstrate the importance of maintaining science-based protections and avoiding decisions driven by political pressure or social conflicts.

I urge the Service to:

• Maintain strong Endangered Species Act protections until grizzly populations are fully recovered and connected.

• Prioritize habitat conservation and wildlife corridors that promote genetic diversity and long-term resilience.

• Expand nonlethal coexistence measures, including conflict prevention programs, public education, and support for communities living alongside grizzly bears.

• Ensure that management decisions are guided by the best available science, transparency, and long-term ecological sustainability.

Grizzly bears are not merely numbers on a spreadsheet. They are an essential part of our natural heritage and play an important ecological role in maintaining healthy ecosystems. We have an ethical responsibility to ensure that future generations inherit a landscape where grizzly bears continue to thrive as wild animals.

Thank you for considering my comments and for your commitment to conserving one of America’s most iconic species.

Sincerely,

Michele Christensen
Longmont, Colorado

title: Comment from Jafari, Katy
printtext:
US Fish and Wildlife Service Public Comments (Grizzly Bear),

I am writing to express my strong support for maintaining federal protections for grizzly bears under the Endangered Species Act. Grizzly bears are an iconic species of American wilderness, yet have been decimated to a fraction of their historical population size and range. Decades of conservation efforts have kept the few remaining grizzly bears from going extinct. However, they still face significant threats from isolation, habitat loss, human-caused death, and climate change. Continued protections are essential to the long-term recovery and survival of grizzly bears.

I support the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service rule that would maintain federal E.S.A. protections for the grizzly bear, which have been the key to preventing their extinction. Grizzly bears are a keystone species that play a critical role in maintaining a healthy ecosystem balance. They hold great ecological and cultural importance- to lose these species would be devastating. The best available science tells us that their long-term recovery depends on treating all grizzly populations as part of a single, interconnected species rather than as isolated groups. I support the Service’s decision to consider grizzly bears as a single distinct population segment in the lower 48. This will allow for a more comprehensive and holistic conservation strategy.

However, I am concerned about two aspects of the proposed rule. Firstly, I do not support the loosened protections that will allow for greater grizzly bear killing in livestock conflicts. The USFWS should be requiring the use of non-lethal strategies to mitigate bear-livestock conflicts. Research and real-world trials show us that non-lethal deterrents are highly effective in preventing conflicts- allowing both grizzly bears and ranchers to co-exist. Secondly, the rule limits recovery zones

title: Comment from Hasan, Terry
printtext:
Thank you for rejecting the state petitions to delist grizzly bears from Endangered Species Act protections. The current science shows that the best way for the species to truly recover is to maintain federal protections under the ESA and manage the bears in a way that allows for natural connectivity between their existing habitats. The science shows that a unified population of grizzly bears is essential for their long-term recovery in the Northern Rockies.

Even with federal protections, last year was the deadliest year for grizzly bears in the Northern Rockies. Bears were killed during surprise encounters with hunters or were exterminated over encounters with livestock or after rummaging through unsecured household trash. Others were hit by cars or trains. Some were electrocuted. A mother bear and two cubs drowned in a concrete drainage ditch. Still more were killed at the hands of poachers.

At least 90 grizzly bear deaths in the Northern Rockies last year were attributable to human causes.

The rising trend in grizzly bear deaths is largely due to the states adopting lethal anti-science policies that allow for the killing and “take” of more bears. Now the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service is considering expanding on some of these types of regressive policies, even allowing for trophy hunting of grizzly bears. Virtually all leading grizzly bear biologists say this is counterproductive to the long-term recovery of grizzly bears on the landscape.

Former U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service Grizzly Bear coordinator Dr. Christopher Servheen’s 2024 report (https://earthjustice.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/12/2024-12-11-usfws-grizzly-petition_with-exhibits.pdf) highlights the importance of fostering natural connectivity for grizzly bears between existing recovery areas. Grizzlies also need enhanced protections against lethal human activities, careful mortality management, and more resources and assistance to communities to reduce human/bear conflicts.

The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service should reject any policy that allows for increased human-caused mortality risks like hunting of grizzly bears, or trapping other species, like wolves and coyotes in grizzly habitats.

I urge the Service to follow the best available science and pass a 4(d) rule that promotes natural connectivity of grizzly bear populations, manages grizzlies as a unified metapopulation, and reduces human-caused threats and risks to their mortality.

Sincerely,
Terry Hasan
Brooklyn, NY

title: Comment from Orsie, Rachel
printtext:
US Fish and Wildlife Service Public Comments (Grizzly Bear),

I am writing to express my strong support for maintaining federal protections for grizzly bears under the Endangered Species Act. Grizzly bears are an iconic species of American wilderness, yet have been decimated to a fraction of their historical population size and range. Decades of conservation efforts have kept the few remaining grizzly bears from going extinct. However, they still face significant threats from isolation, habitat loss, human-caused death, and climate change. Continued protections are essential to the long-term recovery and survival of grizzly bears.

I support the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service rule that would maintain federal E.S.A. protections for the grizzly bear, which have been the key to preventing their extinction. Grizzly bears are a keystone species that play a critical role in maintaining a healthy ecosystem balance. They hold great ecological and cultural importance- to lose these species would be devastating. The best available science tells us that their long-term recovery depends on treating all grizzly populations as part of a single, interconnected species rather than as isolated groups. I support the Service’s decision to consider grizzly bears as a single distinct population segment in the lower 48. This will allow for a more comprehensive and holistic conservation strategy.

However, I am concerned about two aspects of the proposed rule. Firstly, I do not support the loosened protections that will allow for greater grizzly bear killing in livestock conflicts. The USFWS should be requiring the use of non-lethal strategies to mitigate bear-livestock conflicts. Research and real-world trials show us that non-lethal deterrents are highly effective in preventing conflicts- allowing both grizzly bears and ranchers to co-exist. Secondly, the rule limits recovery zones

title: Comment from Kronenberg, Warren and Esther
printtext:
We are opposed to any revision to Fish and Wildlife Service, Part 610 Wilderness Stewardship that would weaken protection for wilderness study areas, lands with wilderness characteristics, or recommended, proposed, and eligible wilderness.

We believe strongly that not all land should be available for human use and exploitation and that it is critical to keep wilderness areas truly wilderness for our physical and spiritual health. We cannot be good stewards of the land if we see all of it as consumable resources. We must remember the future generations and preserve our inheritance for posterity-and for our own survival.

We have enjoyed visiting many wilderness areas in California and would be heartsick to know these magnificent landscapes were scarred by roads.

These policies aren’t as simple as the phrase “non-binding guidance” makes them sound. They carry out the agencies’ duty, rooted in the Wilderness Act and the statutes governing these lands, to keep wild and roadless country managed so as not to impair its suitability for wilderness designation until Congress decides its fate. They hold a finite inheritance of wild land intact so that a future Congress can retain the option to protect it permanently. Once roads, motorized use, or logging are admitted into these places, the wilderness character that makes them eligible is destroyed, and no future Congress can vote it back. The loss is permanent in a way that almost nothing in public lands policy ever is.

The agency has offered no reasoned justification for reversing decades of settled protection. A change of this magnitude, made without a documented basis and against the clear weight of public objection, would be arbitrary and capricious. I ask that the existing standards be preserved in full, that no revision lower the standard of care for these lands, and that our wild lands continue to be protected as they have been.

title: Comment from Eckart, Emily
printtext:
I am writing to declare my strong opposition to any alterations to Part 610 of the Fish and Wildlife Service Manual, Wilderness Stewardship that would weaken existing safeguards for wilderness study areas, lands with distinct wilderness qualities, or tracts currently proposed, recommended, or eligible for formal wilderness designation.

The frameworks outlined in this manual carry far more weight than the label "non-binding guidance" suggests. They are the direct mechanism by which the bureau fulfills its statutory obligation—grounded in the Wilderness Act and core public land laws—to oversee roadless, primitive landscapes so that their suitability for future designation remains uncompromised until Congress renders a final decision. These regulations ensure a limited heritage of pristine country is kept secure, leaving the door open for future legislative bodies to enact permanent protections. Allowing timber extraction, new roads, or motorized vehicles into these spaces permanently strips away the very qualities that make them eligible for preservation. Once that wild character is compromised, no future act of Congress can recreate it; it is a permanent loss unlike almost any other outcome in public lands management.

Moreover, the bureau has offered no logical justification for overturning decades of consistent, protective management. Enacting a sweeping policy reversal of this magnitude without a rational, evidence-based foundation—and against overwhelming public dissent—would be entirely arbitrary and capricious. I ask that the current regulatory standards remain fully intact, that the level of stewardship for these vulnerable lands not be diluted, and that our wild places continue to be defended under the established guidelines.

title: Comment from Fowler, Chris
printtext:
I oppose any revision to Part 610 of the Fish and Wildlife Service Manual, Wilderness Stewardship, that would weaken the protection of lands Congress has already designated as Wilderness. Part 610 is where the Wilderness Act’s core promise gets kept, the ban on roads, motors, machines, permanent structures, and commercial enterprise inside designated Wilderness. Lower the minimum-requirements test that holds those intrusions out, or quietly redefine a road or a motor or an installation until it no longer counts, and you’ve opened Wilderness to the development Congress placed off-limits, without Congress ever voting on it.

title: Comment from Millbrooke, Anne
printtext:

First and foremost, I strongly support the Wilderness Act, Wilderness Areas, and Wilderness Study Areas. Wilderness designation is this country's gold standard of conservation.

Third, wilderness naturally sequesters carbon and cleans our atmosphere, the air. That too is good.

title: Comment from Grisendi, Luca
printtext:
Dear U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service,
I am writing from Italy regarding the review of Part 610 of the Service Manual concerning Wilderness Stewardship.
I strongly urge the Service to preserve and strengthen existing wilderness stewardship standards.
Wilderness areas managed within the National Wildlife Refuge System have exceptional importance because they combine two fundamental conservation purposes: preservation of wilderness character and protection of wildlife and habitat.
Any revision of Service policy should therefore prioritize ecological integrity, natural processes, native biodiversity, habitat connectivity, clean water, natural soundscapes, dark skies and the undeveloped character of Wilderness.
Administrative convenience, commercial interests or increased mechanization should not be allowed to gradually erode wilderness standards.
In particular, the Service should continue to apply rigorous analysis before authorizing structures, motorized equipment, installations or activities that may impair wilderness character.
Wildlife populations increasingly face pressures from habitat fragmentation, climate change, invasive species and development outside protected areas. Intact wilderness refuges consequently serve as increasingly important ecological anchors.
Wilderness also protects areas of cultural and spiritual significance to Indigenous peoples, and meaningful Tribal consultation should remain an essential component of stewardship decisions.
The Wilderness Act was designed to provide enduring protection. Internal policy revisions should implement that purpose faithfully rather than create new pathways for degradation.
Please retain strong Part 610 protections and ensure that wilderness character and wildlife conservation remain paramount.
Thank you for considering my comments.
Kind regards.

title: Comment from Millbrooke, Anne
printtext:
Thank you for the opportunity to comment! Public participation in public matters is a basic right in any democracy, and it is a right protected in the Bill of Rights of the U.S. Constitution, such as right to free speech and right to protest. It is a right and a joy to participate in this matter.

First and foremost, I strongly support the Wilderness Act, Wilderness Areas, and Wilderness Study Areas. Wilderness designation is this country's gold standard of conservation.

Second, wilderness is good! Wilderness designation provides legal protection for watersheds, wildlife, fish, birds, insects, and the entire menagerie collectively called biodiversity.

Third, wilderness naturally sequesters carbon and cleans our atmosphere, the air. That too is good.

Fourth, Congress has delayed too long in completing the process of turning Wilderness Study Areas and other lands with wilderness characteristics into formally designated Wilderness. Please, for your sake, my sake, and the sake of generations following us, please make the strong recommendation for Congress to grant full wilderness status and protection — without of weaselly exceptions and grandfather clauses — to all existing Wilderness Study Areas and addto the wilderness system existing lands with wilderness characteristics.

Fifth, in the crude terminology masking the real values of wilderness, wilderness supports the economy - at the national, state, and local level. There are so many studies showing the economical value of a clean and healthy environment that I think everyone should know this, but it is obviously necessary to point it out in the current profiteering political climate.

Sixth, untrammeled, free from mechanized civilization and motorized contraptions (the list of existing and emerging thrill toys and tools is frightening) are keys to letting natural processes proceed free from human manipulation and monetization. Let nature reign supreme in wilderness areas.

Seventh, roadless areas are so small on the scale of this nation as to be an embarrassment. Every one of them needs effective protection from roadbuilding, regardless of excuse (forest treatment, logging, mining, local economic development, grazing, etc. - all nothing but profiteering excuses).

Eighth, wilderness designation does not exclude anyone. It allows anyone to roam as people have done throughout millennia. It simply excludes mechanized tools and toys.

Ninth, there are enough trails already in wilderness areas. There is no need to build new trails, paths, dirt access lanes, and certainly not roads. Concentrated recreation areas OUTSIDE of and away from wilderness areas can handle crowds as well as the mechanized and motorized items that people find convenient or thrilling.

Tenth, I love wilderness. The idea and reality are part of our national heritage as well as a part of our presence, and I hope our future.

Again, thank you for this opportunity to comment.

title: Comment from Towers Saint Amand, TerryAnn
printtext:
Re: FWS-HQ-NWRS-2026-2575, Part 610 Wilderness Stewardship
I urge the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service to retain the substantive protections in Part 610 and use modernization to improve transparency, science, Tribal consultation, and public accountability rather than weaken wilderness stewardship.
Part 610 governs more than designated Wilderness. Chapter 4 requires periodic wilderness review of eligible refuge lands outside Alaska and protects Wilderness Study Areas and recommended wilderness while decisions are pending. Those safeguards should remain. If a discretionary action could cause irreversible or irretrievable harm while an area is under study, FWS should postpone it rather than allow development to make the future wilderness decision meaningless.
The Minimum Requirement Analysis should remain central. Structures, motorized equipment, ecosystem manipulation, commercial services, prescribed fire, invasive-species treatment, and similar interventions should be authorized only when genuinely necessary and by the least harmful effective means. Convenience, lower cost, staffing shortages, contractor preference, or schedule pressure should not be treated as necessity.
Part 610 appropriately recognizes that refuge Wilderness is both wildlife habitat and wilderness. Natural processes such as fire and predation should not be treated as management failures merely because they are inconvenient. I support retaining the policy that predation is an essential ecological process and should not be manipulated solely to protect livestock, visitors, or other users. I also support restrictions on introducing nonnative species, stocking fish in waters that did not naturally contain fish, and artificially enhancing wildlife or fisheries.
Fire policy should retain the principle that wildland fire is an inherent ecological process and that prescribed fire in Wilderness is justified only where fire naturally belongs, satisfies the Minimum Requirement test, and serves refuge and Wilderness Act purposes. “Resilience” should not become a general authorization for routine mechanical vegetation manipulation.
The Integrated Pest Management framework should remain. Chemical or biological treatment should be used only where justified and with the least impact on non-target species and the wilderness environment. FWS should strengthen transparency by publicly documenting, where sensitive location information does not require protection, the product or agent used, active ingredient, amount, location, method, applicator, target species, and why less harmful methods were inadequate.
Wilderness stewardship plans should continue to include baseline conditions, measurable indicators, thresholds that trigger corrective action, and monitoring of wilderness character. Otherwise cumulative degradation from many small decisions can disappear from view.
FWS should preserve meaningful public participation and Tribal coordination. Consultation should occur early enough to influence decisions, and culturally sensitive information should be protected from unnecessary disclosure.
Compatible hunting, fishing, wildlife observation, photography, education, and other appropriate recreation can continue consistent with refuge purposes and wilderness character. “Access” should not become a rationale to weaken compatibility review, expand motorized use, or build permanent infrastructure where Congress has imposed a different standard.
Alaska requires particular care. Any revision must preserve ANILCA protections and rights, including subsistence priorities, traditional travel and access, and access to inholdings, together with accompanying environmental safeguards. A national rewrite should not casually disturb the balance between wilderness conservation, subsistence, rural life, and lawful access.
Finally, this process is inadequate for substantive revision. The Federal Register notice asks whether all five chapters of Part 610 should be updated, clarified, or revised, but provides no proposed replacement text or redline. The public cannot meaningfully evaluate changes it has not seen. If FWS intends material revisions, it should publish the proposed language, explain substantive changes and their legal basis, and provide another public-comment period before adoption. This request for recommendations should not be treated as approval for an unseen rewrite. Climbing-policy changes should remain in the separate climbing docket where draft language has been provided.
Modernize Part 610 without weakening it. Preserve wilderness review, interim protection, Minimum Requirement Analysis, restraint on ecosystem manipulation, natural-fire and predator principles, invasive-species safeguards, compatible recreation standards, ANILCA protections, and measurable wilderness-character stewardship.
Thank you for considering my comments.

title: Comment from Ramias, Christopher
printtext:
**Re: Docket No. FWS-HQ-NWRS-2026-2575; FXRS12610900000-267-FF09R20000 — Wilderness Stewardship**

I am writing to strongly oppose any changes to the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service's wilderness stewardship policies that would weaken protections for wilderness within the National Wildlife Refuge System.

I value our public lands not simply for the activities they allow, but for the opportunity they provide to experience places that remain wild. Wilderness areas within the National Wildlife Refuge System are among the places where that opportunity is most important. They protect habitat, ecological processes, wildlife, natural landscapes, and opportunities for solitude and primitive recreation that are increasingly difficult to find.

The purpose of wilderness protection is not merely to preserve scenery. Wilderness provides a fundamentally different kind of public-land experience: one in which natural processes are allowed to operate with minimal human interference and where visitors can experience landscapes without the infrastructure, noise, and development that characterize so much of the modern world.

I urge the Fish and Wildlife Service to maintain a strong interpretation of its responsibilities under the Wilderness Act and to manage designated wilderness in a manner that preserves its wilderness character for the long term.

In particular, I am concerned about any policy changes that could make it easier to authorize development, infrastructure, motorized or mechanized use, commercial activities, or other actions that would diminish wilderness character. These impacts are not necessarily reversible. Once a road, facility, utility, or other permanent intrusion is established in a wilderness landscape, the character of that place can be fundamentally altered.

Wilderness management should also recognize that protecting wilderness character means protecting more than individual wildlife species or isolated habitat features. Wilderness provides intact ecological systems in which natural processes—including wildlife movement, predator-prey relationships, fire, flooding, and vegetation change—can continue with minimal human manipulation. These intact systems are increasingly valuable as surrounding landscapes become more fragmented and developed.

The Service should also preserve opportunities for solitude and primitive and unconfined recreation. These are not incidental benefits of wilderness; they are among the qualities Congress specifically sought to protect through the Wilderness Act. Visitors should be able to experience refuge wilderness without encountering the sights, sounds, and infrastructure associated with intensive development.

I am particularly concerned about approaches that would treat wilderness primarily as another designation that can be balanced away whenever another use is considered convenient. Congress established the National Wildlife Refuge System and the wilderness system precisely because some places require a higher level of protection. The absence of development in these areas is itself a management success—not an indication that the land is being underutilized.

The Fish and Wildlife Service should therefore:

* Maintain strong protections for the wilderness character of National Wildlife Refuge System wilderness.
* Continue to manage wilderness consistent with the requirements and purposes of the Wilderness Act.
* Avoid unnecessary roads, structures, facilities, and other permanent infrastructure in wilderness.
* Protect opportunities for solitude and primitive and unconfined recreation.
* Preserve natural ecological processes and intact wildlife habitat.
* Carefully scrutinize actions that could introduce motorized or mechanized use or otherwise diminish wilderness character.
* Consider cumulative impacts rather than evaluating potentially damaging activities only on a project-by-project basis.
* Avoid administrative changes that would weaken existing wilderness protections or make prohibited or incompatible uses easier to authorize.

There are very few places left where people can experience a landscape primarily on nature's terms. Once those places are altered, they cannot simply be recreated elsewhere. The Fish and Wildlife Service therefore has a responsibility to act as a steward of these lands for people who will never have the opportunity to participate in today's decisions.

I urge the Service to maintain—and where appropriate strengthen—its existing wilderness stewardship policies. Wilderness within the National Wildlife Refuge System should remain genuinely wild, protected from unnecessary development and degradation, and managed so that its wilderness character endures for generations to come.

Thank you for considering my comment.

I’m writing to oppose any revision to FWS Part 610: “Part 610 of the Fish and Wildlife Service Manual, Wilderness Stewardship” that would weaken protection for wilderness study areas, lands with wilderness characteristics, or recommended, proposed, and eligible wilderness.

These policies aren’t as simple as the phrase “non-binding guidance” makes them sound. They carry out the agencies’ duty, rooted in the Wilderness Act and the statutes governing these lands, to keep wild and roadless country managed so as not to impair its suitability for wilderness designation until Congress decides its fate. They hold a finite inheritance of wild land intact so that a future Congress can retain the option to protect it permanently. Once roads, motorized use, or logging are admitted into these places, the wilderness character that makes them eligible is destroyed, and no future Congress can vote it back. The loss is permanent in a way that almost nothing in public lands policy ever is.

The agency has offered no reasoned justification for reversing decades of settled protection. A change of this magnitude, made without a documented basis and against the clear weight of public objection, would be arbitrary and capricious. I ask that the existing standards be preserved in full, that no revision lower the standard of care for these lands, and that our wild lands continue to be protected as they have been.

Wilderness

Hardware replacement depends upon: appropriateness determinations, compatibility determinations, refuge planning, possible permits.

title: Comment from Western Montana Climbing Coalition
printtext:
Western Montana Climbing Coalition
Comments on the Proposed Federal Climbing Management Guidance
To Whom It May Concern,
The Western Montana Climbing Coalition (WMTCC) appreciates the opportunity to comment on the proposed climbing management guidance. We support the overall direction of this proposal and commend the agency for recognizing that rock climbing is an appropriate and legitimate use of our public lands while acknowledging the important role that fixed anchors play in climber safety.
Western Montana is home to a diverse collection of climbing resources on Forest Service, Bureau of Land Management, and National Park Service lands. Many of these climbing areas have been developed and cared for over decades through volunteer stewardship, close collaboration with local land managers, and partnerships with organizations such as Access Fund. Our experience has shown that the best conservation outcomes occur when agencies work with the climbing community as active stewardship partners.
The Bitterroot Valley provides an excellent example of this collaborative approach. At Mill Creek, local volunteers have invested hundreds of hours improving trail sustainability, reducing erosion, restoring damaged staging areas, replacing aging anchors, educating visitors, and working alongside the Bitterroot National Forest to improve long-term recreation management. Similar stewardship efforts occur throughout western Montana and demonstrate that climbers are invested in protecting the landscapes where they recreate.
We strongly support the proposal's recognition that limited, safety-based fixed anchors are fundamentally different from larger installations and should not automatically be treated as prohibited developments. Small hand-placed anchors are an essential component of safe climbing and, when thoughtfully placed, have minimal visual or environmental impact while preventing resource damage caused by repeated placement of temporary anchors.
We also appreciate the proposal's recognition that existing climbing routes and anchors established before January 4, 2025, should generally remain available for continued use and maintenance. Western Montana contains many long-established routes that are part of the region's climbing history. Routine one-for-one replacement of aging anchors should remain straightforward so volunteers can continue maintaining these routes safely without unnecessary administrative delays.
While we support the proposal, we encourage several refinements that will improve implementation.
First, the guidance should avoid rigid national numeric standards for fixed anchors or spacing requirements. Montana climbing areas vary tremendously in geology, route length, and terrain. Local conditions, not arbitrary numerical thresholds should guide safe anchor placement.
Second, any authorization process for new routes should be efficient, predictable, and scaled appropriately to the proposed activity. Lengthy permitting processes or requirements for comprehensive climbing management plans before routine decisions can be made would unnecessarily burden both agencies and volunteers while discouraging proactive stewardship.
Third, the guidance should clearly allow timely replacement of unsafe anchors and emergency anchor installation when necessary to protect human life. Volunteers should not have to choose between following administrative procedures and addressing immediate safety hazards.
Finally, we encourage the agency to continue emphasizing partnerships with local climbing organizations. Groups like the Western Montana Climbing Coalition provide volunteer labor, local knowledge, education, monitoring, and long-term stewardship that significantly expands agency capacity. Local organizations should be consulted early when developing climbing management plans, seasonal restrictions, or other management decisions affecting established climbing areas.
As our coalition's work at Mill Creek with the U.S. Forest Service demonstrates, collaborative stewardship creates healthier landscapes, safer climbing opportunities, and stronger partnerships between climbers and land managers. We have also worked closely with the Bureau of Land Management at Rattler, organizing trail stewardship days and updating fixed anchors to improve both resource protection and climber safety. These projects demonstrate that when land managers and the climbing community work together, they can achieve lasting conservation and recreation outcomes. We encourage the agency to adopt a final policy that builds on these successful collaborations by supporting sustainable access, promoting shared stewardship, and protecting the natural resources that make our public lands exceptional for current and future generations.
Thank you for considering our comments and for your continued commitment to collaborative stewardship of America's public lands.
Sincerely,
Western Montana Climbing Coalition

title: Comment from Elliot, Benjamin
printtext:
As Vice President of the Climbing Association of Southern Arizona, I have seen firsthand that climbers care deeply about protecting the wild places where we climb.

One example is the way our community responds to wildlife concerns. CASA regularly communicates seasonal closures and other protections for sensitive species, including the annual Pusch Ridge Wilderness closure for desert bighorn sheep during lambing season. We also share information about nesting raptors and encourage climbers to avoid active nests.

In Cochise Stronghold, formal raptor closures were allowed to lapse after wildlife conditions improved. Even without a mandatory closure, CASA continued asking climbers to stay away from active nests. Climbers listened. They changed plans, avoided particular routes and crags, and gave the birds the space they needed.
That experience has reinforced my belief that climbing access and wilderness protection are not opposing goals. Climbers form lasting relationships with these landscapes. Because we return to the same cliffs, canyons, and wilderness areas over many years, we notice changes, report resource concerns, educate other visitors, and help protect the places we value. I’ve been a recreational climber, a guide, steward of the land, and now I serve as a volunteer in a leadership position. With few exceptions, my experience has shown me that the climbing community cares deeply about public land and is eager to serve as partners to land managers.

It has also shown me that site-specific management, clear communication, and collaboration are often more effective than broad prohibitions. When agencies explain what resource needs protection and why, local climbing organizations can quickly share that information and encourage responsible behavior.

I support guidance that recognizes climbing, including the responsible placement and maintenance of limited fixed anchors, as an appropriate wilderness use. Existing routes should remain available, and aging safety equipment should be eligible for routine, one-for-one replacement. title: Comment from Bedell, Sam
printtext:
As a climber who is most interested in climbing routes in wild places, such as designated wilderness areas, I have done my fair share of rappelling off of spires and peaks to safely reach the ground. In some places, where routes are repeated I see old nylon cord and webbing that had to be left behind to allow retreat. I have cleaned hundreds of pounds of sun bleached, decaying cord and webbing from old rappel anchors as I rappelled off routes over my 20+ years as a climber. In many cases I had to also leave my own, fresh material, to get down, knowing that it would decay with exposure until the next climber was able to remove it. In almost all these cases, if the first ascent party was simply allowed to place two metal bolts in the rock, then there would be no decaying nylon plastic fibers, no trash from needing to descend a route, just two pieces of stainless steel, often painted to blend in, that would allow fast and safe descent. Obviously there are situations where they are not needed, such as a mountain with a trail to the top on another aspect, but in the case of peaks that have technical terrain on all sides, such as many classic peaks that have been climbed regularly for 75 years now, leaving material is the only way to descend safely. Two pieces of metal that can be easily replaced is the least impactful option we have for allowing safe descent from these popular routes. Allowing these to be permitted and replaced rapidly keeps users safe and limits impacts on the environment.

title: Comment from Simpson, Peter
printtext:
As a rock climber who relies on well-maintained fixed anchors to climb safely on public lands, I appreciate the opportunity to comment on the Fish and Wildlife Service's implementation of the EXPLORE Act, but I have several concerns.

First, within Wilderness, hardware replacement is made to depend on appropriateness determinations, compatibility determinations, refuge planning, and possible permits. Layering these requirements onto routine maintenance risks significant delay and could leave deteriorating, unsafe anchors in place while approvals work their way through. Replacement of existing anchors should be broadly authorized so that qualified climbers can keep hardware safe in a timely manner.

Second, "replacement" is never defined, and the guidance gives no indication of whether it includes modernization. Modern anchor replacement rarely means installing identical hardware. The guidance should explicitly allow upgraded hardware, adhesive (glue-in) anchors, modest relocation where rock quality is poor, and improved anchor configurations consistent with accepted best practices.

Outside Wilderness, I recognize that the Refuge System's statutory framework makes climbing access necessarily different, since climbing must first clear an appropriateness determination and a compatibility determination before it is authorized. Even so, handling every subsequent replacement through individual refuge planning is likely to remain more administratively burdensome than on other federal lands. Once climbing is authorized on a refuge, bolt replacement work should be broadly authorized rather than routed through case-by-case planning.

I support responsible climbing management consistent with the Refuge System's mission, but this guidance should enable the ongoing anchor maintenance that keeps climbers safe rather than creating administrative delays that leave dangerous hardware in place.

The approximately 1.76 million-acre proposed leasing area (“RFI Area”) identified in the applicant’s unsolicited mineral release sale request does not exist in isolation.

The consequences of such a high-impact activity in this dynamic and interconnected coastal marine ecosystem could cause extensive harm beyond the defined RFI Area.

I have four main areas of concern:

1. Risk of harm to local and migratory protected and endangered species.
2. Risk of harm to habitat for culturally, commercially, and recreationally important fish species.
3. Risk of exacerbating coastal erosion threats and community resilience due to reduced alongshore and nearshore transport of sediment.
4. Risk of setting a precedent for future coastal seabed mining in the Atlantic without a scientific consensus on the potential impacts of seabed mining on local, regional, and global marine ecosystems, and neighboring communities.

David Quick
[Redacted PII]
Mount Pleasant, SC 29464

title: Comment from Willis, Emily
printtext: Subject: Opposition to Commercial Seabed Mineral Leasing Offshore Virginia — BOEM-2026-0100 Dear BOEM Marine Minerals Division: I live in Virginia Beach, VA, and I am writing in strong opposition to BOEM’s Request for Information on potential commercial mineral leasing offshore Virginia. Virginia’s coast is not an empty industrial zone. It supports our tourism economy, commercial and recreational fisheries, aquaculture industry, military operations, wildlife habitat, and coastal communities. From Virginia Beach to the Eastern Shore, our communities depend on clean water, healthy marine ecosystems, and a thriving ocean economy. The proposed RFI Area covers approximately 2,764 square miles off Virginia’s coast. Marine phosphate and heavy mineral sand mining would likely involve industrial-scale dredging and removal of large volumes of seafloor. That activity could destroy bottom habitat, increase sediment in the water, disrupt fish and shellfish habitat, and threaten the clean coastal waters that support Virginia’s fisheries, aquaculture, tourism, recreation, and quality of life. This proposal would introduce a new and risky industrial use into waters that already sustain major existing industries. Virginia’s marine economy supports more than 130,000 jobs and contributes billions of dollars each year to the Commonwealth. The Eastern Shore also supports nationally significant aquaculture, migratory bird habitat, fish nurseries, tourism destinations, and some of the most important coastal wilderness remaining on the Atlantic seaboard. The risks of commercial seabed mining are too great. This proposal could cause lasting harm to Virginia’s ocean resources, coastal economy, and way of life. I urge BOEM to remove the areas offshore Virginia from consideration for commercial mineral leasing and to abandon any plans for seabed mining off Virginia’s coast. At minimum, BOEM should extend the public comment period and hold public meetings in affected coastal communities, including Hampton Roads and the Eastern Shore. Thank you for considering my comment.

title: Comment from Johnston, Daniel
printtext:
I wish to express my strong opposition to any proposal to permit deep-sea mining off the Virginia coast.

It does not require a degree in marine biology or environmental science to recognize that vacuuming the ocean floor would severely disrupt—perhaps permanently—the delicate ecosystems that have evolved over millions of years. Disturbing these habitats threatens the complex food webs that support fish, marine mammals, and countless other ocean species.

Supporters argue that extracting rare minerals from the seabed is necessary to meet the growing demand for electric vehicle batteries, smartphones, and advanced microchips. However, terrestrial mining remains significantly less expensive and, despite its own environmental impacts, is generally better understood, more tightly regulated, and far less disruptive to fragile deep-ocean ecosystems than industrial-scale seabed mining.

It is also important to recognize that there are currently no active commercial deep-sea mining operations anywhere in the world. That fact alone should give policymakers reason to proceed with great caution. Virginia should not become a testing ground for an industry whose environmental consequences remain largely unknown and could prove irreversible.

Our coastal waters are an invaluable natural resource that support commercial and recreational fisheries, tourism, and marine biodiversity. Once these deep-sea ecosystems are damaged, restoration may be impossible. Virginia has an opportunity to demonstrate responsible stewardship by protecting its offshore environment rather than leading the way in a highly controversial and potentially destructive industry.

I urge our elected officials to reject any proposal that would allow deep-sea mining off Virginia's coast and instead support policies that protect our oceans while encouraging responsible and sustainable sources of the critical minerals our economy requires.

Daniel Johnston M.D.

title: Comment from Wells , Gail
printtext:
I strongly oppose moving forward with commercial leasing for offshore mineral extraction off the coast of Virginia.

The Atlantic Ocean supports diverse marine ecosystems that are already under increasing pressure from climate change, warming waters, pollution, and habitat loss. Introducing industrial-scale seabed mineral exploration and extraction could result in long-lasting and potentially irreversible impacts on marine habitats, fisheries, whales, dolphins, sea turtles, and countless other species that depend on healthy ocean ecosystems.

There remains significant scientific uncertainty regarding the environmental consequences of disturbing the seafloor. Sediment plumes, underwater noise, habitat destruction, and the release of contaminants could have effects that extend well beyond the lease area. Once these ecosystems are damaged, recovery may take decades or may never occur.

Virginia’s coastal economy depends heavily on commercial and recreational fishing, tourism, and healthy marine resources. These industries support thousands of jobs and generate substantial economic activity. Any potential short-term economic benefits from offshore mineral development should not outweigh the long-term risks to existing livelihoods, coastal communities, and natural resources.

I urge BOEM to apply the precautionary principle and refrain from advancing this proposal until comprehensive, independent scientific research demonstrates that offshore mineral extraction can be conducted without causing unacceptable environmental harm. Such research should include extensive baseline studies, cumulative impact assessments, meaningful consultation with Tribes, commercial and recreational fishing interests, scientists, coastal communities, and conservation organizations, and full transparency throughout the decision-making process.

Given the current lack of scientific certainty and the potentially significant environmental and economic consequences, I respectfully request that BOEM not proceed with commercial mineral leasing offshore Virginia.

Thank you for considering my comments.

title: Comment from Ebersberger, Wendy
printtext:
This is to strongly urge BOEM to reject proposed commercial seabed mineral leasing in the 2,764 square miles of waters off Eastern Shore Virginia. The proposal to open up this part of the Atlantic Ocean for industrial mining poses a grave threat to marine habitat, endangered and threatened species, and our local fisheries and tourism economies.

The term "lease" implies that what is leased will be returned in the same condition at the end of the lease as at its start. Extracting heavy minerals from the ocean floor would involve industrial-scale dredging, with heavy machinery designed to break up and remove enormous volumes of seafloor sediment. That process would bring a massive disruption to species and habitat, impacting fish spawning grounds, important migration routes and the complex marine food webs that both species and coastal communities rely on. Marine animals like sea turtles, fish and whale species could face increased vessel collisions, degraded water quality, and other threats to their long-term survival.

It is particularly galling that an out-of-state corporation is seeking this lease, which would adversely impact our local fisheries and tourism by jeopardizing local jobs and millions of dollars in economic activity. The damage done to our environment and economy would long outlast the term of a lease.

This is to strongly urge BOEM to reject proposed commercial seabed mineral leasing in the 2,764 square miles of waters off Eastern Shore Virginia. title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-12725 from E Milford
printtext:
Hello,

I am writing as I am concerned with §200.220 and §200.202(e) regarding international collaborative research. I work at a mathematics institute in the US that receives NSF funding. Our aim is to promote cutting edge mathematical research, which is the technology underlying almost all private sector technological progress. In order to accelerate mathematical research effectively we must carefully curate just the right mixture of expertise, personality, work environment, and research interests. One expert being disallowed from attendance can throw off the entire equilibrium which can stall progress in entire fields of mathematics. Sometimes this mathematician is American. Sometimes they are not. In mathematics researchers are almost always working in the weeds. It is difficult to be an expert in more than one area, and each area comes with its own set of instincts, intuitions, and norms. We have found that giving the experts in a given area the opportunity to significantly shape the invitation list produces the most scientific advances. When we intervene on this process or are unable to invite a notable expert due to regulation, or they are too afraid to attend due to government intimidation, the research suffers.

It is already quite difficult to coordinate international research collaboration due to the need to navigate the visa process. We already have staff dedicated to this task which creates administrative bloat. Adding additional hurdles and administrative checks would hurt the broader research community by stymieing the progress of fundamental mathematics and wasting taxes on unnecessary administrative staff. Gathering the best mathematicians from Yale, Princeton, and Stanford simply does not have the same potential to accelerate research as a carefully curated group of both US and international scholars. We are all about bringing the RIGHT minds together at the RIGHT moment in time. We cannot do that if we do not have significant lead time to develop each program (meaning funding needs to be reliable enough to plan far into the future) or if we are not allowed to invite the scholars that we need on the whim of geo-political disputes.

Technologies like space exploration, medicine, and artificial intelligence are all built on top of years of successful international collaborations between mathematicians from around the world. Any changes and their consequences should be considered extremely carefully. Sweeping changes like the ones proposed here are likely to massively disrupt the progress of mathematics if implemented. There are already signs that the significant cuts to US math funding have allowed China and the EU to pull ahead in areas like biotechnology and AI.

title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-12725 from Anonymous
printtext:
I am writing as a research assistant at an R1 institution to respectfully oppose several aspects of the proposed NSF Guidance on Financial Assistance (GFA) as currently drafted. While I support NSF’s goals of improving clarity, accessibility, and usability, the draft appears to shift substantial compliance burdens onto investigators and institutions without sufficient evidence that the resulting system will reduce confusion or improve research administration in practice.
First, the draft’s reorganization may improve navigation on paper, but the practical effect is to expand procedural complexity across 26 separate guides, each with its own requirements, definitions, and cross-references. For researchers working in fast-moving, collaborative, and often under-resourced environments, especially at R1 institutions where proposal volume is high, this structure risks creating more fragmentation rather than less. A streamlined format should reduce interpretive burden, but the draft still requires users to locate and reconcile multiple guides, regulatory citations, executive orders, and external policies to understand a single obligation.
Second, I am concerned that several provisions intensify compliance and surveillance obligations in ways that may chill legitimate research activity. The expanded research security, foreign disclosure, and risk assessment requirements may be especially burdensome for early-career researchers, international collaborators, and scholars working in politically sensitive or globally connected fields. As open science grows in popularity and efficacy in assuring reproducible, accredited research distillation, NSF should ensure that safeguards are narrowly tailored, clearly defined, and supported by transparent procedures so that compliance obligations do not become de facto barriers to collaboration, mobility, or participation in federally funded science.
Third, the draft appears to increase administrative demands around mentoring plans, data management and sharing, collaboration documentation, and reporting requirements without adequately distinguishing between large well-resourced institutions and smaller or less administratively supported organizations. Although R1 institutions may have infrastructure to absorb some of these changes, the policy should still be designed to avoid reinforcing inequities in who can participate in NSF funding. Ethical policy construction requires attention not only to accountability, but also to feasibility, proportionality, and the unequal administrative capacity of different recipients.
Fourth, some of the language in the draft is overly vague or overly deferential to future implementation details. Where key terms such as “substantial support,” “risk mitigation,” and disclosure-related expectations have major consequences for researchers, NSF should define them with greater precision and provide concrete examples, appeal pathways, and implementation guidance. Clear standards are essential for fairness, consistency, and due process.
I urge NSF to revise the final GFA so that it is not merely more organized but genuinely more usable, equitable, and transparent. NSF should reduce duplicative reporting, limit compliance expansions to what is demonstrably necessary, preserve space for open and collaborative inquiry, and provide implementation guidance that is accessible to investigators at all career stages and institutional types.
I support NSF’s effort to modernize and reorganize its financial assistance rules, but I strongly oppose the draft GFA as written because it increases administrative burden, expands compliance obligations, and may create unequal impacts across institutions and researchers. A policy intended to improve clarity should not rely on more fragmented guidance, broader surveillance-like reporting, or vague standards that shift interpretive risk onto investigators and institutions. NSF should revise the guidance to ensure proportionality, precision, due process, and real usability for the research community.

title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-12725 from Anonymous
printtext:
I have worked as a research administrator of federal grant awards for 20 years. Throughout my career, it has been a source of great pride to support the groundbreaking and life-saving work of American institutions funded by our federal government. I am deeply disappointed to see changes to the OMB rules that could fundamentally disrupt and discontinue this important work, directly causing the loss of thousands of jobs and ending projects that put America in first place in the race of scientific and technological development.
Specifically, the proposed new rules would impact my work and my institution in the following negative ways:
•Movement away from peer review (§200.205) introduces uncertainty in award decisions, reducing predictability for faculty and administrators.
•Undefined evaluation criteria (e.g., “national interest,” “anti-American values”) create non-transparent funding risks.
•Smaller institutions, such as the one I currently work for, may face disproportionate disadvantage due to limited political visibility and advocacy capacity.
•Expanded termination authority (§200.340) allows mid-project cancellation without cause, exposing the institution to:
oUnrecoverable personnel and infrastructure costs
oDisruption of multi-year research investments
•Increased volatility in federal funding may impact:
oHiring plans
oCapital investments (labs, equipment)
oIndirect cost recovery stability. In addition, giving preference to institutions with lower indirect cost rates only preferences those without the world-class infrastructure that is supported by indirect cost recovery. Indirect cost rates are not arbitrary percentages; rather, rates are calculated based on the actual institutional facilities, and rates even vary within the same institution based on the type of award. The current leadership of the OMB appears to lack basic understanding of how indirect costs work.

•Conversion of Uniform Guidance from “guidance” to binding regulation significantly expands compliance obligations.
•New areas of administrative responsibility:
oMonitoring for political/ideological compliance risks
oManaging conflicts between federal rules and civil rights laws
oIncreased documentation and audit exposure
•Pre-award processes will become more complex, requiring:
oEnhanced proposal risk screening
oGreater coordination with legal counsel and leadership
•Restrictions on program design (§200.202) may limit allowable research topics, particularly in policy-relevant fields (e.g., climate, public health, infrastructure).
•Communication limits (§200.421, §200.450) may:
oRestrict faculty from sharing findings with policymakers or the public
oReduce institutional visibility and impact
•Barriers to dissemination:
oConference participation requires prior approval
oPublication and journal costs may become unallowable. Why would you block the research community from accessing the research they paid for with their tax dollars?
Result: Likely decline in faculty research activity, morale, and retention.
•Engineering research, such as in energy, environment, infrastructure, and emerging technologies, may face heightened scrutiny.
•Restrictions on international collaboration (§200.220) affect:
oJoint research initiatives
oGlobal partnerships
oAccess to data and expertise
•Reduced access to conferences and journals limits ability to stay current in rapidly evolving fields.
•Capstone and applied research projects tied to federal funding face instability risks.
•Increased barriers to employing international researchers (E-Verify requirements; collaboration limits).
•Reduced attractiveness in faculty recruitment due to:
oConstraints on academic freedom
oFunding instability
•Graduate students and research staff face:
oUncertain funding continuity
oInterrupted research pathways
•Fewer federally funded research opportunities for undergraduate and graduate students.
•Potential disruption of:
oSenior design/capstone projects
oThesis and dissertation work
•Reduced exposure to:
oConferences
oPublication opportunities
oIndustry-aligned research experiences
•Fewer federally funded research opportunities for undergraduate and graduate students.
•Direct conflicts between proposed provisions and existing federal obligations (e.g., Title VI, Title IX).
•Increased risk of:
oNoncompliance due to ambiguous standards
oFederal audit findings or enforcement inconsistencies
•Potential need for new institutional policies governing:
oCommunications
oaffiliations
oresearch scope
•Reduced ability to collaborate internationally or across sectors.
•Potential reputational impact as:
oA constrained research environment
oLess competitive compared to peer or global institutions
•Industry partnerships may become more critical but insufficient to replace federal funding.

title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-12725 from John O'Donnell
printtext:
I am a neuroscientist whose research on brain injury has been supported by federal grants for 16 years. OMB's recently proposed rule, Regulation for Federal Financial Assistance, has been derided as deeply corrupt and harmful to America and Americans. This new proposal from NSF is intended to force feed this corruption into our government after we widely rejected the OMB rule. NSF's proposal aims to preemptively align its grantmaking rules with OMB's corrupt Regulation for Federal Financial Assistance, conforming to requirements like all grants needing approval by political appointees, bans on international collaborations, and restricting communications and publishing.

The NSF proposal creates additional institutional requirements, imposes significant economic impacts on grantees, and implements sweeping regulatory control over institutes of higher education via information collection. This attempt to regulate speech and academic freedom at independent universities is a gross overreach of NSF's authority.

This is another direct threat to scientific independence, public health, and evidence-based decision-making. This rule would give unqualified political appointees the power to override transparent scientific review committees to fund pet publicity projects with no benefit to discovery or health, and to do it all secretly behind closed doors. The United States has been the wealthiest, most stable nation on the planet due to our position as the greatest scientific and technological powerhouse in history. American research provides health, safety, and $2.50 in economic output for every $1 invested. There has never been a system so unequivocally beneficial to society. Do not throw it all away for some misguided attempt at gaining political power. For the sake of the country, I sincerely urge NSF not to implement this deeply corrupt rule.
