title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-12725 from Bob Rudis
printtext:
I ask NSF to withdraw the draft Guidance on Financial Assistance in full. If NSF does not withdraw the draft, I ask NSF to hold it until OMB completes its rulemaking on 2 CFR 200.

I am a security engineer. I work on internet measurement and internet intelligence. I do not hold an NSF award. I write because my field is a direct product of NSF-supported research.

The ZMap scanner started in a university laboratory & was the first public result of that work. The authors of the ZMap paper state that NSF grant CNS-1255153 and an NSF Graduate Research Fellowship gave partial support for it. That scanner became a commercial internet intelligence platform. Thousands of defenders now use tools that descend from it. This pattern is common in security. Federal research money produced the transport-layer-security measurements, the botnet studies, and the certificate-ecosystem work that defenders apply each day.

The current PAPPG (NSF 24-1), Chapter XII.A.2.a(i), lists the specific situations in which NSF can suspend or terminate an award. NSF wrote that list. NSF owns it.

The draft removes the list. Guide 25, Section A, Policies, item 1, keeps only a reference to 2 CFR 200.339 and 2 CFR 200.340. The reference gives no date and no version. The summary of changes for Guide 25 states that the guide aligns the termination provisions with the proposed revisions to 2 CFR 200.

Those revisions are not final. OMB published them on May 29, 2026 (Docket OMB-2026-0034, 91 FR 32198). The comment period closed on July 13, 2026. OMB has not published a final rule.

This construction has an effect that NSF should state plainly. If OMB changes 2 CFR 200.340, the NSF standard changes at the same moment. NSF holds no further rulemaking. The public gets no further comment period. NSF adopts a standard that it has not read in final form.

The proposed 2 CFR 200.340 permits termination when an award does not effectuate program goals, agency priorities, or the national interest as those exist at the time of termination. The proposed text does not define "national interest." An undefined term applied at the moment of termination is not a standard. It is a permission.

Guide 25, Section A, Procedures, item 1(a) keeps NSF's authority to suspend or terminate an award immediately to protect the interests of the government. Item 1(e) confirms that NSF will not issue a notice of non-compliance in that case. The recipient gets no statement of the deficiency and no time to correct it.

That authority is not new. Its combination with an undefined and self-updating standard is new.

The introduction to Section A also gives "changes in priorities" as a common reason to pause or end an award. A change in priorities is not a failure by the recipient. The recipient cannot correct it, cannot predict it, and cannot plan against it.

Guide 26 gives review rights. Those rights have less value when the recipient receives no written basis for the action. NSF should not create a path in which an award ends before the recipient learns the reason.

Guide 13, Section D, defines Gold Standard Science and cites Executive Order 14303. The section contains one policy sentence. It gives no review criteria, no scoring method, no process, and no point in the award lifecycle at which NSF applies it.

NSF staff cannot apply this section in a consistent manner. A proposer cannot show compliance with it. A recipient cannot defend against a claim of non-compliance with it. A standard that no party can measure does not improve science. It supplies a reason for a decision that was made on other grounds.

Guide 19 removes the references to Section 504 coordinators, Title IX coordinators, and age discrimination evaluations. The underlying statutes stay in force. Recipients keep the legal duty and lose the guidance that helped them meet it. This change adds risk for recipients and removes no burden from them.

I read the primary security literature each week and write about it for practitioners. The results that matter to defenders come from long work. Internet-scale measurement, protocol analysis, botnet study, and post-quantum readiness each need several years before they give an operational result. Short projects do not produce them.

An award that a political actor can end at any time is not a basis for a multi-year project. Investigators will choose small and safe work. Universities will admit fewer graduate students. The pipeline that supplies the security industry will narrow.

Adversaries do not change their schedule when United States funding priorities change. A reduction in long-horizon defensive research is a national security cost. NSF should weigh that cost in this collection.

NSF paid for the research that lets defenders see the internet. The rules in this draft make that kind of research harder to start and harder to finish. I ask NSF to reconsider them.

title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-12725 from Walter Leal
printtext:
[G8.Authorities] The language in the proposed NSF Guidance on Financial Assistance (GFA) regarding proposal processing and merit review is ambiguous. The summary accompanying the draft states that "no significant changes are made." However, the GFA also specifies that 2 CFR Part 200 supersedes the GFA where applicable. The proposed revisions to 2 CFR Part 200 call for senior appointees to play a central role in funding decisions and state that discretionary awards should advance the President's policy priorities, while emphasizing that peer review is advisory.

If this provision is intended to apply to NSF merit review, it would represent a fundamental departure from the long-standing principle that scientific proposals are evaluated primarily on their intellectual merit and broader impacts by experts in the relevant fields. Regardless of the administration in office, decisions about the scientific merit of innovative, high-risk research are best made through rigorous peer review rather than by political appointees or based on alignment with presidential priorities.

In the interest of full disclosure, although I have previously received NSF funding, I do not anticipate submitting a proposal during the anticipated three-year duration of this guidance. Nevertheless, as a taxpayer and a member of the scientific community, I have a strong interest in ensuring that federal research funds continue to be allocated through a transparent, merit-based process that maximizes scientific excellence, innovation, and long-term national competitiveness.

Accordingly, I respectfully request that the NSF clarify, in unambiguous terms, that final funding decisions will continue to be grounded in NSF's established merit-review process and will not be determined by senior political appointees or by considerations unrelated to the scientific merits of the proposed research.

title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-12725 from Susan Harrison
printtext:
This is a comment in opposition to the proposed Guidance on Financial Assistance (GFA), which replaces the NSF Proposal and Award Policies and Procedures Guide (PAPPG). This comment focuses on three provisions of the GFA:

[G8.Authorities]
The GFA Summary of Changes states that “no significant changes are made to Proposal Processing and Merit Review,” but this appears not to be the case. The GFA explicitly states that 2 CFR Part 200 takes precedence over any conflicting provisions in the GFA, where 2 CFR Part 200 is the proposed revisions to the Office of Management and Budget’s Uniform Guidance published on May 29, 2026. The proposed revisions to 2 CFR 200.205 provide that senior agency appointees must ensure that discretionary awards advance the President’s policy priorities. Also, 2 CFR Part 200 states that peer review remains advisory and does not replace agency discretion. Clearly, then, the GFA (because it incorporates 2 CFR Part 200) will alter the balance between scientific peer review and political discretion in funding decisions.
Making Federal research grants subject to the political wishes of the executive branch undoes the fundamental independence and integrity that has made U.S. science the envy of the world.

[G25.A.Term 2]
Guide 25 aligns NSF’s termination provisions with the proposed revisions to 2 CFR Part 200, granting agencies broad discretionary authority to suspend or terminate awards. Under these provisions, recipients must accept these terms as a condition of receiving an award. This provision appears to be a mechanism for the executive branch to curtail scientific independence by threatening scientists with the loss of vital funding for any arbitrary and potentially politically motivated reason.
Again, this strikes at the independence and integrity that underlie the success of U.S. science.

[G12.A.Term 1]
The proposed GFA incorporates changes from 2 CFR 200.432 (Conferences) and 2 CFR 200.461 (Publication and Printing Costs), under which conference attendance would be allowable only if expressly approved by the funding agency, and publication costs are characterized as not inherently necessary to carry out the objectives of most federal awards. Conferences and publications are the fundamental ways that scientists communicate their work with each other and the broader public.
These changes are inexplicable except as mechanisms to control and curtail U.S. science at the discretion of political appointees.

title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-12725 from Nicola McGillicuddy
printtext:
I am writing to strongly oppose the National Science Foundation's proposed updates to its Proposal and Award Policies and Procedures Guide, which align NSF grantmaking with OMB's proposed Regulation for Federal Financial Assistance.

As someone who cares deeply about environmental conservation, public health, and evidence based decision making, I rely on independent scientific research to understand the challenges facing our planet and to advocate for meaningful solutions. This proposal threatens that foundation in ways that will harm every American.

Requiring NSF grants to be approved by political appointees rather than career scientists and peer reviewers fundamentally corrupts the scientific process. Science must follow evidence, not political agendas. When research funding is contingent on alignment with Administration priorities, we lose the independence that makes science trustworthy and effective in the first place.

The proposed bans on international collaborations are particularly alarming. The greatest scientific breakthroughs of our time have come from researchers working across borders, sharing data, and building on each other's discoveries. Isolating American science from the global scientific community does not make us stronger. It makes us weaker.

Restricting communications and publishing is an attack on academic freedom and free speech that has no place in a democracy. Independent universities must remain free to pursue knowledge without government interference in what their researchers can say, publish, or share.

I am also deeply concerned about the economic impact on research institutions and the chilling effect these regulations would have on the next generation of scientists.

The NSF's mission is to advance the progress of science for the benefit of the nation. This proposal does the opposite. I urge the NSF to withdraw these proposed changes and protect the independence of American science.

Science belongs to the people. Not to political appointees.
Thank You,
Nicola

title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-12725 from Stephen Evola

I am seriously concerned about the National Science Foundation's apparent pre-emptive implementation of OMB's unapproved proposal for the "Regulation fro Federal Financial Assistance" rule. This rule is unnecessary and a grave threat to the principle and practice of expert reviews of proposals and conduct of scientific research, subordinating it to potential political partisan interference in research that will benefit our nation and keep it from falling behind not just our allies but, far worse, our enemies. I spent my career engaged in scientific research and know the damage caused by political interference. Do not let this rule be implemented, by choice or by dictate, because it will put our nation at a disadvantage in producing research results that will benefit our citizens for no good reason but only to impose detrimental control by political entities who have no idea what they would be interfering with.
Sincerely,
Stephen Evola, PhD

title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-12725 from Christopher Jones
printtext:
I am submitting this comment in opposition to the National Science Foundation's proposed revision of the Proposal & Award Policies & Procedures Guide (PAPPG) into the "Guidance on Financial Assistance" (GFA), Docket No. NSF-2026-OTR-0001.

Who I am: I am a Computer Scientist and have 10 of experience with NSF-funded research in Neuroscience (data analysis).

Why I am concerned:

1. This is a substantive policy rewrite disguised as a paperwork update. NSF frames the GFA as a plain-language, non-substantive revision under the Paperwork Reduction Act. In fact, it is explicitly designed to align NSF's grantmaking with OMB's not-yet-finalized "Regulation for Federal Financial Assistance" and Executive Order 14332. Using a routine information-collection renewal to pre-adopt a controversial, still-pending rule circumvents the normal notice-and-comment process for substantive rulemaking and denies the public a meaningful opportunity to weigh in before the underlying policy takes effect.

2. Political control over grant approvals threatens scientific merit review. Requirements that route grant approvals through political appointees undermine NSF's long-standing peer-review and merit-based funding model, which has historically insulated funding decisions from partisan interference.

3. Restrictions on international collaboration will damage American science. Broad bans or new barriers on international collaboration would cut off U.S. researchers from partnerships that are often essential to major scientific advances and would put American researchers at a disadvantage relative to international peers who continue to collaborate freely.

4. New restrictions on communications and publishing conflict with academic freedom. Provisions restricting how researchers communicate about or publish their federally funded work raise serious First Amendment and academic freedom concerns, and would chill scientific communication that the public relies on for evidence-based decision-making.

5. The proposal imposes real administrative and economic burdens on institutions. New institutional compliance and information-collection requirements will increase costs for universities and grantees - costs that ultimately reduce the funds available for actual research.

6. This is regulatory overreach into the governance of independent institutions of higher education. NSF's statutory mission is to promote the progress of science; using funding conditions to regulate the internal speech and governance practices of independent universities exceeds that mandate.

What I am asking NSF to do:

- Withdraw this information-collection request until the underlying OMB "Regulation for Federal Financial Assistance" is finalized through a full, transparent notice-and-comment rulemaking process, so the public can comment on the substance rather than a fait accompli.
- Preserve NSF's independent, merit-based peer review process for funding decisions.
- Reject provisions that restrict international scientific collaboration, publication, and communication.
- Conduct and publish a full economic and administrative burden analysis before proceeding.

Thank you for considering this comment.

title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-12725 from Anonymous
printtext:
I am an academic researcher that has been federally funded at multiple stages of my career. The changes proposed by NSF will cripple our national scientific enterprise. These harms are not balanced by benefits. It is both unethical and deceptive for the NSF to quietly propose rules to preemptively align with a recent OMB proposal that has garnered a vast number of concerned comments from the public. I have many concerns about these new rules and outline those concerns below.

The proposed changes will lead to arbitrary, rather than evidence based, decisions in research funding. These changes will transfer decision-making power from scientifically trained staff and reviewers to political appointees. I hold an NIH grant and the merit of my proposal was evaluated by peers with expertise required to assess a research program. These peer evaluations guided the funding decision, ensuring that innovative and sound research was prioritized. OMB has not provided any evidence that this decision-making process is ineffective. Yet, they propose to require all grants to be reviewed by political appointees, that majority of whom lack any relevant scientific training. In addition, the changes reclassify peer review as “advisory”, ensuring that grant scores can be easily ignored by appointees, regardless of institute paylines. These changes shift decision making from evidence-based scientific evaluation to ideological evaluation, obliterating objectivity in scientific funding. What possible benefit does oversight by untrained, ideological appointees bring to evaluating scientific proposals? These appointees will misunderstand proposed work and cause irreparable harm to researchers. In addition, basic research is often undervalued, perhaps because many are unaware that it has underpinned every major scientific advance, from antibiotics to vaccines, that has benefited our society. Had my grant proposals been reviewed by political appointees, they may very well have over-ruled trained scientists because they lacked the relevant training and insight to foresee the potential benefits of my fundamental questions. Moreover, we have recently seen political appointees flag research proposals for certain words, such as “diversity”, without any understanding for how those terms may be applied in a scientific field. Finally, these proposed changes depend on an administration’s definitions of “gold standard science”, which is often not informed by the broader scientific community.
I am also concerned by the changes that propose new limitations on using federal funds for open access publications. Publication fees for open access journals are quite high but allow broader dissemination of research worldwide. As science is a collaborative pursuit, broad dissemination of results is required to support further advances. Most institutions provide little to no support for faculty publishing costs. Should the federal government prevent grants from funding many publication costs, researchers would be unable to broadly disseminate key findings, or perhaps, even publish their work at all. For example, my institution provides a very little support for research publication. Without the funding in my grant, I would be unable to continue my research and publish my findings.
The proposed changes limiting conference travel are also ill advised. Science is unpredictable, and researchers must follow projects wherever they lead. Thus, the best venues for sharing research and gathering feedback are not clear at the start of a project. Researchers require flexibility to attend conferences as they become relevant for their projects. What possible benefit is there for the government to attempt to arbitrarily limit which conferences I can attend using funding from my grant? In addition to this change, the changes that target “lobbying or issue advocacy” organizations are extremely concerning. Scientific societies, such as the American Society for Microbiology, advocate on behalf of their members (scientists!). In our current governmental structure, advocacy must take the form of “lobbying or issue advocacy”. This rule change allows the government to arbitrarily bar funding for memberships in scientific societies that advocate for policies they dislike. How is this supportive of free speech or independent scientific thought?

Finally, the proposed changes make it easier for agencies to terminate grants based solely on administrative priorities, rather than a sound scientific reason. This change inserts great uncertainty into a system where researchers rely on funding to advance their projects and support trainees. Will a grant be cancelled simply because the presiding administration dislikes the results, without any legitimate concerns about the validity of the study? The proposed changes open the door for funding to be terminated on a whim, simply because political appointees are ideologically unhappy with a study outcome.

title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-12725 from Neil Losin
printtext:
As a Ph.D. biologist, a faculty affiliate at a R1 University, and a full-time science media producer, I strongly oppose the NSF's recent updates to its Proposal & Award Policies & Procedures Guide, which align with the not-yet-finalized OMB rules with similar effect.

By requiring that NSF grants be approved by political appointees -- rather than scientific peers and career NSF staff, who have the expertise to evaluate the scientific merit and public benefit of NSF-funded research -- the new rules will undercut American leadership in basic and applied research, with potential impacts for generations to come.

The new regulations hinder scientific progress in a number of other ways, including banning international collaborations (long a foundation of American scientific leadership), imposing arbitrary restrictions on publishing and other communications (when the entire purpose of science is to disseminate the results to our scientific peers and the general public who funds our work), and implementing burdensome information-collection requirements on institutions of higher education.

In short, the proposed regulations will cripple American science, to the long-term detriment of American global leadership and economic prosperity. I oppose these rule changes, along with the OMB proposal with which these NSF rule changes are meant to align. Both are certain to harm the U.S.'s capacity to conduct basic and applied research (and by extension, our ability to benefit all Americans through our continued scientific excellence).

Thank you in advance for considering this comment, and all the other comments submitted by my countless colleagues who are united in our opposition of this short-sighted policy.

Regards,

Neil Losin

printtext: I am a professor of chemistry at Stony Brook University and have been funded by the National Science Foundation and served on grant review panels for the NSF over the last 25 years. Requiring discretionary grants that have been reviewed and recommended by scientific experts to undergo an additional round of review by senior political appointees who at best will have minimal familiarity with the science involved will not only introduce delays in funding of critical research, but it will also have a significant negative impact on the careers and training of scientists whose grants are affected. I strongly urge NSF to withdraw the proposed changes.

title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-12725 from Anonymous
printtext:
I am a federally funded researcher in computer science. I write to express concern about provisions in the proposed GFA that would subordinate peer review to political appointee oversight.

The strength of NSF's grant program has always rested on the principle that scientific merit is evaluated by scientific peers. The proposed change, requiring senior political appointees to review grants with discretion that will not defer to peer reviewers, replaces domain expertise with political judgment. This is not a procedural refinement. It is a structural change that will systematically disadvantage research that is rigorous but politically inconvenient, including work on privacy and the social consequences of technology.

I also note concern about the elimination of Special Creativity Extensions, which have supported exactly the kind of long-horizon, high-risk research that produces outsized scientific returns.

The peer review system is not perfect, but it is the best available mechanism for allocating research funding on the basis of scientific merit. These changes move in the wrong direction.

title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-12725 from Eric Pettersen
printtext:
Putting decisions about the funding of scientific research into the hands of political appointees with little grasp of the merits of such research will greatly damage America's leadership in scientific advancement and the concomitant advantages it confers on our economy through technological innovation.

It is important to fund basic research whose "payoff" may not be immediately evident, particularly to a political appointee. The development of CRISPR gene-editing technology and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) technology were offshoots of basic research into natural phenomena, and were in no way foreseen when the research was initiated.

Failing to fund either or both of these will greatly reduce the value produced by research grants.

title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-12725 from Nicola McGillicuddy
printtext:
I am writing to strongly oppose the National Science Foundation's proposed updates to its Proposal and Award Policies and Procedures Guide, which align NSF grantmaking with OMB's proposed Regulation for Federal Financial Assistance.

As someone who cares deeply about environmental conservation, public health, and evidence based decision making, I rely on independent scientific research to understand the challenges facing our planet and to advocate for meaningful solutions. This proposal threatens that foundation in ways that will harm every American.

Requiring NSF grants to be approved by political appointees rather than career scientists and peer reviewers fundamentally corrupts the scientific process. Science must follow evidence, not political agendas. When research funding is contingent on alignment with Administration priorities, we lose the independence that makes science trustworthy and effective in the first place.

The greatest scientific breakthroughs of our time have come from researchers working across borders, sharing data, and building on each other's discoveries. Isolating American science from the global scientific community does not make us stronger. It makes us weaker.

Restricting communications and publishing is an attack on academic freedom and free speech that has no place in a democracy. Independent universities must remain free to pursue knowledge without government interference in what their researchers can say, publish, or share.

I am also deeply concerned about the economic impact on research institutions and the chilling effect these regulations would have on the next generation of scientists.

The NSF's mission is to advance the progress of science for the benefit of the nation. This proposal does the opposite. I urge the NSF to withdraw these proposed changes and protect the independence of American science.

Science belongs to the people. Not to political appointees.
Thank You,
Nicola

title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-12725 from Robert Neches
printtext:
My qualifications to offer informed commentary on this topic include 50 years as a research scientist and manager, experience as a DARPA program manager, and as a senior executive level official who served in both what was then called the Office of Secretary of Defense, and in the Office of the Director of National Intelligence. I have worked with NSF as a proposal reviewer, and as a collaborator on joint projects with DARPA and OSD.

NSF proposes to adapt to Office of Management and Budget's (OMB) Uniform Guidance at 2 CFR 200 through the proposed rule published on May 29, 2026 (see 91 Fed. Reg. 32, 198, May 29, 2026). This is flawed for multiple reasons:

1.NSF’s changes should not be proposed and opened for comment unless and until all adaptations to external rules are based on finalized versions of those rules. OMB’s guidance is not final and may change, NSF’s proposed changes therefore cannot be properly evaluated because the context for evaluation is incomplete.

2.Should OMB’s ill-advised guidance be adopted, mooting the preceding objection, NSF’s failure to revise the merit review guidance (draft Guidance on Assistance, Guide 8, pp. 104-110) to reflect the proposed effective politicization of selection decisions to, “ensur[e] that discretionary award advance the President’s policy priorities,” (OMB Section 200.205). Following this requirement in the absence of substantial revisions to Guide 8 would make it impossible for proposal respondants to make submission decisions. This would create an enormous waste of both submitter and government time preparing and reviewing doomed proposals, accompanied by a signficant loss of quality when potential quality submitters refrain from proposing over uncertainty about their prospects. Proposal submission cost and quality on both government and submitter sides will be irreparably damaged if submitters do not have sufficient information to ensure whether their proposals have viable prospects. This will be impossible in the absence of a reliable mechanism for NSF to convey to potential proposers: what those priorities are, how they are relevant to the topic at hand, and how long those priorities will be in place before changing. The possibility of creating such a mechanism is vanishingly small. The current proposed revisions are therefore fboth flawed and incomplete, and will only reduce performance and effectiveness.

3.Even should the preceding concerns be addressable, two additional fundamental problems remain bearing on the bureaucratic load that will be introduced:

a.It is not at all clear that Presidential policy priorities are a permissable consideration under laws governing the establishment of the NSF, as well as those governing Congressional Authorizations and Appropriations. Selection decisions made under them are potentially subject to legal action.

b.The logistics of requiring senior appointees to determine compliance with those policies given the volume and complexity of NSF submissions renders the requirement logistically infeasible. Proposal processing will be bottlenecked to the point of breakdown.

4.Finally, by incorporating political decisionmaking into the process, NSF will both damage its ability to do the best science, and reduce US international competitive prospects through the loss of scientists, e.g., Forbes Magazine, July 15 article: “Why a Nobel Laureate is Leaving UC Berkeley for China.”

title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-12725 from Christopher Jones
printtext:
I am submitting this comment in opposition to the National Science Foundation's proposed revision of the Proposal & Award Policies & Procedures Guide (PAPPG) into the "Guidance on Financial Assistance" (GFA), Docket No. NSF-2026-OTR-0001.

Who I am: I am a Computer Scientist and have 10 of experience with NSF-funded research in Neuroscience (data analysis).

Why I am concerned:

1. This is a substantive policy rewrite disguised as a paperwork update. NSF frames the GFA as a plain-language, non-substantive revision under the Paperwork Reduction Act. In fact, it is explicitly designed to align NSF's grantmaking with OMB's not-yet-finalized "Regulation for Federal Financial Assistance" and Executive Order 14332. Using a routine information-collection renewal to pre-adopt a controversial, still-pending rule circumvents the normal notice-and-comment process for substantive rulemaking and denies the public a meaningful opportunity to weigh in before the underlying policy takes effect.

2. Political control over grant approvals threatens scientific merit review. Requirements that route grant approvals through political appointees undermine NSF's long-standing peer-review and merit-based funding model, which has historically insulated funding decisions from partisan interference.

3. Restrictions on international collaboration will damage American science. Broad bans or new barriers on international collaboration would cut off U.S. researchers from partnerships that are often essential to major scientific advances and would put American researchers at a disadvantage relative to international peers who continue to collaborate freely.

4. New restrictions on communications and publishing conflict with academic freedom. Provisions restricting how researchers communicate about or publish their federally funded work raise serious First Amendment and academic freedom concerns, and would chill scientific communication that the public relies on for evidence-based decision-making.

5. The proposal imposes real administrative and economic burdens on institutions. New institutional compliance and information-collection requirements will increase costs for universities and grantees - costs that ultimately reduce the funds available for actual research.

6. This is regulatory overreach into the governance of independent institutions of higher education. NSF's statutory mission is to promote the progress of science; using funding conditions to regulate the internal speech and governance practices of independent universities exceeds that mandate.

What I am asking NSF to do:

- Withdraw this information-collection request until the underlying OMB "Regulation for Federal Financial Assistance" is finalized through a full, transparent notice-and-comment rulemaking process, so the public can comment on the substance rather than a fait accompli.
- Preserve NSF's independent, merit-based peer review process for funding decisions.
- Reject provisions that restrict international scientific collaboration, publication, and communication.
- Conduct and publish a full economic and administrative burden analysis before proceeding.

Thank you for considering this comment.

title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-12725 from Erika Lin
printtext: I am writing to express my opposition to the NSF's updated Proposal and Award Policies and Procedures Guide, NSF-2026-OTR-0001-0002. This change aligns with the OMB's Regulation for Federal Financial Assistance rule, which aims to give political appointees oversight over federal grant funding. Peer review is the heart of our scientific system. It requires experts who are SPECIALISTS IN THEIR SUBFIELDS (not just their disciplines in general) to make nuanced judgment calls regarding the quality of research proposals and methodologies. To give political appointees the final word on such matters will completely undermine this process. As a cancer survivor and a university professor, I cannot stress enough the importance of the rigor of peer review. It is crucial that research be evaluated by experts with decades of training in particular relevant subspecializations. You don't ask your dentist for advice about your brain tumor. You don't ask your heart surgeon to operate on your cataracts. Specialized expertise is crucial. This kind of rigor in peer review is what enables us to have new treatments for medical conditions as well as innovative solutions to other public problems, such as climate change. Do you want to have this summer's air quality problems become so common that you have to live your life indoors forever? Can't we study better solutions to wildfires? But what if political appointees decide this kind of research is troubling? Without peer review's rigorous standards, everyone's quality of life will decline. The NSF's updated Proposal and Award Policies and Procedures Guide will completely compromise the value and validity of research findings by interfering with the peer review process. The ultimate cost, financially not just in terms of human lives, will be enormous. Moreover, in interfering with research projects developed and implemented in conjunction with colleagues around the world, the proposed rule completely goes against how the best research is done. Experts rely on other experts, no matter whether they are based in the US or abroad. There are often only a handful of people who really understand the intricacies of a specific kind of research. The whole world should be working together to solve problems like cancer and climate change--these are things that affect us all across national borders! The NSF should not allow non-specialists to arbitrarily declare that talented experts who have unique experience and knowledge in a certain subfield be restricted (or, worse, banned entirely) from participating in specific research projects. As well, the limitations being imposed on communications and publishing make no sense. Are we no longer going to be allowed to share our research with colleagues, so as to learn and grow from their expertise? Last but certainly not least, the NSF rule's regulatory changes and new information collection policies are a major infringement on speech and academic freedom at universities and other independent research institutions. The proposed rule change attempts to codify unprecedented political overreach. I oppose it strongly.

title: Comment from Anonymous
printtext:
I am an individual air traveler. I oppose the proposed amendment to 14 CFR 399.84(a), I oppose more strongly the full or partial repeal floated in Section C, and I oppose the wholesale rescission of the nine guidance documents. A fuller version is attached.

The proposal is larger than the font-size framing suggests.

The operative change is deleting the prohibition on displaying components "prominently." Font size is one lever among many. The Department's own 2012 guidance explained that prominence includes placement, bolding, underlining and highlighting, and this NPRM would rescind that guidance in the same action. The standard is loosened while the only material explaining what it means is destroyed. "No more prominent than the total price" becomes an undefined phrase applied to interfaces carriers can A/B test at scale.

The preamble also says the Department "remains committed" to total-price display while, pages later, asking whether to eliminate it. Both cannot be the agency's position.

Equal prominence is not neutral, and the evidence is not close.

Two numbers set at identical size are not read identically by someone scanning results on a phone. Position, color, contrast and sequence determine what gets encoded, and equal typographic weight hands the advertiser every remaining variable.

Gabaix and Laibson showed that with inattentive consumers the unraveling result fails and shrouding persists in equilibrium (121 Q.J. Econ. 505 (2006)). Chetty, Looney and Kroft found that taxes in the posted price suppress demand more than identical taxes added at the register (99 Am. Econ. Rev. 1145 (2009)). Blake, Moshary, Sweeney and Tadelis found in a StubHub field experiment that back-end fees raised spending, and that the platform lost volume when it moved to all-in pricing while rivals did not (40 Marketing Sci. 619 (2021)).

That last finding is the argument for a floor. A seller who shows the honest number loses to sellers who do not. That is a coordination failure, and removing the floor drags every carrier toward the least legible presentation its rivals adopt. Hotel resort fees are the proof of concept, and the reason the FTC promulgated Part 464.

The FTC comparison runs against the proposal.

The FTC requires the total price to be more prominent than any other pricing information. This NPRM would permit equal prominence, leaving air travel with a weaker standard than concert tickets. If harmonization is the goal, the Department picked the one option that fails to achieve it.

The constitutional rationale defeats itself.

The proposed rule still forbids components from being "more prominent than the total price." That is a government restriction on the size and appearance of commercial speech. If the preamble's theory is right, the proposed rule fails for the same reason as the current one and cures nothing. If the theory is wrong, there is no constitutional basis for the change. Zauderer, 471 U.S. 626, and Milavetz, 559 U.S. 229, govern factual disclosures about the terms of the transaction advertised. NIFLA expressly distinguished Zauderer; it involved compelled speech on a contested moral question unrelated to the services offered. A ticket price is the paradigm Zauderer case.

Section 7275 cannot carry this weight.

It is a tax-code misdemeanor capped at one hundred dollars, not enforced by DOT, creating no consumer remedy. A 1970 revenue provision does not displace 49 U.S.C. 41712, which the Fifth Circuit panel confirmed authorizes prescriptive rulemaking (127 F.4th 563 (2025)). The en banc vacatur was procedural and did not reach authority. A floor is not a ceiling.

One guidance rescission deserves specific attention.

The February 21, 2012 guidance advises carriers that labeling their own fees as "taxes" or "taxes and fees" is deceptive. Rescinding it while permitting prominent component display produces a foreseeable result: bold line items reading "taxes and fees" that consist substantially of charges the carrier sets and keeps. That misattributes the seller's own price to the government.

Requested action.

Withdraw the amendment and retain the existing provisions. Reject the Section C alternatives. State affirmatively that advertised prices must include all government and carrier-imposed mandatory charges. If any change is made, adopt the FTC standard (total more prominent) rather than equal prominence. Retain the February 2012 labeling guidance and the EAPP #2 prominence provisions. Conduct consumer testing of the newly permitted formats and docket it for comment.

Price competition only works when buyers can compare prices cheaply. When that erodes, firms stop competing on being cheaper and start competing on appearing cheaper. Different contest, different winner. We have already watched it play out in hotels and event ticketing. Please retain the Full Fare Rule.

title: Comment from Anonymous
printtext:
oppose the Department's proposal to amend 14 CFR 399.84 to let individual fare components be shown as prominently as the total fare, and the related request for comment on repealing the "full fare rule" outright. Both should be withdrawn; the current total-price disclosure requirement should stand unweakened.

1. The rule was adopted, and upheld in court, to prevent exactly this harm. DOT adopted the full fare rule in 2011 after finding that consumers need "a full picture of the total price... the first time the air fare is presented to them" in order to compare fares. Spirit Airlines, Allegiant Air, and Southwest Airlines challenged this same prominence requirement in court and lost: Spirit Airlines, Inc. v. U.S. Dep't of Transp., 687 F.3d 403 (D.C. Cir. 2012). The NPRM cites no change in law, market structure, or consumer behavior since 2012 that justifies reversing a rule courts have already upheld as lawful and necessary. Fourteen years of reliance on a judicially affirmed protection deserves more than an unsupported reversal.

2. Peer-reviewed research confirms the harm this proposal would reintroduce. Santana, Dallas & Morwitz, "Consumer Reactions to Drip Pricing," Marketing Science 39(3) (2020), found that when charges are shown separately rather than up front, consumers systematically underestimate total cost, are more likely to pick an option that looks cheaper but costs more overall, and stay dissatisfied even after learning the full price. Totzek, "Many a Little Makes a Mickle," Psychology & Marketing 38(11) (2021), found partitioned price disclosure erodes consumer trust, worsening as more components are shown separately. This is also why the FTC has separately pursued rulemaking against "junk fees" and drip pricing economy-wide. Letting fare components match or exceed the total price in size recreates the exact visual conditions this research shows cause consumers to misjudge what they'll pay.

3. This proposal conflicts with DOT's own 2024 rulemaking. The Department's 2024 Transparency of Airline Ancillary Fees rule required upfront fee disclosure specifically because piecemeal disclosure confuses consumers and frustrates comparison shopping. Letting base fares be advertised alongside equally or more prominent add-on charges undermines the total-price anchor that ancillary fee disclosures depend on, and works against the 2024 rule's own purpose. The Department should reconcile this contradiction before proceeding.

4. The Internal Revenue Code cannot substitute for the full fare rule. The NPRM notes an IRC provision governing tax display in air fare ads, suggesting it could replace the full fare rule if repealed. But that provision covers only taxes, not the larger and growing category of mandatory carrier fees and surcharges. Repealing the full fare rule on this basis would leave a significant gap and weaken the Department's authority to address deceptive fare advertising under 49 U.S.C. 41712.

5. The record doesn't yet support a change this significant. The Department's own comment-period extension reflects unresolved complexity, including admitted Constitutional and interagency questions. Before repealing a fourteen-year-old, court-tested protection or rescinding the related guidance documents, the Department should publish consumer-comprehension testing showing its approach won't increase confusion about true fare costs. No such testing is in the docket.

Recommendation: Decline to amend 14 CFR 399.84, decline to repeal the full fare rule, and decline to rescind the related guidance documents absent empirical evidence that doing so will not increase consumer confusion about airfare pricing. Total-price-first advertising is what lets travelers actually comparison-shop; weakening it serves a lower headline number for industry, not the traveling public's interest in knowing what they will pay.

title: Comment from Dan Elliott
printtext:
I oppose any change that weakens the requirement that airlines advertise the full price a consumer will pay.

What public purpose would this rule change serve other than to make costs less transparent, permit potentially misleading advertising, and place a greater burden on consumers to determine the actual price of a flight?

Taxes and mandatory government fees generally apply consistently across airlines. Including those charges in the advertised fare does not distort price comparisons. It allows consumers to compare the total cost of competing flights quickly and accurately.

By contrast, weakening the full-fare requirement would give airlines greater latitude to emphasize a lower base fare while disclosing mandatory charges less prominently. It could also encourage airlines to separate additional required fees from the advertised price, making the ultimate cost less clear.

Consumers should not have to proceed through the entire booking process for every airline they are considering simply to determine the true price of a ticket. That creates unnecessary work, makes meaningful comparison more difficult, and increases the likelihood that consumers will make decisions based on incomplete or misleading information.

The current full-fare rule promotes transparency, fair competition, and informed consumer choice. Weakening or repealing it would move in the opposite direction.

The Department should retain and enforce the requirement that the full price, including all mandatory taxes and fees, be displayed clearly and prominently whenever an airfare is advertised.

I submit this comment in strong support of the Department of Transportation’s proposal to amend its air fare advertising rules and rescind outdated guidance documents. The core change—allowing the total fare, including taxes and fees, to be displayed with the same prominence as individual components—rightly centers what matters most to consumers: a clear, honest understanding of the full price they will pay.

Current prescriptive formatting rules about font size and relative prominence of fare components can actually make price information more confusing and less intuitive, especially in complex digital booking environments. The proposed approach keeps the key safeguard in place—that the advertised fare must reflect the total amount due, including mandatory taxes and fees—while removing rigid design mandates that do not meaningfully advance consumer protection. This is a balanced, modern solution: it preserves transparency and bans deception, but gives sellers the flexibility to present price information in ways users can quickly understand.

For travelers with disabilities, clear, consolidated price information is especially important. Fragmented fare displays and overly rigid formatting can increase cognitive load, create screen reader compatibility issues, and make it harder to compare options. Allowing straightforward presentation of the total fare, with accessible details on taxes and fees, better supports inclusive design and reduces the risk that people with disabilities are misled or disadvantaged by confusing price structures. Flexibility in layout also helps developers build interfaces that work more smoothly across assistive technologies, devices, and literacy levels.

The proposal’s alignment with Internal Revenue Code standards on how taxes should be displayed in air transportation advertising further strengthens its legal soundness. By ensuring that the total cost is at least as prominent as any separate tax or fee amount, DOT’s approach harmonizes regulatory practice with statutory requirements. Rescinding the nine outdated guidance documents is also an important corrective; these materials are no longer necessary and, in some instances, have functioned as de facto regulation without going through proper notice-and-comment procedures. Removing them will simplify compliance, reduce confusion, and ensure that regulated parties and advocates alike can rely on clear statutory and regulatory text.

title: Comment from Air Traveler
printtext:
I am an individual air traveler. I oppose the proposed amendment to 14 CFR 399.84(a), oppose rescinding the nine price advertising guidance documents, and strongly oppose the full or partial repeal of the Full Fare Rule raised as an alternative.

1. The proposed text does not do what the preamble says it does.

The preamble states the rule would "prohibit any components of the fare from being displayed more prominently than the total price." The proposed regulatory text contains no such prohibition. It says only that components "may be displayed with the same prominence as the total price itself." Nothing in the operative text forbids displaying a component more prominently than the total, and it is the text that binds. The public is being asked to comment on a proposal whose stated effect and actual language diverge. If the Department proceeds, it must re-propose language that states the limit it describes.

2. "Same prominence" is not enforceable.

The current font-size provision is the only part of the rule that can be applied objectively, by looking at a screenshot. Prominence in practice is a product of size, weight, color, contrast, position, and whitespace. Under this proposal an advertiser could set the base fare and the tax line in identical font sizes while the total sits in plain text below — technically compliant, designed so the low base fare is the number the eye lands on. Whether two elements are "equally prominent" when they differ along five design dimensions is a case-by-case judgment, which is worse for consumers, for enforcement staff, and for sellers who want to know what compliance looks like.

3. The Department identifies no consumer-side evidence.

The 2011 rule rested on consumer complaints and a finding that travelers need the entire price the first time a fare is presented in order to compare fares and routings. This NPRM does not dispute that finding, and cites no evidence that the current provision has harmed consumers or that equal-prominence display leaves them equally informed. An agency changing course must confront the factual findings underlying the prior rule. Executive Orders and industry comments are not a substitute.

Note also the asymmetry the Department itself identifies: the FTC's fee rule requires the total price to be more prominent than other pricing information. This proposal would place airline advertising on a weaker standard than live-event tickets and lodging.

4. Rescinding the guidance would cost real protections.

Several documents are not obsolete housekeeping. The February 21, 2012 guidance advises that labeling carrier-imposed fees as "taxes" or "taxes and fees" is deceptive. Rescinding it, in the same action that lets fee components be displayed more prominently, would let airlines highlight their own revenue as though it were a government charge. I see no consumer benefit in permitting that. The rounding guidance and the "free" fare and award travel guidance likewise govern the advertisements most likely to mislead. At minimum, retain the guidance prohibiting mislabeling of carrier-imposed fees as taxes.

5. The Internal Revenue Code does not displace this rule.

26 U.S.C. 7275 is a criminal tax penalty provision carrying a maximum $100 fine, governing how taxes appear in advertisements. It is a floor for tax display, not a consumer protection scheme, and nothing in it limits the Department's separate authority under 49 U.S.C. 41712. A $100 misdemeanor is not a meaningful deterrent against a pricing display seen by millions.

6. The First Amendment concern is overstated.

Spirit Airlines v. DOT upheld this rule as a disclosure requirement aimed at preventing deception about total price, and it has not been overruled. NIFLA concerned compelled speech on a contested subject; a ticket's total price is a purely factual disclosure. Airlines remain free to itemize every tax and fee.

7. I oppose full or partial repeal.

Repeal would return advertising to the pre-2011 environment in which the advertised fare was not the price I could actually buy. The claim that consumers can calculate the total themselves because taxes are roughly uniform is wrong in my experience: taxes and fees vary substantially by itinerary, and international and multi-stop routings are where the base fare diverges most from the total, and where an error costs most. Case-by-case enforcement is slow and discretionary, and gives no guidance to a consumer comparing fares this afternoon.

Requested action: withdraw the proposal and retain 14 CFR 399.84(a) as written, including the prominence and font-size provisions; decline to repeal § 399.84 in whole or in part; retain the price advertising guidance; and if the Department proceeds, re-propose text containing the limitation described in the preamble, supported by evidence on consumer comprehension rather than industry comment alone.

title: Comment from Daniel Kanouff
printtext:
Public Comment Submission
Docket Title: Enhancing Flexibility of Air Fare Price Advertising

Docket ID: DOT-OST-2025-0831

RIN: 2105-AF37

Re: Opposition to Proposed Revisions to Full-Fare Advertising Rules (14 CFR 399.84)

Comment:

I am writing to express my strong opposition to the Department of Transportation’s proposed rule changes regarding airfare price advertising. Weakening or rolling back the longstanding Full-Fare Advertising Rule under 14 CFR 399.84 represents a significant step backward for consumer protection, market transparency, and price competition.

1. Disruption of True Comparison Shopping
The current Full-Fare Advertising Rule mandates that the first price a consumer sees is the complete, mandatory cost of travel. Unbundling mandatory government taxes, segment fees, and airport charges from the advertised base fare will re-introduce deceptive "bait-and-switch" pricing practices into airline retail.

When baseline fares are stripped of mandatory fees, comparison shopping across carriers and search engines becomes frustratingly complex and inefficient. Consumers will be forced to advance multiple itineraries through complex checkout funnels simply to determine the true, total cost of a single flight. This intentional friction hurts price discovery and disproportionately benefits carriers that rely on opaque fee structures.

2. The Flawed "Sales Tax" Analogy
Proponents of this rule change often argue that American consumers are accustomed to retail environments where taxes are added at checkout. This comparison relies on a fundamental misconception of how aviation fees work:

Sales tax is simple and predictable: In traditional retail, local and state sales taxes are standard, fixed percentages applied uniformly across goods within a jurisdiction.

Aviation fees are highly complex and variable: Airfare taxes and charges are not a simple flat percentage. They comprise a tangled matrix of government-imposed taxes, segment fees, Passenger Facility Charges (PFCs), TSA security fees, and international departure/arrival taxes. These charges vary dramatically depending on origin, destination, connecting airports, transit hubs, and international borders.

Expecting a traveler to calculate or anticipate these airport- and route-specific fee variations before reaching the final payment screen is entirely unrealistic.

3. Mandatory Costs Belong in the Headline Price
A core principle of fair advertising is that any non-negotiable cost required to consume a product or service must be included in the advertised headline price. Because passengers cannot opt out of government-imposed airport fees, security charges, or mandatory taxes, separating them from the initial price quote serves no legitimate consumer benefit—it serves only to artificially deflate advertised costs until the final stage of purchase.

Conclusion
The existing Full-Fare Advertising Rule has successfully provided clear, transparent, and honest pricing for over a decade. Weakening it will degrade the consumer experience, increase transaction friction, and obscure true price competition across the industry.

I urge the Department of Transportation to abandon this proposed rollback and preserve the mandatory full-fare disclosure standard in its current form.

While markets function best with limited regulation, certain rules are necessary to ensure that competitors present prices in a consistent and honest manner so consumers can make informed purchasing decisions. Airlines should compete on the quality of their service, reliability, and the actual total price consumers pay—not on how effectively they can advertise only portions of that price.

The Department states in the background discussion that airlines could display taxes and mandatory fees later in the booking process because consumers can calculate the total price themselves, noting that taxes are generally uniform across purchases. This overlooks the unique nature of air travel. Unlike local retail purchases, airline tickets are frequently purchased by travelers who are unfamiliar with the taxes, fees, airport charges, and other mandatory costs associated with their destination or connecting airports. Consumers should not be expected to estimate these unavoidable charges in order to determine the true cost of travel. The purpose of advertising is to allow meaningful comparisons before investing time in the booking process.

Consider a family of four searching for flights within a fixed vacation budget. If fares are advertised without prominently displaying the total mandatory cost, the family may spend considerable time comparing itineraries only to discover at the final booking page that the actual price exceeds their budget. Requiring airlines to display the full price at the outset saves consumers time, reduces frustration, and allows meaningful comparison shopping across carriers.

The proposed rule could also undermine fair competition among airlines. Carriers that continue to advertise the complete, all-in price would appear more expensive than competitors that emphasize only a lower base fare while relegating mandatory taxes and fees to less prominent disclosures. Consumers naturally gravitate toward the lowest advertised price, even when the final cost is ultimately the same or higher. This creates an incentive for airlines to compete on marketing tactics rather than on the actual price consumers pay. A marketplace functions most efficiently when every competitor presents prices using the same transparent standard, allowing consumers to compare true costs quickly and accurately. Retaining the current requirement that the total airfare be the most prominent price promotes honest competition and rewards airlines that offer genuine value rather than those that simply advertise more strategically.

The existing full-fare advertising rule has promoted transparency and fair competition for years. The Department has not demonstrated that the current requirements have harmed competition or innovation. Instead, the proposal appears more likely to encourage advertising practices that emphasize lower headline prices while obscuring unavoidable costs. Consumers deserve to know the actual price they will pay before investing their time in comparing flights and making travel decisions.

For these reasons, I respectfully urge the Department to retain the current requirement that the total airfare, including all mandatory taxes and fees, be displayed prominently in all airfare advertisements. Doing so will protect consumers, promote honest competition, and preserve an efficient marketplace where airlines compete on the value they deliver rather than on the presentation of incomplete prices.

title: Comment from Savage, Sandra
printtext:
To the Federal Trade Commission:
I support transparency in AI systems. I do not support this proposed statement as written, for three reasons.
First — this framework is selectively applied.

The Commission has never proposed truth enforcement for cable news, social media, search engines, or talk radio — all of which influence consumer decisions at massive scale and have demonstrably spread false information. Fox News settled a \$787 million defamation case after its own hosts privately acknowledged broadcasting claims they knew to be false. No FTC action followed. Social media algorithms amplify misinformation to billions daily. No equivalent oversight exists.

The Commission owes the public a principled explanation for why AI specifically warrants content-level regulation that no previous information medium has faced. Without that explanation, this statement appears designed to target a medium that particular interests find threatening — not to protect consumers neutrally.

Second — "who defines accuracy" is the most important question this statement never answers.
The statement prohibits AI outputs steered by "undisclosed ideological objectives" but never addresses what happens when scientific consensus conflicts with current political positions. Is an AI reflecting peer-reviewed climate science engaging in ideological distortion? The statement's silence on this is not neutral — it is an open invitation for future enforcement to define inconvenient facts as bias.

Every comparable democracy has explicitly avoided placing government in the role of AI truth arbiter for exactly this reason. This proposal is a dangerous international outlier.

Third — perceived AI bias deserves a more honest explanation.
Many Americans perceive AI as biased. Before acting on that perception, the Commission should consider an alternative explanation:
AI may feel biased simply because people are accustomed to information that was curated before it reached them — selected by algorithms optimized for engagement, filtered through ideologically consistent media choices, and delivered by hosts whose job is narrative, not accuracy.
When information arrives without that curation, it feels unfamiliar. Unfamiliar feels wrong. Wrong feels like bias.

That is not an AI problem. That is an information environment problem. And regulating AI outputs to match expectations formed inside curated information ecosystems does not protect consumers — it protects the ecosystems.

What I support instead:

Require AI companies to clearly and prominently disclose their methodologies, guardrails, and values. That transparency remedy — which the statement itself acknowledges — is sufficient, appropriate, and does not require the Commission to become an arbiter of correct answers.

Respectfully submitted 7/13/2026

[Your Name]
[Date]
[City, State]

title: Comment from Anonymous
printtext:
We are an independently owned collision repair facility that has served our community since 1997. We support the FTC’s effort to protect consumers from AI systems whose outputs are manipulated or directed toward undisclosed objectives.

We urge the FTC to apply its final policy to undisclosed financial and commercial objectives, including AI used by insurers, claims administrators, estimating companies, and vendors to reduce claim severity at the expense of accuracy, safety, and consumer rights.

We do not work for an insurance company. We work for vehicle owners and policyholders. Our responsibility is to perform complete repairs based on documented damage, pre-loss condition, applicable law, and manufacturer-required procedures. An insurer’s estimate represents what it proposes to pay. It should not override what is required to safely repair the vehicle.

AI is increasingly used to photograph damage, prepare estimates, review repair plans, modify operations, and approve or deny claim costs. AI may improve efficiency when properly supervised. However, when a system is trained or evaluated according to claim-severity reductions, average repair costs, or cost-containment goals, it may appear objective while producing an incomplete or artificially low estimate.

This creates serious safety and consumer protection concerns. AI may overlook hidden or structural damage, omit necessary labor, undervalue rates and materials, select inappropriate parts, or exclude manufacturer-required procedures. Missing operations may include scans, diagnostics, ADAS calibrations, measurements, corrosion protection, seam sealer, weld preparation, refinishing requirements, and safety inspections.

These are not optional charges. They may be required to return a vehicle to its pre-loss condition and ensure that its structural, mechanical, electrical, and safety systems operate as intended.

Consumers may believe that an insurer’s AI estimate is accurate, complete, and neutral. They may not know that the system could be influenced by an undisclosed objective to lower claim payments. Consumers and repairers may have no way to examine its data, rules, limitations, or financial objectives.

Independent repairers regularly identify damage and required procedures missing from insurer estimates. When AI reinforces an incomplete estimate, repairers must document the damage, submit supplements, explain manufacturer requirements, and challenge automated decisions. This can delay repairs, increase rental expenses, create disputes, pressure consumers to accept incomplete repairs, and leave vehicle owners responsible for costs that should have been properly evaluated.

We respectfully ask the FTC to establish that:

1. AI may be deceptive when presented as accurate or objective while directed toward undisclosed claim-severity or cost-containment goals.

2. Insurers and vendors must disclose when AI creates, reviews, modifies, reduces, approves, or denies any part of an estimate or claim.

3. Consumers and repairers must be informed when AI causes the omission, reduction, or denial of a repair operation, part, material, procedure, or labor amount.

4. AI estimates must be supported by documented damage, current manufacturer procedures, identifiable vehicle data, and verifiable estimating information.

5. AI must not disregard OEM procedures, scans, calibrations, structural operations, corrosion protection, refinishing requirements, or safety inspections to reduce costs.

6. Consumers and their repair professionals must have prompt access to a qualified human reviewer with authority to correct an automated decision.

7. Insurers and AI vendors must maintain auditable records showing how estimates and decisions were produced, including material inputs and known limitations.

8. Insurers and AI providers should be accountable when inaccurate estimates cause underpayment, unreasonable delays, unsafe repair pressure, or other consumer harm.

9. AI should serve only as an estimating aid. It must not replace physical inspections, necessary teardown, repair documentation, manufacturer procedures, or qualified professional judgment.

We support technology that improves accuracy, efficiency, and consumer service. We strongly oppose the undisclosed use of AI to suppress legitimate repair costs, omit documented damage, disregard manufacturer requirements, or produce estimates primarily designed to reduce claim severity.

Collision repair accuracy is a consumer safety issue. A vehicle is safely repaired only when all damage is properly evaluated and necessary procedures are performed according to manufacturer requirements and applicable law.

We ask the FTC to include insurance estimating and claims-handling systems within its final policy and recognize undisclosed cost-containment objectives as potential sources of deceptive AI output.

Respectfully,

Independent Collision Repair Shop Owner

title: Comment from Eisenmann, Peter
printtext:
I am submitting this comment in strong opposition to the FTC’s proposed policy statement on AI accuracy, Matter No. P264200 / Docket FTC-2026-0859. This proposed statement does not protect consumers from AI harm. It protects AI companies from accountability for discriminatory and structurally harmful outputs by reframing equity-centered correction and anti-discrimination safeguards as potential consumer deception.

AI systems are not neutral. They are trained on datasets shaped by historical inequality, colonial archives, racial hierarchy, gender hierarchy, ableist assumptions, language dominance, and institutional exclusion. When those systems are used in consequential decisions, the harms are real. They affect jobs, housing, credit, healthcare, education, public benefits, legal systems, immigration, and personal safety.

The FTC’s own prior interagency position recognized that automated systems can perpetuate unlawful bias, automate unlawful discrimination, and produce harmful outcomes. The FTC must not now adopt a policy that treats correction of those harms as suspicious steering.

The proposed policy statement’s treatment of Colorado’s AI accountability law is dangerous. State laws that require companies to address algorithmic discrimination are not ideological coercion. They are consumer protection. They are civil-rights protection. They are public accountability.

Section 5 of the FTC Act must not be used to preempt state-level AI accountability and anti-discrimination protections. State protections against algorithmic discrimination do not conflict with consumer protection. They are a necessary form of consumer protection.

The proposed statement does not center the communities most harmed by uncorrected AI bias, including people of the global majority, disabled people, immigrants, LGBTQIA+ communities, women, workers, tenants, patients, students, and people targeted by surveillance and criminal legal systems.

I urge the Commission to withdraw this proposed policy statement. I urge the Commission to commission independent research on the documented harms of algorithmic discrimination. I urge the Commission to develop any future AI accuracy guidance through a process that centers the communities most harmed by AI systems, not the companies most protected by them.

Signed, Peter Eisenmann, Durham, NC, Real Estate Broker
