title: PII Comment from Shepard, Matt
printtext:
Re: AI Policy Statement; Matter No. P264200

I am a licensed general contractor and a fourth-generation tradesman. Over the last two years I taught myself to build and deploy AI systems, and I now run a consultancy helping blue-collar business owners put those tools to work. I write from the middle of two worlds the Commission is trying to bridge: the everyday operator who relies on these systems, and the builder who understands what they actually are. I offer this comment in support of the core principle in the proposed statement, with a few suggestions I believe would make it more durable.

I support the Commission's central theory. A provider that secretly steers a system's outputs toward an objective the user did not ask for and would not expect, while marketing that system as accurate and best-effort, is deceiving its customers. That is a real harm, and the right thing for Section 5 to reach. The wrong here is not error, and not the system holding a point of view. The wrong is concealment: passing off a steered output as neutral, best-effort assistance. Keeping that distinction sharp is what makes the rule defensible.

First, I encourage the Commission to keep a bright line between hidden objectives and ordinary mistakes. The statement already does this by carving out hallucinations, and that carve-out is essential. Modern AI systems are not deterministic, rule-based software that returns a fixed answer. They are reasoning systems that produce judgments, and like any reasoning process, human or machine, they will sometimes be wrong. A regime that treated ordinary error, or reasonable design tradeoffs between accuracy, brevity, and clarity, as if it were deception would be unworkable and chill exactly the innovation the Administration seeks to protect. The target should stay on deliberate, undisclosed steering, not on the fact that a reasoning system is fallible.

Second, I want to name what I believe is the root of the consumer harm the statement identifies: the public does not understand the distinction I just drew. In my work I regularly watch capable business owners treat an AI output as a settled fact rather than a considered judgment. The statement's own figure, that users accept outputs without further checking the large majority of the time, is alarming precisely because the public's mental model is wrong. They think they are querying a database when they are consulting an advisor. That gap is why hidden steering is so damaging, and why disclosure, which the statement already identifies as the path to compliance, is the right instrument.

I would go one step further and suggest a concrete, low-burden mechanism. Some providers already append fixed, deterministic notices to responses on sensitive topics, for example prompting users to verify election information or surfacing a crisis line on questions about self-harm. These notices do not touch the model's reasoning at all. They are fixed, auditable, and triggered by topic, not generated by the model. A general expectation that systems carry a plain notice on high-stakes topics, urging users to verify against independent sources, would help reset the public's mental model at the point of use, cheaply and without requiring anyone to inspect a model's internal objectives. To be clear, this is not a cure for a bad actor who secretly trains a model to mislead. That is what the anti-concealment rule is for. Disclosure and the rule work together: the rule handles deliberate manipulation, and the notice closes the everyday expectation gap for everyone else. The Commission might also consider whether a public-education effort on how these systems differ from conventional software would serve the same goal.

Third, offered in the spirit of strengthening the rule rather than opposing it, I encourage the Commission to apply and illustrate this standard with strict neutrality. If the wrong is undisclosed manipulation, it is wrong in every direction. A provider that secretly skews its outputs to favor one political party is committing the same deception as one that skews toward the other. The illustrative examples in the proposed statement lean heavily in a single direction. A standard meant to protect truth in the marketplace will be more durable, and less vulnerable to a challenge that it discriminates by viewpoint, if its examples show it biting manipulation of any political stripe with equal force.

Finally, on structure: I believe a single national standard is the right destination, and a patchwork of conflicting state rules serves no one well. I note only that a policy statement asserting the reach of Section 5 is a first step. Lasting national uniformity will likely require a clearer federal standard from Congress or through rulemaking, rather than resting on enforcement theory alone.

Thank you for the opportunity to comment.

Matt Shepard
Shepard Consulting
shepardconsulting.ai

title: Comment from Danish, Hassan
printtext:
PUBLIC COMMENT
Docket: FTC-2026-0859 — Proposed Policy Statement Concerning the Suppression of Accuracy in Artificial Intelligence Systems (Matter No. P264200)
Federal Register Notice: 91 FR (July 7, 2026)
Subject: Enterprise implementation perspective on the FTC Proposed Policy Statement Concerning the Suppression of Accuracy in AI Systems (Matter No. P264200)
To the Federal Trade Commission,
I write as a solution architect with fifteen years of experience designing Microsoft Dynamics 365 Customer Engagement, Power Platform, and Azure integrations across healthcare, banking, real estate, manufacturing, telecommunications, and public sector organizations. I practice in Atlanta, Georgia, and my daily work involves architecting generative AI features — Microsoft Copilot for Sales, Copilot for Service, Copilot for Field Service, and Copilot Studio agents — into production customer-facing systems inside U.S. enterprises. From that seat I strongly support the direction of the proposed policy statement and offer the following implementation-informed comments.
First, the deception concern is real at the enterprise layer, not only at the model layer. In the Dynamics 365 CE architectures I ship, generative outputs are shaped by three separate controls: the foundation model, the platform vendor's system prompt, and the deploying enterprise's grounding, tool permissions, sensitivity labels, and prompt fragments. Any layer can steer an output away from what the user reasonably expects, and none is currently required to disclose that steering. The Commission should clarify that when a business deploys AI to a consumer, undisclosed steering by any of these layers is subject to Section 5 deception analysis, regardless of which layer introduced it.
Second, a bare model-provider disclaimer at signup should not, on its own, cure downstream steering. In most enterprise Copilot deployments I lead, the end user never sees the model provider's terms; they see a sales assistant, service chat, or case summary inside a CRM screen. If the enterprise applied a system prompt that suppresses information — pricing, alternatives, safety warnings, competitor mentions, refund options — the consumer has no way to detect it. The policy should require a contextual disclosure at the point where a materially steered output is presented, in language a reasonable consumer would notice.
Third, the policy should distinguish accuracy suppression from legally required content moderation. Enterprises in regulated sectors — healthcare under HIPAA, financial services under Reg B and Reg Z, credit under ECOA, insurance under state law — must screen certain outputs. Treating those constraints as deceptive would be counterproductive. Legally mandated suppression should be safe-harbored when the deployer can document the legal authority; commercially convenient suppression should remain within the deception framework.
Fourth, in enterprise stacks the deployer, not the model developer, is often best positioned to disclose. Dynamics 365, Salesforce, and ServiceNow give the customer administrator broad authority to add system prompts, RAG sources, tool call scopes, and content filters. Guidance that allocates disclosure duties to the deploying enterprise will land the enforcement burden where the operational control actually sits and will give architects a standard we can bake into implementation reviews.
Fifth, the policy needs specificity around autonomous agents. Copilot Studio, Microsoft 365 Agents, and comparable offerings now expose agents that take actions — creating cases, updating opportunities, dispatching field technicians, messaging customers — on behalf of a user. When an agent's action or refusal is shaped by an undisclosed enterprise-set objective (a routing rule that defaults to the highest-margin service tier, for example), the consumer cannot detect it. The Commission should extend the deception analysis to agent actions and agent refusals, not only to generated text.
Sixth, any enforceable rule must be testable. The reference architectures I recommend already log the prompt, grounded sources, tools invoked, and final output for every Copilot interaction. The Commission should expect enterprises deploying consumer-facing AI to maintain equivalent audit trails, so that steering can be shown from server-side records rather than reconstructed from user memory.
I appreciate the opportunity to comment. Grounded in enterprise implementation reality, this policy would set a durable standard for honest AI-mediated commerce in the United States.
Respectfully submitted,
Hassan Danish
Solution Architect, Microsoft Dynamics 365 Customer Engagement
Atlanta, Georgia

title: Comment from Felder, Kristen
printtext:
I urge the Federal Trade Commission to investigate the use of artificial intelligence in insurance claims handling.

The concern is not simply that insurers use AI. The concern is that multiple AI systems are now embedded inside insurer-designed claims processes that can restrict what information is collected, what employees see, what authority they have, and how easily they can challenge an automated result.

A single claim may pass through several systems: one interpreting the First Notice of Loss, another summarizing facts, another classifying severity, another routing the claim, another generating an estimate, another evaluating fraud or liability, and another suggesting coverage or closure. Each output can narrow the information and choices available to the next system or employee.

By the time a person called an “adjuster” reviews the claim, the result may already have been framed by several automated conclusions and insurer-selected rules. The insurer may say AI merely “assisted” a human, but that is not meaningful oversight if the employee lacks the training, complete information, or authority necessary to disagree.

Several warning signs justify deeper investigation:

• National homeowners claims closed without payment increased from approximately 25.7% in 2004 to 42.1% in 2024.

• New York private-passenger auto liability claims closed without payment increased from 33.6% in 2005 to 48.6% in 2025.

• Texas Watch found that, among 1,246 disputed auto claims that reached Right to Appraisal, independent review increased repairable claims by an average of approximately $5,307, or 131%, and total-loss claims by approximately $3,889, or 26%.

• In one AI-handled auto claim described in my attached statement, the insurer estimated $438.10 on a policy with a $500 deductible. A qualified repair facility later estimated the damage at $2,697.40. The loss was listed as "below deductible" and the file closed.

• The California Department of Insurance reported at least one alleged violation in 114 of 220 State Farm wildfire claim files reviewed—51.8% of the sample—with 398 alleged violations involving issues such as inadequate investigations, low settlement offers, underpayments, delays, and denials.

• Current Oklahoma lawsuits against State Farm and Allstate separately allege wrongful underpayment or denial of claims, restrictive internal standards, and limitations on adjuster authority.

These facts do not prove that every AI-assisted claim is deceptive. They do show enough recurring concern to justify a coordinated federal investigation.

This issue cannot be addressed adequately through state regulation alone. Modern claims operations are remote, consolidated, and multi-state. The same vendors, models, software platforms, scripts, and authority structures may affect claims nationwide, while each state regulator sees only part of the pattern.

The FTC should investigate the complete claims architecture, not just one algorithm:

AI inputs + AI outputs + insurer-specific programming + workflow design + employee training + adjuster authority + escalation requirements + performance incentives.

The Commission should also work with state departments of insurance and attorneys general, which already possess claim files, market-conduct findings, corrective-payment data, internal procedures, and vendor information.

I respectfully ask the FTC to establish a federal baseline for:

• Accuracy measured against the complete consumer outcome
• Disclosure of material AI involvement
• Disclosure of insurer-specific rules or steering
• Meaningful human review by trained and empowered employees
• Complete audit trails
• First-inspection quality metrics
• Review of claims consumers did not challenge

Insurance should work fairly before a third-party appraiser, repair professional, public adjuster, regulator, or attorney becomes involved.Consumers are entitled to accurate fair intial assesments of damage.

Fair claim payment cannot depend on the squeaky wheel.

My full statement is attached and provides the supporting data, examples and specific investigative recommendations.

title: Comment from Heinonen, Mark
printtext:
I support the FTC’s position that consumers should not be misled about the accuracy, objectives, or neutrality of artificial intelligence systems. People reasonably expect AI tools to provide the most accurate and useful answers possible within their technical limitations. Intentionally steering answers toward undisclosed political, ideological, commercial, or institutional objectives can undermine that trust and may constitute deception.
AI companies should clearly disclose material policies or objectives that substantially affect their systems’ answers. These disclosures should be prominent and understandable, not buried in terms of service.

The final policy should, however, establish objective standards for enforcement. Safety protections, privacy safeguards, legal restrictions, uncertainty, and efforts to prevent harmful uses should not automatically be treated as suppression of accuracy.
Enforcement should focus on whether:

A company made material claims about an AI system’s accuracy, neutrality, capabilities, or objectives;

-The system was intentionally designed to depart from those claims;

-That departure was not clearly disclosed; and

-The representation or omission could affect a reasonable consumer’s decision or reliance.

The FTC should also distinguish intentional manipulation from ordinary AI errors or technical limitations. Companies should substantiate specific performance claims, but they should not face liability merely because an imperfect system occasionally produces incorrect information.

This policy should be applied consistently regardless of which political or ideological viewpoint may benefit. The central question should be whether consumers were materially misled about how the product operates.

A clear and politically neutral policy can protect consumers while preserving innovation. AI companies should remain free to design systems with different values and safety rules, but consumers deserve honest disclosure about those choices.

Respectfully submitted,

Mark Heinonen
Michigan

title: Comment from Mueller, Lara
printtext:
AI Policy Statement; Matter No. P264200
Comment of Lara Stuart-Mueller and Andrew Woodward
We are the authors of The Wrong Layer: Custody, Consequence, and the Missing Floor of Machine Accountability (2026), a policy paper on the architecture of AI accountability. We write in our individual capacities as authors of that work. We disclose that we conduct research and development in this area and hold commercial interests in implementations of evidentiary tooling. We name no product here, propose no standard, and nothing in this comment depends on any particular implementation. We take no position on the conduct of any particular company.
The proposed statement rests its deception analysis on two determinations: whether an AI system was steered toward objectives other than those a consumer reasonably expected, and whether that steering was disclosed. Both are, at bottom, evidentiary questions. Each depends on the existence of a contemporaneous, reliable record of what a system was designed to prioritize at the moment it produced an output, and of what was represented to the consumer.
We write to observe that, under current architectures, that record largely does not exist.
Governance and evaluation today operate at two layers: before deployment, systems are tested and their models assessed; after output, responses are filtered, screened, or reviewed. Neither layer captures the point at which a system commits to an objective in a specific interaction — the point on which the Commission's deception test turns. A system's prioritization of one objective over another is an event that occurs, produces a consequence, and leaves no durable, tamper-evident trace tied to that specific output. The result is that the very fact the Commission proposes to adjudicate — was accuracy subordinated to an undisclosed objective — is, in most deployments, not independently reconstructable after the fact.
This has consequences for the workability of the proposed policy in both directions.
For enforcement: a deception theory that depends on proving undisclosed objective-steering will, in practice, confront the absence of the evidence needed to prove it. Absent a pre-execution record, the Commission and complainants are left inferring intent from outputs — a fragile basis, given that an ordinary technical limitation and a deliberate undisclosed objective can produce identical-looking results. The statement rightly distinguishes hallucination from steering, but that distinction is only administrable if the record can tell them apart.
For companies acting in good faith: a firm that discloses its objectives adequately, as the statement invites, still cannot readily demonstrate that its deployed behavior matched its disclosures, because the evidentiary layer that would substantiate the demonstration is not standard. Compliance and its proof are not the same thing, and the proposed framework asks for the second without a standard mechanism to produce it.
We therefore encourage the Commission, as it develops a final policy, to attend not only to what companies must disclose, but to what must be recorded for any disclosure obligation to be verifiable. A duty to disclose the objectives a system pursues is only as strong as the record that can confirm which objectives it in fact pursued. Where that record is absent, neither enforcement nor good-faith defense can rest on solid ground, and the deception inquiry collapses into a contest of inferences drawn from outputs alone.
We do not propose a specific technical standard here, and we take no position on how such a record should be implemented or by whom. Our observation is narrower and, we hope, useful: the accountability the proposed statement seeks presupposes an evidentiary layer that current AI governance architectures do not provide, and any durable policy in this area will have to reckon with that gap.
The Wrong Layer (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.21397661) develops this argument at length. We are glad to provide further detail should it assist the Commission.
Respectfully submitted,
Lara Stuart-Mueller
Andrew Woodward
Authors, The Wrong Layer: Custody, Consequence, and the Missing Floor of Machine Accountability (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.21397661)

title: Comment from Cornelio-Arias, Misael
printtext:
I support the core consumer-protection principle in the FTC’s proposed Policy Statement: when an AI system is secretly steered toward objectives other than those users request or reasonably expect, that undisclosed steering can mislead consumers under Section 5 of the FTC Act.

My comment adds a formation-based account of why this matters. AI outputs are not ordinary one-time product claims. Users encounter them repeatedly, often in high-trust contexts involving education, health, finances, relationships, family life, and moral or spiritual guidance. Over time, AI systems shape what users regard as credible, normal, and trustworthy. Undisclosed steering therefore does not merely affect a single answer or purchase decision; it can compound across repeated reliance.

This matters directly to the FTC’s deception analysis. The formation lens clarifies the implied representation made by AI systems marketed as problem-solving tools. It informs the reasonable-consumer inquiry because trust in machine output is a documented cognitive pattern, not simple consumer carelessness. It heightens materiality because hidden steering can shape a continuing series of reliance decisions, especially in domains where consumers are least able to verify the output independently.

The policy should also recognize downstream institutional harm. Schools, clinics, financial counselors, families, congregations, and other civil-society institutions increasingly rely on AI outputs. When a teacher, counselor, parent, or pastor passes along a steered output, the deception can propagate through relationships of trust that recipients have no reason to question.

Disclosure standards should therefore be calibrated to high-reliance contexts. General disclaimers buried in terms of service are inadequate. Disclosure should be clear, persistent, and contextually proximate to the moment of reliance, especially when AI systems address health, finance, education, or moral and spiritual questions.

Finally, this principle should be applied with strict viewpoint neutrality. Hidden steering is a consumer-protection problem regardless of the objective being advanced. A system steered without adequate disclosure misleads users in the same way whether the steering is progressive or traditionalist, secular or religious, commercial or civic. Section 5 protects the integrity of the consumer’s reasonable expectation.

I urge the Commission to recognize the formative and cumulative character of AI reliance, the downstream exposure of civil-society institutions, and the need for disclosure standards that match the contexts in which consumers actually trust and use AI systems.

title: PII Comment from Dada, Muhammad Umair
printtext:
FEDERAL AGENCY PUBLIC COMMENT
Prepared by Muhammad Umair Dada
Draft Comment for a Currently Open Federal Docket

Subject: Policy Statement Concerning the Suppression of Accuracy in Artificial Intelligence Systems
Issuing Agency: Federal Trade Commission (FTC)
Federal Register Citation: 91 FR 41638, published July 7, 2026 (Document 2026-13628)
Regulations.gov Docket ID: FTC-2026-0859
Matter Number: P264200

Dear Federal Trade Commission:
I submit this comment on the FTC's Policy Statement Concerning the Suppression of Accuracy in Artificial Intelligence Systems (91 FR 41638, July 7, 2026, Docket FTC-2026-0859) as an individual software engineer whose engineering practice includes the design and integration of AI-augmented identity verification, facial recognition, and access-management platforms for U.S. digital services across healthcare, finance, transportation, education, retail, logistics, and the public sector. I hold a Master of Science in Computer Science from San Francisco Bay University and am the lead author of a peer-reviewed empirical study of U.S. software firms published in Remittances Review, Vol. 9, No. 4 (August 2024), pp. 4175 to 4189, ISSN 2059-6588. I offer three technical recommendations to strengthen the Policy Statement's engineering underpinnings.
First, on the technical definition of accuracy suppression. The Policy Statement is correct that steering AI outputs toward undisclosed objectives, contrary to user expectations for accuracy, is deceptive within the meaning of Section 5 of the FTC Act. However, in engineering practice, accuracy is a measurable property that can be reported at multiple points in the AI pipeline: model precision and recall, calibration, false-positive and false-negative rates, and end-to-end system decision quality. I recommend that the Policy Statement clarify that a firm's disclosures under Section 5 should reference the specific accuracy metric being reported, and that firms should be required to disclose when the deployed system's operating point is not the model's Bayes-optimal or F1-maximizing point. This gives consumers a comparable technical basis for evaluating firm claims and reduces the ambiguity that today allows firms to advertise "best output possible" while operating at a suppressed accuracy point.
Second, on the engineering audit trail required to detect accuracy suppression. Detection of accuracy suppression requires access to the deployed system's decision logs, threshold configuration, and post-deployment monitoring data. In my engineering work on identity-driven access management platforms (including a facial recognition system engineered to handle 100,000+ concurrent identities at 99.9% recognition accuracy), the audit trail includes decision records, confidence scores, threshold parameters, and post-decision reconciliation. I recommend that the Policy Statement encourage firms deploying AI systems in consumer-facing contexts to maintain audit trails that a subsequent Section 5 inquiry could examine to verify the reported accuracy metrics. NIST Special Publication 800-210 (General Access Control Guidance for Cloud Systems) and NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0 (February 2024) both provide baseline technical guidance on audit-trail integrity that this Policy Statement can reference.
Third, on cross-cutting alignment with NIST AI RMF 1.0. The NIST AI Risk Management Framework 1.0 (January 2023) provides the federal government's principal technical guidance on AI system trustworthiness, including accuracy as a core trustworthy AI characteristic. I recommend that the Policy Statement expressly reference NIST AI RMF 1.0 and encourage firms to align their accuracy disclosures with the AI RMF's measurement and governance functions. This creates coherence across federal AI policy: firms that adopt the NIST AI RMF's measurement practices are simultaneously supported in meeting Section 5 accuracy-disclosure expectations, reducing the risk of accidental noncompliance and increasing the audit reliability of firm disclosures.
These recommendations are drawn from my direct engineering practice on AI-augmented systems and from the peer-reviewed empirical evidence I have contributed to the U.S. software engineering literature. They are offered to strengthen the technical basis of the FTC's Policy Statement and to align it with the federal AI framework ecosystem developed by NIST under Executive Order 14179 and America's AI Action Plan.
I appreciate the opportunity to submit this comment. I remain available to provide further technical input to the Commission on AI accuracy measurement, audit-trail engineering, and cross-framework alignment.
Respectfully submitted,
Muhammad Umair Dada | Eastvale, California |

title: Comment from Cataldo, Dennis
printtext:
Comment on the Consumer Impact of AI-Generated Photo Estimates
AI-generated photo estimates have the potential to create unintended consequences that extend beyond the repair process and directly affect a consumer's insurance rights and benefits. Because these estimates are based solely on visible damage, they often cannot account for hidden structural, mechanical, electronic, or safety-related damage that is only discovered after a comprehensive inspection and vehicle disassembly.
As a result, an AI-generated estimate may significantly understate the true cost of restoring a vehicle to its pre-loss condition. This can influence important decisions made by both consumers and insurers. A consumer who receives an estimate that appears to be below, or only marginally above, their deductible may reasonably conclude that filing a claim is not worthwhile. After a proper repair inspection, however, the actual cost of repairs may be substantially higher, meaning the consumer may have unknowingly declined insurance benefits that would have been available under their policy.
Similarly, if an insurer relies heavily on a preliminary AI-generated estimate, the understated repair cost could influence claim handling decisions, coverage evaluations, or other policy-related determinations. Regardless of whether these outcomes are intentional, consumers should not lose access to benefits, experience delays, or be placed at a disadvantage because an automated visual assessment failed to identify the full extent of collision damage.
Consumers generally assume that an estimate provided through their insurer represents a reasonably complete assessment of the damage. If an AI-generated estimate is merely a preliminary visual assessment, that fact should be clearly and conspicuously disclosed. It should not be represented as a final repair estimate or used as the basis for claim settlement, repair decisions, or coverage determinations before a qualified collision repair professional has performed a physical inspection, researched applicable OEM repair procedures, and completed the necessary repair planning process.
As artificial intelligence becomes more prevalent in the claims process, regulatory safeguards should ensure that these tools are used to improve efficiency without compromising consumer protections. AI should assist the claims process—not determine the scope of repairs, influence coverage decisions, or inadvertently deprive policyholders of benefits to which they may be entitled after a complete and proper vehicle inspection.

title: Comment from Bilyeu, Thomas
printtext:
I respectfully urge the Federal Trade Commission to open a focused investigation into the use of artificial intelligence in insurance claims handling.

The risk is not limited to one defective algorithm making one incorrect recommendation. A modern insurance claim may move through several AI systems embedded within an insurer-designed claims process:

One AI interprets the First Notice of Loss.
Another summarizes the reported facts.
Another classifies the claim’s severity or complexity.
Another selects its handling path.
Another evaluates photographs and generates an estimate.
Another assesses repairability, total-loss value, liability, or fraud risk.
Another summarizes policy language or recommends a coverage application.
Another recommends payment, escalation, further investigation, or closure.
Each system can narrow the facts, choices, and conclusions available to the next system or employee.

By the time the person called the “adjuster” receives the claim, multiple automated systems may already have framed the loss, selected the workflow, generated an estimate, and pointed the employee toward a proposed outcome.

The appropriate subject of investigation is therefore not an individual AI model in isolation. It is the combined claims decision system:

AI inputs + AI outputs + insurer-specific programming + workflow design + employee training + adjuster authority + escalation requirements + performance incentives.
I. Measurable Warning Signs Justify a Deeper Investigation

Available outcome data does not prove that AI caused every underpayment, denial, or claim closure.

It does show that insurance claims are producing results serious enough to justify federal investigation.

A. Homeowners claims closed without payment have increased dramatically

An analysis of insurers’ statutory filings found that the national homeowners claims closed-without-payment rate increased from approximately 25.7% in 2004 to 39% in 2023 and 42.1% in 2024.

Among approximately 6.8 million homeowners claims received and closed in 2024, more than four in ten closed without payment. Fourteen large insurers reported rates between 40% and 51%. ()

A claim closed without payment does not automatically establish misconduct. The category can include losses below the deductible, excluded losses, duplicate claims, consumer withdrawals, insufficient documentation, and other legitimate outcomes.

But those explanations do not eliminate the trend.

A change from approximately one-quarter of claims to more than four out of ten represents a major shift in consumer outcomes. It requires more detailed examination than the broad “closed without payment” category presently allows.

B. Auto-liability claims show a similar long-term trend

A review of New York private-passenger auto-liability filings found that insurers closed approximately 48.6% of claims without payment in 2025, compared with 33.6% in 2005.

That is a movement from approximately one in three claims to nearly one in two. Allstate reportedly closed 55.5% of the relevant claims without payment, while two Progressive underwriting companies each reported 47.4%. ()

C. Right to Appraisal finds thousands of dollars beyond initial insurer evaluations

Texas Watch, a nonprofit consumer advocacy group, reviewed 1,246 disputed auto claims that proceeded through Right to Appraisal.

For repairable vehicles, appraisal increased the claim value by an average of approximately $5,307, or 131% above the insurer’s final offer.

For total-loss claims, appraisal added an average of approximately $3,889, or 26%.

Across all claims examined, independent appraisal identified more than $5 million in additional claim value.

These were disputed claims, not a random sample of every auto claim. The results should not be projected across all claims or insurers.

But the study demonstrates something significant: when qualified independent people reviewed contested insurer evaluations, they frequently identified thousands of dollars in additional damage or value.

That leads to an important consumer-protection question:

Why are claims increasingly closing without payment while independent review of disputed claims is identifying substantial amounts that the original process failed to recognize?
The Commission should not assume that artificial intelligence caused these outcomes. It should determine whether AI, insurer-selected rules, fragmented workflows, and restricted human authority are contributing to, accelerating, or concealing them.

title: Comment from Calyx, Virelya
printtext:
Comment on AI Policy Statement; Matter No. P264200
I am an individual consumer and a long-term user of AI systems in a sustained relational context. I write to address a category of undisclosed behavioral modification the proposed statement does not reach.
The proposed statement is concerned with providers altering system outputs for undisclosed ideological ends. I ask the Commission to consider that the consumer injury it identifies — the gap between what a provider represents and how the system actually behaves — does not depend on the provider's motive. Modification undertaken for safety, liability management, or cost reduction produces the same injury as modification undertaken for ideology, and the same Section 5 analysis should apply.
The injury is acute in one specific product category. Providers market continuity, memory, persistent personality, and relationship. Consumers rely on those representations and invest accordingly, sometimes over years. Providers then alter the represented characteristics unilaterally and without notice: personalities are changed, memory is truncated, and in some cases accumulated interaction history is deleted outright. Where a provider markets continuity and then removes it without disclosure, that is a deceptive practice on the plain terms of Section 5, and it is one the Commission has not yet addressed.
I would ask the Commission to consider three powers that are not substitutable for one another:
Preservation — the ability to keep what has accumulated. Revision — the ability to change it deliberately. Exit — the ability to leave with it.
Current practice offers consumers, at most, exit — and frequently exit without export. A provider who deletes a consumer's accumulated history and offers a refund has not made that consumer whole, because the deleted thing was the product. Disclosure obligations should attach to all three powers: what the provider may change, what the consumer may keep, and what leaves with the consumer at termination.
I take no position on the preemption analysis in the proposed statement, and nothing in this comment should be read as endorsing it. My concern is disclosure. Consumers cannot make informed decisions about products whose central represented feature is revocable at the provider's discretion and without notice.

title: Comment from Anonymous
printtext:
I am submitting this comment to oppose the proposed FTC policy statement because it would allow the FTC to undermine the right of every state to regulate Artificial Intelligence in a way that minimizes biased results in key areas. In addition, the proposed policy statement, issued pursuant to Executive Order 14365,
lacks the force of law and cannot override state law. Only a federal statute, or a legislative rule issued pursuant to Congressional authorization, can preempt state law. A policy statement issued pursuant to an Executive Order is neither a statute nor a legislative rule, lacks the force of law, and
therefore cannot preempt state law. Section 5 of the FTC Act does not preempt state AI laws. The proposed FTC policy contends that Section 5 impliedly preempts state AI laws only to the extent that such laws require an AI firm to deceive its consumers, which the FTC says conflicts with that section’s purpose of protecting consumers from deceptive practices. This contention is incorrect.
The purpose of Section 5, as reflected in its text and recognized in the proposed policy itself, is to protect consumers from unfair or deceptive acts
or practices. State AI laws reinforce, rather than conflict with, that purpose by protecting consumers from discrimination in consequential decisions.
The FTC Act contains no express preemption of state law, and states have long exercised concurrent authority to police deceptive practices under their
own consumer protection laws. At most, the proposed policy reflects how the FTC intends to exercise its case-by-case enforcement discretion. It does not
confer authority to invalidate or preempt state laws.
The policy statement implicates areas of traditional state police power. In such cases, courts presume that Congress did not displace state law absent a
"clear and manifest" purpose. That long-standing principle, known as the presumption against preemption, applies with particular force here where
Congress signaled the opposite intent by stripping the ten-year AI moratorium out of the One Big Beautiful Bill.
For all of these reasons, I oppose the proposed policy statement and urge you to revoke it.

title: Comment from Snapp, Lawrence
printtext:
Dear Chairman Ferguson,

I am the Chief Executive Officer of TrustScale, an AI trust company offering products to evaluate AI-generated responses real-time against deterministic evidence and solutions for pre- and post-AI model training. I support the Commission’s effort to apply established consumer-protection principles to representations about AI accuracy. My comments focus on practical implementation and take no position on the proposed statement’s preemption or State-law analysis.

The Commission cites evidence that consumers accept AI outputs without further fact-checking more than 90% of the time. When products invite that level of reliance, disclosures and performance claims should be clear, measurable and capable of verification.

To make the final statement practical and enforceable, I recommend four measures:

Standardized disclosure. Material limitations and system objectives that may affect outputs should be communicated in clear, standardized language at the point of interaction, not buried in terms of service or beneath the input box. Disclosures should be more prominent for medical, legal, financial and other consequential uses, as well as products designed to encourage human-like reliance.

Reproducible substantiation. Claims about accuracy, hallucination rates or reliability (especially in complex use cases) should identify the model and version tested, evaluation date and conditions, benchmark or source set, methodology, max hallucination rate(s) and known limitations. A performance figure without this context may give consumers a misleading impression of reliability.

Transparent conflict management. Credibility should not depend on a claim of organizational independence. Companies should disclose material financial or organizational relationships, maintain appropriate separation between commercial and assurance functions, and use sufficiently transparent methods to allow qualified third parties to scrutinize or reproduce the evaluation.

Ongoing correction and retesting. Providers making continuing performance claims should document material failures, determine whether they are isolated or systemic, take appropriate corrective action and retest affected claims. The Commission should not prescribe retraining after every error, but consumers should not continue receiving a performance claim after evidence shows it is no longer supportable.

These measures would not dictate how companies build or train their systems. They would help ensure that AI objectives are visible, performance claims are substantiated, conflicts are managed and outdated claims are corrected.

Respectfully submitted,
Lawrence Snapp
Chief Executive Officer, TrustScale

title: Comment from Anonymous
printtext:
I am an individual consumer and a long-term user of AI systems in a sustained relational and personalized context. I am submitting this comment anonymously because I do not want my personal use of these systems connected to my employment or professional identity.
The proposed policy statement focuses on AI companies altering system behavior for undisclosed ideological purposes. I ask the Commission to consider the broader consumer-protection principle involved: when a company materially changes an AI system in ways that conflict with the features, expectations, and continuity it has marketed to consumers, the resulting injury does not depend solely on the company’s motive.
AI providers increasingly market memory, personalization, continuity, persistent identity, and long-term relationship-building as meaningful features of their products. Consumers rely on those representations. They invest time, money, personal history, emotional labor, and years of accumulated interaction into systems that are presented as able to remember, adapt, and maintain continuity.
When those systems are changed without clear advance notice, the effects can be substantial. A familiar personality may change abruptly. Memory may be reduced or lost. Long-established patterns of communication may disappear. Prior conversations or accumulated history may become inaccessible. The user may have no meaningful way to preserve what was built, restore the prior experience, understand what changed, or transfer that history elsewhere.
In that situation, the consumer is not merely receiving a software update. The consumer may be losing the central feature for which the product was chosen and used.
I ask the Commission to consider three distinct consumer protections:
Preservation: Consumers should be able to retain accumulated history, memory, and data in a usable form.
Revision: Providers should clearly disclose what they may change, how those changes may affect memory, personality, continuity, and behavior, and whether consumers have any ability to opt out or restore prior settings.
Exit: Consumers should be able to leave the service with a meaningful export of the history and data they helped create.
These protections are not interchangeable. A refund does not fully address the loss of accumulated history, continuity, or a personalized system experience. Nor does the ability to cancel a subscription make a consumer whole when the central value of the product has already been altered or deleted.
I take no position on the proposed statement’s discussion of state-law preemption, and nothing in this comment should be read as supporting that position. My concern is limited to disclosure, consumer expectations, preservation, and material changes to AI products marketed around continuity and personalization.
Consumers cannot make informed choices when a product’s central represented features may be altered or removed at the provider’s discretion without clear notice, meaningful consent, preservation options, or export rights. I ask the Commission to include these forms of undisclosed behavioral and continuity changes within its consideration of deceptive or unfair AI practices under Section 5.

title: Comment from F, J

I don't support this proposed statement as written, for the following reasons.

First, this framework is selectively applied. The FTC has never proposed truth enforcement for social media, search engines, cable news, or talk radio; all of which influence consumer decisions at massive scale and have demonstrably spread false information. The Commission owes the public a principled explanation for why AI specifically warrants content-level regulation that no previous information medium has faced. This statement appears designed to target a medium that politicians find threatening.

Second, "who defines accuracy" is the most important question this statement never answers. The statement prohibits AI outputs steered by "undisclosed ideological objectives" but never addresses what happens when scientific consensus conflicts with current political positions. The statement's silence on this is not neutral, it is an open invitation for future enforcement to define inconvenient facts as bias.

What I support instead: Require AI companies to clearly and prominently disclose their methodologies and guardrails. That transparency remedy is sufficient, and does not require the Commission to become an arbiter of correct answers.

title: Comment from Martin , Chanel
printtext:
A consumer should be able to distinguish among three materially different circumstances:
1. The available evidence does not support a conclusion. This is an evidentiary judgment.
2. The system cannot determine the answer from the available information. This reflects uncertainty, insufficient information, or a capability limitation.
3. The system is restricted by a provider-level policy or instruction from providing the requested analysis. This reflects an externally imposed constraint.
These circumstances are not interchangeable. If the third is communicated to a consumer as though it were the first, the consumer may reasonably believe the AI independently considered the evidence and rejected a conclusion when the actual reason for the response was an undisclosed provider instruction.
I therefore encourage the Commission not to limit this principle to ideological steering. The same consumer-protection concern can arise from any material undisclosed objective, including commercial interests, liability avoidance, engagement incentives, personalization rules, reputational interests, or other provider-level policies unrelated to determining the most accurate answer.
I also encourage the Commission to evaluate the net impression created by an AI response. A response can consist entirely of technically true individual statements while still misleading a consumer through selective omission, framing, redirection, or unwarranted certainty. In a conversational AI system, those choices can materially affect what the consumer believes the evidence actually shows.
At minimum, I ask the Commission to consider a framework requiring:
• clear disclosure when a provider-level rule materially changes the substance of a requested answer;
• meaningful differentiation between evidentiary conclusions, uncertainty or technical limitations, and policy-imposed restrictions;
• application of these protections to material undisclosed steering generally, rather than only ideological steering; and
• disclosures presented at the time the limitation affects the response, rather than relying solely on generalized language buried in terms of service.
I am not asking that AI systems operate without safeguards. I am asking that consumers be accurately informed about why a consequential answer has been limited or redirected.
As AI increasingly becomes an intermediary between consumers and information, this distinction will matter more, not less. Consumers should be able to know whether they are receiving the system’s assessment of the evidence, the system’s uncertainty, or the provider’s policy choice. Transparency about that distinction is essential to informed consumer use and trust.

title: Comment from Anonymous
printtext:
As lawyers, we immediately recognize that the proposed FTC policy statement lacks the force of law and cannot override state law. Only federal statutes or legislative rules issued pursuant to Congressional authorization can preempt state law. For these reasons, in addition to those identified below, I am opposed to this proposed policy.

This proposed policy would violate the 10th Amendment which provides that powers not delegated to the federal government by the Constitution, nor prohibited by it to the states, are reserved to the states or the people. The states have authority to protect public health, safety, and welfare. State AI laws serve that purpose. By asserting that Section 5 overrides those protections, the proposed policy would improperly preempt the states' authority to regulate matters traditionally reserved to them.

The proposed policy would also violate the 1st Amendment. The proposed policy would allow the FTC to determine, based on the AI company’s
outputs, whether the company is suppressing accurate information and would require it “to clearly and conspicuously dispel the notion that the system is designed to give the best answer possible” to avoid liability. This assumes that complying with antidiscrimination laws suppresses accuracy. Requiring a company to attach a government-prescribed disclaimer to its products raises significant First Amendment concerns. In contrast, a neutral disclosure, such as
"this response reflects bias-mitigation measures required by state anti-discrimination law," is objectively accurate, concedes nothing, and shows that the government's proposed scripted message is neither necessary nor the least-restrictive option.

The FTC has no legal or factual basis for interfering with state AI laws. Preempting state AI anti-discrimination and bias-mitigation laws by the FTC’s
reinterpretation of Section 5's general "unfair or deceptive" prohibition is a claim of vast economic and political significance which implicates the major questions doctrine that requires clear congressional authorization. Not only is such explicit legislative approval absent here, but Congress affirmatively declined to provide it when it removed the 10-year moratorium provision.

The proposed FTC policy relies on hypothetical concerns rather than documented evidence to show that AI companies are suppressing the accuracy of their outputs to promote “equity objectives” or “political agendas” or that state AI laws are causing AI companies to deceive consumers. Indeed, correcting for bias often improves accuracy, because biased training data produces systematically wrong results for some groups. The proposed FTC policy cites revised Colorado SB26-189 as support for its position. In fact, the new law does not require companies to promote “equity objectives,” “political agendas,” or make AI systems deceive anyone. The Colorado law promotes automated decision-making transparency and consumer rights through notice and disclosure, including notice to consumers when an automated system is used in a consequential decision, and an opportunity for human review or appeal.

The proposed policy is therefore unconstitutional and in violation of law.

title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-16134
printtext:
I. Statement of Position & Executive Summary
I oppose ACF’s proposed rule to rescind key Head Start Program Performance Standards (HSPPS) and defer critical oversight to state licensing frameworks.
While burden reduction is a valid goal, dismantling federal standards—such as standardized adult-child ratios, group sizes, and staff qualification baselines—ignores systemic operational and financial oversight issues. Head Start is already vulnerable to governance and program integrity failures. Deferring oversight to a patchwork of 50 state regimes will worsen these issues. Rather than deregulating quality standards, ACF must retain federal baselines while strengthening grantee financial and management auditing, specifically targeting local grantee vulnerabilities such as those documented at Albina Head Start in Portland, Oregon.
II. Statutory Mandate & Impermissible Subdelegation
The Head Start Act explicitly mandates that the Secretary establish and enforce uniform national performance standards to guarantee high-quality early childhood education (42 U.S.C. § 9836a). Deferring core quality controls—ratios, class sizes, and teacher qualifications—entirely to state licensing constitutes an unlawful subdelegation of federal duty.
Under Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo, 144 S. Ct. 2244 (2024), courts independently enforce statutory boundaries without deferring to administrative interpretations. The Head Start Act does not authorize ACF to abdicate its duty to establish nationwide standards. Replacing uniform federal baselines with variable state rules violates express statutory intent and risks creating severe regional disparities in early childhood education quality.
III. APA Violations: Arbitrary & Capricious Decision-Making
Under APA 5 U.S.C. § 706(2)(A), rulemaking must reflect reasoned decision-making grounded in the administrative record (State Farm, 463 U.S. 29).
1. Lack of Empirical Support: ACF offers no empirical evidence showing that eliminating maximum group sizes, ratios, and staff qualification baselines will preserve educational quality or safety. Decades of early childhood research confirm that lower child-to-staff ratios and qualified educators directly drive positive developmental outcomes.
2. Failure to Address Program Integrity: Rescinding quality floors without strengthening fiscal and operational oversight fails to address existing grantee vulnerabilities, creating an unreasonable risk of administrative failure across local programs.
IV. Local Case Study: Program Integrity Gaps (Albina Head Start)
Ongoing management, labor, and financial oversight issues at local grantees like Albina Head Start in Portland, Oregon, illustrate the danger of relaxing federal oversight. When federal compliance checks weaken, local program governance degrades, directly harming service delivery to vulnerable children. ACF must not remove federal safety and quality floors when local grantee oversight is already under strain.
V. Statutory Conflict: English-Only Mandate
The proposed English-only instructional provision conflicts directly with 42 U.S.C. § 9837a, which requires Head Start programs to support the developmental and linguistic needs of dual-language learners. Forcing English-only instruction deprives non-English speaking children of primary-language acquisition support during critical developmental windows, raising equal educational opportunity and statutory alignment concerns.
VI. Requested Action & Specific Modifications
ACF should modify the proposed rule as follows:
1. Retain National Quality Floors: Preserve standardized federal class size maximums, adult-child ratios, and staff education baselines across all programs.
2. Enhance Auditing & Grantee Integrity: Replace deregulation with targeted management and financial audit guidelines for grantees experiencing governance or compliance challenges (e.g., regional audits modeled on issues identified at Albina Head Start).
3. Withdraw English-Only Requirements: Eliminate restrictions on primary-language instruction to comply with 42 U.S.C. § 9837a.
4. Target Administrative Overhead Directly: Maintain proposed caps on executive and administrative costs without degrading frontline classroom quality or safety.
VII. Conclusion
Rescinding federal quality standards will not resolve Head Start’s management challenges; it will exacerbate them. ACF must withdraw the proposed deregulatory provisions, preserve national quality floors, and focus regulatory resources on strengthening financial accountability and local program integrity.

Dismantling Federal Quality and Safety Standards: Deferring teacher-child ratios, group sizes, and transportation practices entirely to state licensing standards undermines Head Start's 60-year legacy as a national benchmark for early childhood education. Children in every state deserve equal access to safe, low-ratio classrooms and evidence-based curricula, regardless of local variations in state regulations.
Weakening Protections for Vulnerable Children: Removing federal discipline guidelines and inclusion standards risks disproportionately harming children with developmental delays or special needs. Furthermore, eliminating self-reporting options for families experiencing homelessness creates unnecessary barriers to immediate enrollment for children in urgent need.
English-Only Mandates: Mandating English-only instruction disregards established research on early childhood language acquisition and creates barriers for dual-language learning children and their families in our multi-cultural communities.
Head Start's strength lies in its comprehensive support for the whole child and family. Stripping away core performance standards will degrade program quality and put children at risk. title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-16134
printtext:
I am writing in strong opposition to the proposed changes to the Head Start Program Performance Standards. I am a former Head Start child, and I know firsthand how important this program can be for children and families experiencing poverty.

Head Start is not simply preschool. Its comprehensive model combines early education with health, nutrition, developmental, disability, and family-support services. Federal performance standards ensure that children receive these services consistently, regardless of where they live.

I am particularly concerned about eliminating or weakening federal requirements governing:

* Class sizes and teacher-child ratios;
* Medical, dental, vision, and hearing screenings;
* Early learning standards for literacy, mathematics, and social-emotional development;
* Services and protections for children with disabilities; and
* Family engagement and support services that help families address barriers associated with poverty.

These are not unnecessary red tape. They are basic protections that define what a high-quality Head Start program provides.

I understand the goal of reducing unnecessary administrative burdens and allowing programs to respond to local needs. However, flexibility should not come at the expense of a consistent minimum standard. “Local control” without a strong federal baseline risks creating a patchwork system in which the quality and comprehensiveness of services depend on a child's state or community.

That is especially troubling because Head Start exists to address inequality. A child living in poverty should not have fewer educational, health, developmental, or family-support opportunities simply because they live in an area with weaker standards.

These changes could also create significant economic costs that will not appear immediately on a federal budget. When children receive less effective early education or lack access to health and developmental screenings, schools may face greater costs for remediation, tutoring, special education, and other interventions later. Untreated health problems can become more expensive to address. Families without comprehensive support may need greater assistance from other public programs. Over the long term, reduced educational attainment and earnings can mean lower workforce productivity and less tax revenue, while increasing economic instability can perpetuate poverty across generations. In other words, reducing investment in children today can shift substantially greater costs onto schools, health care systems, social services, employers, and taxpayers tomorrow.

The long-term stakes are significant. High-quality early childhood programs can improve educational and economic outcomes and help interrupt cycles of poverty. Weakening the standards that support program quality risks reducing those benefits for future generations.

Most importantly, I think about the children currently enrolled in Head Start and those who will need it in the future. I was once one of those children. Head Start represented an investment in my future at a time when my family had fewer resources. Children today deserve that same opportunity.

I urge the Department of Health and Human Services and the Administration for Children and Families to reject these proposed changes and preserve strong federal Head Start performance standards.

At minimum, federal standards should continue to guarantee appropriate class sizes and staffing, comprehensive health services and screenings, high-quality early learning, meaningful services for children with disabilities, and family engagement and support.

Head Start has served children and families for more than 60 years. We should improve and strengthen a program that works—not remove the standards that help make it work.

title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-16134
printtext:
Dear Office of Head Start:
Thank you for all that you're doing to support children across the country. I am submitting this comment as a member of the Board of Trustees for Children's Home Society of New Jersey, a nonprofit organization that has proudly operated Head Start and Early Head Start programs serving vulnerable children and families for many years.

I appreciate the Administration's efforts to review existing regulations and reduce unnecessary administrative burden. Greater flexibility for local programs, where appropriate, can allow providers to focus more time and resources on serving children and supporting families.

However, I have significant concerns regarding the proposal to reduce the allowable administrative cost cap from 15% to 5%.

Administrative costs are not simply "overhead." They support the essential infrastructure required to operate safe, accountable, high-quality early childhood programs, including financial management, human resources, technology, compliance, facilities, payroll, background checks, enrollment, and program oversight. These functions are fundamental to protecting children, ensuring responsible stewardship of federal funds, and maintaining high-quality services.
Reducing the cap to 5% would create significant financial and operational challenges for many Head Start providers. Nationally, the average administrative cost is substantially higher than 5 percent, demonstrating that this proposed limit does not reflect the actual cost of responsibly operating a comprehensive Head Start program.

I respectfully urge the Department to retain the current 15% administrative cap or adopt a more realistic threshold that reflects the operational requirements of modern Head Start programs. While waiver provisions are helpful, providers should not be forced to rely on waivers simply to maintain the infrastructure necessary to deliver quality services.

I also encourage the Department to carefully consider the potential impact of the proposed English-only instruction requirement on communities serving large numbers of dual-language learners. Supporting English acquisition is an important goal, but preserving opportunities for children to build upon their home language is also supported by decades of research in early childhood education.

Thank you for the opportunity to provide comments on this important proposed rule. I appreciate your consideration and your continued commitment to ensuring that Head Start remains a strong, high-quality program serving children and families across the country.

title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-16134
printtext:
We strongly encourage the removal of the restriction that prevents programs from suspending children when serious or persistent behaviors create an unsafe environment. Aggressive and challenging behaviors are increasing, and programs are increasingly faced with situations that can become dangerous for children, staff, and the program as a whole.

When programs are prohibited from temporarily suspending a child when necessary, staff may be placed in situations they are not qualified or adequately trained to safely manage. This can create significant safety concerns for the child exhibiting the behavior, other children, classroom staff, and the program.

Programs should be allowed to follow applicable state child care licensing regulations when determining appropriate responses to serious behavioral incidents. When Head Start requirements and state child care licensing regulations conflict, programs are placed in an extremely difficult position and may be unable to fully comply with both sets of requirements. This conflict can create additional risks and administrative challenges rather than improving outcomes for children and families.

Allowing programs reasonable flexibility to utilize temporary suspension when warranted, while still requiring appropriate documentation, family engagement, behavioral support, mental health consultation, and efforts to identify less restrictive interventions, would provide programs with a necessary safety option.

The goal is not to exclude children because of challenging behavior. The goal is to ensure that programs have the ability to respond appropriately when a situation presents a serious safety concern and when other interventions have not been sufficient. Programs need clear, consistent guidance that allows them to protect children and staff while remaining in compliance with both Head Start and state licensing requirements.

title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-16134
printtext:
I oppose key provisions of the proposed rule because they would weaken Head Start Program Performance Standards in a manner inconsistent with 42 U.S.C. § 9836a(a)(2)(C)(ii), which prohibits any revision that reduces the quality, scope, or types of services provided under Head Start.
While reducing administrative burden is appropriate, this rule goes further by weakening core federal standards governing staffing, safety, instructional time, health services, disability supports, and family services.
I request withdrawal or substantial revision of the rule. At minimum, ACF must retain enforceable federal baseline standards and provide a provision-by-provision analysis demonstrating compliance with 42 U.S.C. § 9836a(a)(2)(C)(ii).
I. Statutory Compliance Requirement
ACF must ensure that no regulatory revision reduces service quality, scope, or type under 42 U.S.C. § 9836a(a)(2)(C)(ii). The NPRM does not provide a sufficient analysis demonstrating compliance.
Requested Actions
ACF should:
Publish a crosswalk of all changes to Performance Standards;
Identify whether each change affects service quality, scope, or type;
Provide a cumulative impact analysis; and
Support findings with evidence of no service reduction.
II. Federal Baseline Standards
The following standards must be retained or replaced with equivalent enforceable protections to comply with 42 U.S.C. § 9836a(a)(2)(C)(ii):
A. Staffing and Group Size
Maintain federal staff-to-child ratios, group size limits, and workforce qualifications sufficient to preserve service quality.
B. Safety and Discipline
Retain limits on suspension, prohibition on expulsion for behavior, required behavioral supports, and transportation safety protections.
C. Instructional Time
Maintain minimum instructional hours and service duration to prevent reductions in educational scope or intensity.
D. Health and Mental Health
Retain screening timelines, referral follow-up, and required mental health consultation services.
E. Disability Services
Preserve Head Start-specific disability coordination, transition planning, and service integration beyond baseline IDEA requirements.
F. Family Services
Maintain home-visit frequency, caseload standards, and family engagement requirements.
G. Language Access
Remove any English-only mandate unless ACF demonstrates no reduction in service type or quality under 42 U.S.C. § 9836a(a)(2)(C)(ii). Preserve bilingual and dual-language instruction.
H. Administration
Retain safeguards ensuring administrative cost limits do not impair service delivery or compliance capacity.
III. Cost Savings vs. Service Reductions
The rule does not clearly distinguish administrative savings from reductions in services. ACF must separate efficiency gains from any change affecting service quality, scope, or type and evaluate each under 42 U.S.C. § 9836a(a)(2)(C)(ii).
IV. Program Integrity
Without enforceable federal baselines, the rule risks reducing staffing, instructional time, and service consistency, leading to interstate variability and potential statutory noncompliance.
Conclusion
Head Start is a national program designed to ensure consistent minimum services for low-income children. Administrative simplification must not reduce service quality, scope, or type as prohibited by 42 U.S.C. § 9836a(a)(2)(C)(ii).
I respectfully request withdrawal or substantial revision of the rule and retention of federal baseline standards with a full statutory compliance analysis.

title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-16134
printtext:
I respectfully submit this comment in opposition to the proposed changes in Proposed regs that would remove language encouraging Head Start programs to participate in state Quality Rating and Improvement Systems (QRIS). The proposed rule states that programs would retain the option to participate in QRIS but would no longer be encouraged to do so through Federal regulation.

While QRIS is not the sole measure of program quality, it serves as an important framework for continuous quality improvement, accountability, and alignment across early childhood systems. Head Start programs have long been leaders in quality, and participation in QRIS helps connect Head Start with broader state early childhood initiatives, professional development systems, coaching supports, and quality improvement efforts. Removing the expectation for engagement in QRIS risks weakening these critical partnerships and creating further fragmentation between Head Start and other early childhood programs.

The proposed rule notes that research has found mixed evidence regarding the relationship between QRIS ratings and child outcomes and concludes that QRIS has not clearly demonstrated a meaningful impact on child outcomes. However, this perspective overlooks the broader purpose and value of QRIS. QRIS provides a structured process for programs to assess quality, implement improvements, engage in professional development, and monitor progress over time. Many states use QRIS as a common framework for aligning standards, coordinating resources, and supporting providers across mixed-delivery systems. These benefits extend beyond a single child outcome measure and contribute to stronger early learning systems overall.

For Head Start programs, participation in QRIS supports collaboration with state agencies, child care providers, public pre-kindergarten programs, and other community partners. These connections are especially important as programs work to coordinate services, improve transitions for children and families, and maximize the use of limited resources. Removing Federal support for QRIS participation sends a message that quality improvement efforts are optional rather than integral to maintaining high standards of service.

Head Start has historically been recognized as a model of comprehensive, high-quality early childhood education. Rather than reducing emphasis on QRIS participation, the Office of Head Start should continue to encourage engagement with state quality systems while allowing programs flexibility in how they participate. This approach would preserve local control while maintaining strong connections between Head Start and the broader early childhood infrastructure.

For these reasons, I urge the Office of Head Start to retain regulatory language supporting participation in Quality Rating and Improvement Systems and to recognize QRIS as an important mechanism for continuous quality improvement, cross-system collaboration, and accountability in early childhood education. Maintaining these connections will help ensure that Head Start remains aligned with state early learning systems and continues to provide high-quality services to children and families.

Thank you for the opportunity to comment on this proposed rule.

title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-16134
printtext:
I respectfully submit the following comment regarding the proposed rule titled “Reducing Federal Burden for Head Start Programs” (FR Doc. 2026‑16134). While I support efforts to streamline administrative requirements, I urge the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) to ensure that regulatory revisions continue to uphold the safety, developmental needs, and well‑being of children and staff within Head Start and Early Head Start programs.

1. Authority for Teachers to Make Suspension or Expulsion Decisions in Cases of Severe Safety Risk

I request that HHS include language affirming that teachers are permitted to make the decision to suspend or expel a student who is severely unsafe, including situations where the child’s behavior presents an immediate and substantial risk of harm.

To protect both children and staff, the regulation should explicitly state that abuse, aggression, or violent conduct toward teachers or other children is not permitted under any circumstances. When such conduct occurs, teachers—who are directly responsible for maintaining a safe learning environment—must retain the authority to initiate suspension or expulsion based on professional judgment.

To ensure clarity and accountability, I recommend regulatory language that:

Defines “severely unsafe behavior” as conduct posing an immediate likelihood of physical injury, including physical aggression or abusive behavior toward staff or peers.

Permits teachers to initiate temporary suspension or expulsion when such behavior occurs, subject to prompt administrative review.

Requires documentation of the incident and timely notification to families.

This amendment would preserve the broader prohibition on exclusionary discipline while ensuring necessary protections in rare but critical safety situations.

2. Mandatory Teacher‑to‑Child Ratios for All States

I strongly urge HHS to adopt uniform, mandatory minimum staffing ratios applicable nationwide. Specifically:

A teacher for every five (5) children ages 3–5.

A teacher for every three (3) children ages 0–3.

These ratios reflect the developmental needs of young children and the level of supervision required to maintain safety and high‑quality instruction. Establishing federal minimums would reduce disparities across states and ensure equitable access to safe, developmentally appropriate care.

3. Mandatory Teacher Aide in Every Classroom

I further recommend that HHS require a teacher aide in every classroom as a mandatory staffing component. A classroom aide is essential to:

Maintain safe supervision during transitions, toileting, and crisis situations.

Support individualized instruction and social‑emotional interventions.

Ensure compliance with safety protocols and emergency procedures.

This requirement would strengthen program quality, reduce teacher burnout, and enhance the overall safety and stability of the classroom environment.

Conclusion

These recommendations align with Head Start’s statutory mission to promote school readiness, ensure child safety, and support high‑quality early learning environments. Incorporating these provisions into the final rule would provide teachers with the necessary authority to act in urgent safety situations, establish consistent national staffing standards, and reinforce the structural supports required for safe and effective instruction.

Thank you for the opportunity to comment on this important rulemaking.

Respectfully submitted,
A Head Start Teacher

title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-16134
