I am deeply concerned about the proposed "deregulation" of Head Start. I was a Head Start teacher up until recently, and I am concerned that the chosen policies to deregulate will affect the safety and well-being of some of the country's most vulnerable children and families. Because Head Start is specifically an anti-poverty program, the students who attend have higher needs than students in other schools. They need the extra protections that things like strict student:teacher ratios, extra background checks, etc provide. Teachers need to be especially qualified to teach this group of children, who attend school with a variety of needs and trauma caused directly by poverty.

While the proposal says that states can continue to uphold the already established guidelines if they choose, I wonder how they will be able to pay for it without the support of the federal government. It doesn't seem fair that a child in need in Massachusetts and a child in need on West Virginia don't have the same access to the same level of quality education. This is why federal guidelines are important. Again, because Head Start is more than a preschool program - it exists as an anti-poverty program.

While it is true that there is research that says gains made in Head Start disappear by third grade, that is not necessarily the point of Head Start. The point of Head Start is to level the playing field so that children living in poverty do not have a disadvantage entering kindergarten.

In regards to "giving parents more control", families have always had a strong connection to the Head Start program. Home visits occur twice per year, policy counsel and family engagement events happen multiple times per year, and in my own program, families were invited to share input on what students learned. Head Start is already doing these things.

I am confused as to why we are deregulating safety standards such as ratios, background checks an qualifications of teachers, but using resources to provide information about why marriage is important. I am not opposed to marriage and am married myself, but I think that if we really are trying to save money, why add? If you go forward with resources about the importance of marriage it will be equally important to include resources on what it looks like when marriage is unhealthy and how to find support for victims of domestic abuse. I have encountered enough two parent homes during my time at Head Start where the marriage was toxic. We should not be encouraging anyone to stay and "work it out" with someone who puts them and the children in danger for the sake of having a two parent home. It will be VERY important for us to have resources available for those who need to leave a relationship, and to empower single parents and other caregivers.

Once again, I oppose the proposed changes to the Head Start program. These changes reduce the quality of the program. These proposals are not "efficiency" as much as they are a cheap shell of what this program really is. Our most vulnerable families deserve better.

title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-16134
printtext:
Head Start is one of the few rigorously studied early‑childhood programs that consistently demonstrates positive, long‑term outcomes. Its benefits extend far beyond kindergarten readiness: participation is associated with improved lifelong health, higher adult earnings, and a reduced likelihood of involvement with the juvenile or criminal justice system. Weakening Head Start standards will almost certainly diminish these proven effects. Additionally, the states most likely to adopt only the minimum requirements are, unfortunately, the same states where students already face the greatest academic challenges.

Particularly harmful is the decision to increase student‑to‑teacher ratios. Many children in Head Start have experienced significant adversity linked to poverty, which often manifests as challenging classroom behaviors. Increasing class sizes will make it harder for teachers to provide the individualized support these children need and risks driving already scarce early‑childhood educators out of the profession. And discontinuing the vital ancillary services would make the teachers jobs immeasurably harder.

Compounding the problem, current Head Start funding does not come close to covering the true cost of delivering this intensive, high‑touch program. Maintaining the 15% administrative reimbursement is essential if programs are to uphold the level of quality, oversight, and accountability that Head Start rightly demands.

Please recognize the extreme repercussions of the changes proposed and reconsider this drastic reduction in the very elements that have made this program tremendously successful over the last 60 years.

I am writing to respectfully oppose the proposed rule, “Reducing Federal Burden for Head Start Programs.”

I have worked in Head Start for many years, first as a teacher and now as a Center Director. I have seen firsthand how the Head Start Program Performance Standards help us provide consistent, high-quality services to children and families. These standards are not simply regulations on paper. They guide the work we do every day to keep children safe, support their development, partner with families, and ensure that children receive the comprehensive services they need.

I understand the importance of reducing unnecessary paperwork and administrative burden. However, reducing paperwork should not mean reducing protections and quality standards for children.

I am particularly concerned about removing or weakening federal requirements related to health and safety, staff-to-child ratios, mental health services, family support, services for children with disabilities, staff qualifications, and support for children who are learning more than one language.

Head Start serves some of our country’s most vulnerable children and families. A child’s access to high-quality and safe early education should not depend on which state or community they live in. Strong national standards help ensure that every Head Start child receives a consistent level of care, safety, education, and support.

As an early childhood educator and Head Start leader, I have seen the difference that comprehensive Head Start services make. We do much more than prepare children academically. We support children’s social-emotional development, health, nutrition, mental health, disabilities, language development, and families.

I respectfully ask HHS to preserve the Head Start Program Performance Standards that protect quality, safety, comprehensive services, and equitable opportunities for children and families. Please work with Head Start educators, families, program leaders, and communities to identify ways to reduce unnecessary administrative burden without eliminating the standards that have helped make Head Start successful for generations.

Our children deserve strong protections, high expectations, and the same opportunity to receive a high-quality Head Start experience regardless of where they live.

Thank you for considering my perspective and for the opportunity to comment.

Re: Reducing Federal Burden for Head Start Programs (RIN: 0970-AD30)

Dear Secretary Kennedy,

I am writing to urge the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services to protect the Head Start Program Performance Standards and withdraw the proposed rule.

I work across Arizona to improve the way our state meets the needs of families. I've spoken with many families whose children and families have been transformed by Head Start. I live in a rural community and a child care desert. Parents report difficulty navigating finances in early childhood. K-12 teacher report a lack of readiness in kindergarten, which affects all students. Head Start is s solution. When rural communities struggle to find child care, preschool, and other early learning environments, they often do have Head Start. We don't need less of the program - we need more!

The proposed rule would fundamentally upend those standards and make it harder for Head Start programs to deliver the high-quality services children and families deserve.

Specifically, the proposal would:

- Eliminate research-based standards that support educational quality, child safety and healthy development.
- Remove evidence-based teacher-child ratio requirements that support individualized learning and safe learning environments.
- Reduce protections and services for infants, children with disabilities and multilingual learners.
- Limit opportunities for parents to shape their local Head Start programs.
- Make it more difficult for communities, especially rural communities, to sustain high-quality Head Start services.

For these reasons, I respectfully urge HHS to withdraw this proposed rule.

Thank you for considering my comments.

Sincerely,

Molly Peterson
Mother of two young boys, ages 1 and 4
Impact Strategist at Prevent Child Abuse Arizona

title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-16134
printtext:
Comment on Parent Committees and Parent Voice
I strongly oppose the proposal to make parent committees optional. In many Head Start programs, parents’ voices are not consistently heard or meaningfully considered by the organizations operating the programs. Parent committees provide an important, structured opportunity for parents to raise concerns, share recommendations, volunteer, and help guide services so they meet the needs of children and families.
Making parent committees optional would give organizations a clear path to eliminate or weaken one of the primary avenues through which parents participate in program decision-making. If a Head Start organization is allowed to make parent committee participation optional, there will likely be far less parent involvement than there is now. Without a consistent, required structure for engagement, many parents may not know how to participate, may not attend meetings, or may not have an opportunity to contribute their time and skills to the program.
This reduction in participation could also affect a program’s ability to meet its required 20 percent non-Federal match, often referred to as the in-kind requirement. Parent volunteer hours, meeting participation, and other contributions are important sources of in-kind support. When parent committees are required and parents are encouraged to participate, programs have a reliable way to document volunteer involvement and community support. If parent committees become optional, fewer parents may volunteer, and programs may have greater difficulty meeting the required in-kind match.
Although the proposed rule would retain statutory requirements for governing bodies, Policy Councils, and Policy Committees where applicable, those bodies do not replace the direct, regular, and accessible participation provided by center-based parent committees. Parents should not have to rely solely on the organization’s governing body or staff to decide whether their concerns are heard. Parent committees create an essential connection between individual families, program centers, and the broader Head Start governance structure.
Removing this requirement would likely reduce parent participation, weaken transparency, limit volunteer contributions, and make Head Start programs less responsive and less effective. The committee participation requirement needs to be mandatory, not optional. A mandatory parent committee helps ensure that every center provides parents with a meaningful voice, a regular opportunity to participate, and a clear way to support their children’s program.
I recommend that ACF retain the requirement for each Head Start center to establish and support a mandatory parent committee. The final rule should require programs to provide reasonable meeting times, transportation, interpretation, child care when appropriate, and other supports that reduce barriers to participation. Programs should also document parent concerns and recommendations, provide written responses when appropriate, and show how parent input was considered in program planning and decision-making.
Parents are their children’s first and most important teachers. Their participation must be strengthened—not reduced—within the Head Start program.

printtext:
I would like to provide an additional comment specifically about family engagement and parent voice in Head Start.

As both a former Head Start parent and someone who has spent the past eight years working as a Family Support Specialist in early childhood education, I have experienced family engagement from both sides. I have been the parent receiving support, and I have also had the privilege of supporting families as they set goals, access resources, advocate for their children, and become more involved in their children's education.

I am concerned about reducing federal requirements related to family engagement because meaningful family engagement does not happen simply because programs believe it is important. Strong standards help ensure that every family has opportunities to participate, build relationships with staff, identify their strengths and goals, and have a voice in decisions affecting their children.

Families come to early childhood programs with different experiences, cultures, languages, resources, and challenges. Some parents may already feel comfortable speaking up, while others may need someone to recognize their strengths and invite them into the conversation. When we intentionally create those opportunities, parents begin to see themselves differently. They realize that they are their child's first and most important advocate.

I have seen families accomplish goals that extend far beyond their child's classroom. I have seen parents gain confidence, learn how to navigate systems, connect with community resources, and advocate for what their children need. Those outcomes may be difficult to measure on a compliance checklist, but they are an important part of what makes Head Start successful.

My own journey demonstrates the long-term impact of family engagement. I entered Head Start as a parent looking for opportunities for my children. Through that experience, I found my own voice and eventually a professional calling supporting other families. Eight years later, I am still working in this field and advocating for children and families.

I understand and support efforts to reduce unnecessary paperwork that takes staff away from families. However, there is an important difference between reducing paperwork and reducing expectations for meaningful family engagement. We should make it easier for staff to spend time building relationships with families without weakening the standards that ensure those relationships remain a priority.

I respectfully ask HHS and ACF to preserve strong federal expectations for family engagement and parent voice as the proposed regulations are reconsidered. Where administrative requirements can be simplified without harming families, I support doing so. But the answer should be giving staff more time to engage families, not making meaningful family engagement less central to Head Start.

Head Start should continue to recognize parents not simply as recipients of services, but as partners, leaders, and advocates with the ability to create lasting change for their children, their families, and their communities.

title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-16134
printtext:
I respectfully oppose the proposed rule, Reducing Federal Burden for Head Start Programs.

While reducing unnecessary administrative burden is a worthwhile goal, this proposal goes far beyond streamlining paperwork. It would rescind and replace nearly the entire Head Start Program Performance Standards framework and shift substantial authority over program operations to states and local entities.

Head Start was created as a comprehensive federal program to support children's education, health, nutrition, development, and family well-being. The current performance standards help ensure that children and families receive a consistent baseline of quality services regardless of where they live. Eliminating detailed federal standards in favor of a patchwork of state requirements risks creating significant inequities in access, safety, and program quality.

I am particularly concerned about the proposal to make parent committees optional. Parents are central to the Head Start model, and meaningful family engagement has been a defining feature of the program for decades. While statutory governance requirements would remain, removing regulatory requirements for parent committees would likely reduce opportunities for family leadership and shared decision-making, especially for families whose voices are often underrepresented in public systems.

I am also concerned that the proposal understates the importance of the comprehensive services model. Head Start is more than a preschool program. It connects families to developmental screenings, health services, nutrition support, family services, and school readiness resources. These services are fundamental to the program's mission and are especially important for children experiencing poverty and other barriers to opportunity.

The rule's projected cost savings and expansion of funded slots should not be viewed as sufficient justification for removing longstanding quality standards. Serving more children is important, but the goal of Head Start is to provide high-quality, comprehensive services that support healthy development and school readiness. The proposed rule does not adequately demonstrate that these protections can be removed without harming service quality or increasing disparities across states and communities.

For these reasons, I urge ACF to withdraw or substantially revise the proposed rule, retain core federal performance standards, preserve strong family engagement requirements, and maintain federal safeguards that have helped make Head Start a nationally recognized model for comprehensive early childhood services.

Thank you for considering my comment.

title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-16134

Dear Office of Head Start:
Thank you for all that you're doing to support children across the country. I am submitting this comment as a member of the Board of Trustees for Children's Home Society of New Jersey, a nonprofit organization that has proudly operated Head Start and Early Head Start programs serving vulnerable children and families for many years.

I appreciate the Administration's efforts to review existing regulations and reduce unnecessary administrative burden. Greater flexibility for local programs, where appropriate, can allow providers to focus more time and resources on serving children and supporting families.

Administrative costs are not simply "overhead." They support the essential infrastructure required to operate safe, accountable, high-quality early childhood programs, including financial management, human resources, technology, compliance, facilities, payroll, background checks, enrollment, and program oversight. These functions are fundamental to protecting children, ensuring responsible stewardship of federal funds, and maintaining high-quality services.
Reducing the cap to 5% would create significant financial and operational challenges for many Head Start providers. Nationally, the average administrative cost is substantially higher than 5 percent, demonstrating that this proposed limit does not reflect the actual cost of responsibly operating a comprehensive Head Start program.

I respectfully urge the Department to retain the current 15% administrative cap or adopt a more realistic threshold that reflects the operational requirements of modern Head Start programs. While waiver provisions are helpful, providers should not be forced to rely on waivers simply to maintain the infrastructure necessary to deliver quality services.

I also encourage the Department to carefully consider the potential impact of the proposed English-only instruction requirement on communities serving large numbers of dual-language learners. Thank you for the opportunity to provide comments on this important proposed rule. I appreciate your consideration and your continued commitment to ensuring that Head Start remains a strong, high-quality program serving children and families across the country.

Agency: Administration for Children and Families (ACF), Department of Health and Human Services (HHS)

To: Administration for Children and Families, U.S. Department of Health and Human Services
Re: Public Comment on Proposed Rule: Reducing Federal Burden for Head Start Programs

Date: August 9, 2026
Submitted By: Concerned Citizen

1. Introduction & Overview
I am submitting comments on the proposed rule, Reducing Federal Burden for Head Start Programs. As a mother and concerned citizen, I care deeply about the quality, accessibility, and long-term impact of Head Start for low-income children and families. While I support administrative efficiency and prioritizing children’s health and nutrition, I strongly urge HHS to reconsider provisions that risk diluting the comprehensive standards that make Head Start effective.

2. Specific Feedback on Key Proposed Provisions

* Classroom Overcrowding & State Ratios
I am deeply concerned about eliminating federal limits on staff-to-child ratios and maximum class sizes. Head Start maintains low ratios (1:4 for toddlers, 1:8 to 1:10 for preschoolers) to ensure safe, individualized care. Defaulting to state licensing minimums—which often permit far higher ratios—will lead to classroom overcrowding. Overcrowded rooms make it nearly impossible for teachers to provide the specialized attention, trauma-informed care, and early intervention low-income children need to thrive.

* Administrative Overhead Cap (15% to 5%)
While directing maximum funding to classrooms is a worthy goal, reducing the administrative cap from 15% to 5% is unrealistic for local grantees, especially rural and smaller nonprofits. These funds cover required audits, regulatory compliance, legal oversight, and evaluations. A strict 5% cap without reduced reporting requirements will create operational bottlenecks or force program closures.

* Comprehensive Family Supports & Health Screenings
Head Start’s success stems from treating child development holistically by combining education with health screenings, parent engagement, and family support. Removing federal requirements for structured health screenings, home visits, and family goal-setting weakens the safety net for children experiencing trauma, housing instability, or developmental delays.

* Instructional Language Flexibility
Mandating English-only instruction (outside of tribal programs) ignores extensive research on dual-language learners. Young children build literacy most effectively when their home language is supported alongside English. Local programs need flexibility to offer dual-language support based on community demographics.

* Nutrition & Physical Activity
I support offering whole foods and guaranteeing daily physical activity (30 minutes per 3.5 hours of classroom time). However, HHS must ensure local centers receive adequate funding and flexibility to source whole foods and adapt activities for children with physical disabilities or severe weather constraints.

3. Conclusion & Recommendations
Head Start’s strength lies in combining high federal standards with local delivery. Rather than replacing federal standards with varying state minimums, I urge HHS to:
1. Retain federal baselines for maximum class sizes, staff-to-child ratios, and teacher qualifications.
2. Set a phased, realistic administrative cap (e.g., 10%) rather than an immediate drop to 5%.
3. Maintain mandatory comprehensive health, dental, and developmental screening frameworks.

Thank you for the opportunity to comment on this critical rule.

Sincerely,
Concerned Citizen

Head Start has, for the past 60 years, been the trailblazer for all other Early Childhood Programs nationwide because it is a FEDERAL program and is not left in the hands of irresponsible, ever-changing and inconsistent State governments. In Indiana, Early Childhood Education has been systematically deconstructed and destroyed over the past year and a half. The resulting consequences have been swift and disturbingly negative. This statement is full of commentary about returning educational decisions to parents. You want to rescind performance standards 1301-1305. title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-16134
printtext: Cutting federal Head Start standards risks eliminating critical health, dental, and developmental screenings, weakening teacher-to-student ratios, and lowering the quality of care for over 700,000 vulnerable low-income children. Critics and educators argue that deregulation removes essential safeguards and leaves children without vital wraparound support. Current rules mandate checks for vision, hearing, immunizations, and mental health. Basic preventative care like daily tooth-brushing routines and dental exams could be lost, which is particularly harmful in rural areas where alternative dental care is hours away. Staff screen children for developmental delays and disabilities, helping catch issues early. Federal limits on class sizes and supervision numbers would be erased, letting states or local groups apply looser rules. Without specific federal protections, children with disabilities face a higher risk of suspension or expulsion if local programs lack strict oversight. Shifting rules entirely to state and local levels could create a patchwork of lower-quality care, serving as a step backward from a proven national gold standard.

title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-16134
printtext:
I am strongly opposed to the proposed changes to Early Head Start. Early Head Start is not simply a childcare program—it provides children and families with access to early education, developmental support, family resources, and a strong foundation during some of the most important years of a child’s life.

A child who attended Head Start or Early Head Start may be in third grade and performing at a third-grade level today. But what you may not see is where that child started. You may not see the developmental progress, growth, support, and early intervention that happened along the way. Without Head Start/Early Head Start, that child may not have had the same opportunity to reach grade level. We cannot measure the success of the program only by where a child is today without looking at where that child began.

Early Head Start is also not daycare. It is an early childhood education and family-support program. Moving away from the model that allows programs to meet families where they are and going back to a strictly center-based approach does not necessarily benefit parents or children. Families have different needs, schedules, circumstances, and barriers, and Early Head Start should continue to provide services in ways that actually support the families it serves.

The documentation and data collected by Early Head Start staff are also not meaningless paperwork—they are part of our job and an important part of the work we do. Documentation allows us to track children’s development, identify needs, monitor progress, communicate with families, and ensure that children are receiving the services and support they need. Taking those responsibilities away could take away an important part of how we know whether we are truly making a difference.

For many families, Early Head Start is the difference between having access to essential early education and family services and going without. Changes that reduce access, services, staffing, or the ability to properly document and support children could have a lasting impact on infants, toddlers, parents, and communities.

We should be investing more in Early Head Start—not making changes that could weaken the very services that have helped so many children succeed.

Every child deserves the opportunity to have a safe, supportive, educational start in life, regardless of their family’s income or circumstances. Please listen to the families, educators, and communities who depend on Early Head Start.

I am strongly against these proposed changes. Our youngest children and their families deserve better, and the work of Early Head Start deserves to be protected.

title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-16134
printtext:
I oppose the proposed Head Start rule, Docket No. ACF-2026-0595. I am a school psychologist who works directly with children and families, and I strongly believe that Head Start is an essential program that should be protected and strengthened, not diminished.

High-quality early childhood education can have a profound impact on a child’s development and readiness for school. Children enter kindergarten with vastly different levels of exposure to language, literacy, numbers, classroom routines, social interaction, and structured learning. Preschool programs help reduce those disparities before children ever enter a kindergarten classroom. Research has repeatedly demonstrated positive effects of high-quality early childhood education, particularly for children from economically disadvantaged or otherwise at-risk backgrounds.

Head Start is especially important because it reaches children who might otherwise have little or no access to early childhood education. Without programs like Head Start, the children who could benefit most from early intervention may instead begin kindergarten already at a disadvantage compared with peers whose families were able to afford private preschool or had access to other high-quality early learning opportunities. We should be working to close those opportunity gaps, not widening them.

Head Start is also imperative for working families. Parents should not have to choose between maintaining employment and providing their children with developmentally appropriate early learning experiences. Accessible early childhood programs support both children and the economic stability of their families.

As a mental health professional, I am also deeply concerned about any changes that weaken protections or supports for young children with disabilities, developmental delays, or behavioral needs. Challenging behavior in young children is often communication of an unmet developmental, emotional, environmental, or disability-related need. Removing a child from an educational setting rather than providing appropriate assessment, intervention, and support does not address that need; it simply removes the child from an opportunity to learn. Early childhood is precisely when we should be intervening and providing support.

Head Start should continue to be available to families, with strong standards for staffing, disability and behavioral supports, health and family services, and developmentally and linguistically appropriate education.

In fact, I believe our country should be moving in the opposite direction. High-quality universal prekindergarten should ultimately be available to every child whose family wants it, regardless of income or ZIP code. Access to early education should not depend upon whether a family can afford private preschool.

Reducing administrative burden is a worthwhile goal when it eliminates unnecessary bureaucracy. It should not come at the expense of educational quality, children’s protections, or access to services. I urge HHS to withdraw or substantially revise provisions of this proposed rule that would weaken Head Start standards or reduce the comprehensive supports available to children and families.

title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-16134
printtext:
Reducing unnecessary administrative burden is an important goal. The question is whether the proposed changes reduce burden while preserving the core features that make Head Start effective. In my view, several provisions do not.

Through my work with Community Equity Collaborative (CEC), a California organization focused on early childhood and community-based systems change, I have worked for years alongside early educators, Head Start programs, families, community organizations, and local government. Duplicative requirements can divert time and resources from children and families. But burden reduction should not come at the expense of quality, workforce stability, or comprehensive support.

WORKFORCE IMPACTS SHOULD BE PART OF THE ANALYSIS
Early childhood programs already face a severe educator shortage. I have worked directly on efforts to strengthen the early educator pipeline, and one lesson is clear: we will not solve that shortage by asking fewer educators to do more.

ACF estimates that the proposed staffing changes would increase the average number of children per teacher by approximately 16 percent while reducing the number of teachers needed by roughly 13 percent. That could make recruitment and retention even harder.

The proposed English-only instruction requirement raises related workforce and family engagement concerns. Bilingual and multilingual educators bring language skills and cultural knowledge that strengthen relationships with families. ACF itself acknowledges that reduced language capacity may "negatively affect communication with non-English speaking families and weaken family engagement."

At a time when programs struggle to recruit staff, policy should expand the educator pool, not narrow it.
Children should develop strong English-language skills. English acquisition and support for a child's home language are complementary goals, not competing ones.

HEAD START'S INTEGRATED MODEL SHOULD BE EVALUATED AS A WHOLE
Head Start's effectiveness comes from the interaction of its supports, not from any single requirement in isolation. Classroom quality, family engagement, mental health services, and early intervention reinforce one another.

Changes to staffing, mental health consultation, family service capacity, language requirements, eligibility procedures, and protections against exclusion may appear modest individually. Taken together, they risk weakening the comprehensive model that distinguishes Head Start from child care alone.

ACF estimates that approximately 8 percent of currently enrolled children could lose eligibility unless their families provide alternative documentation, while acknowledging that families experiencing homelessness may have greater difficulty doing so. Creating new barriers for families Head Start was designed to reach is not simply an administrative change.

FISCAL RESPONSIBILITY SHOULD INCLUDE PREVENTION
A reduction in Head Start expenditures is not necessarily a reduction in taxpayer costs. When needs go unaddressed, families receive less support, classroom quality declines, or experienced educators leave the field, costs can reappear later in public education, health care, and social services.

Some proposed savings may shift costs directly to families. ACF acknowledges that reducing annual hours or days of service may require families to secure alternative child care, resulting in additional costs or lost work time.

Only about 3.7 percent of Head Start grants currently operate at or below the proposed 5 percent administrative cost threshold. Responsible administration, including fiscal oversight, enrollment, data systems, compliance, and organizational leadership, is part of delivering high-quality services.

Administrative savings should not come at the expense of the capacity needed to operate programs effectively and responsibly.

LOCAL FLEXIBILITY SHOULD BUILD ON A MEANINGFUL FEDERAL FLOOR
I strongly support locally designed solutions. But local flexibility and federal standards serve different purposes. Flexibility allows communities to determine how best to achieve outcomes, while federal standards establish the minimum quality and protections children should receive regardless of where they live.

My experience is rooted in California, which has significant early childhood investments and its own regulatory framework. That experience has reinforced for me why a meaningful federal floor matters. A child's Head Start experience should not depend on whether they live in a state with stronger or weaker early childhood standards.

There is a real opportunity to improve Head Start by reducing duplicative requirements that do not improve outcomes while preserving standards that support children, families, and educators.

For these reasons, I urge ACF not to finalize these provisions as proposed. Head Start can be easier to administer without becoming less effective.

title: Comment from The Black Veteran Newsletter, LLC on VA-2026-VACO-0001-0027
printtext:
I respectfully submit the following comments regarding the proposed revision of VA Form 10-8678 under the Paperwork Reduction Act.
The statutory and regulatory authority for the annual clothing allowance under 38 U.S.C. § 1162 and 38 C.F.R. § 3.810 is clear. However, practical access to this benefit remains inconsistent due to gaps in cross-referencing, notification practices, and system integration.
VA does provide information about the clothing allowance on its website and within certain VHA prosthetics processes. However, eligibility is not consistently cross-referenced against service-connected conditions, prescribed medications, or issued appliances. Many veterans prescribed medications for service-connected dermatological conditions, or issued orthopedic appliances that damage outer garments, are never affirmatively notified of potential eligibility.
When a condition is granted service connection and involves appliances or medications that may qualify under 38 C.F.R. § 3.810, VA should include standardized language in the rating decision notification letter advising the veteran of potential eligibility for the annual clothing allowance, along with a direct link to apply.
There is also an equity concern that warrants attention. Women veterans with service-connected gynecological conditions that cause excessive or irregular menstrual bleeding frequently report denial of clothing allowance benefits or lack of notice that they may qualify. In contrast, male veterans with service-connected urinary incontinence or gastrointestinal conditions that result in appliance use or garment damage more commonly receive notification or awards. If clothing damage is the qualifying standard, it must be applied consistently and without gender disparity.
VA should evaluate whether current adjudication guidance and internal training sufficiently address gender-specific medical conditions and their real-world impact on clothing damage.
In addition, veterans should be able to apply electronically through VA.gov, My HealtheVet, and the VA mobile application, with automated annual reminders prior to the August 1 deadline. Improved interoperability between Veterans Benefits Administration and Veterans Health Administration systems would allow appliance issuance, medication profiles, and service-connected conditions to trigger proactive notice.
If the “One VA” framework is to be fully realized, systems must communicate in a way that reduces the burden on veterans rather than requiring them to navigate internal administrative divisions.
Finally, structured veteran user feedback should be incorporated into future redesign efforts. Veterans who rely on this benefit are best positioned to identify barriers in clarity, notification, and functionality.
The annual clothing allowance is a recurring benefit. Improved cross-referencing, equitable application, proactive notice, and integrated technology would significantly enhance its practical utility while reducing administrative burden.
Thank you for the opportunity to provide comment.

EPA testing in the early 1980's resulted in a "Super Fund" site designation with long term mitigation activites initiated. for references sake the level of contaminants was reported to be 4600 ppm at the USDB water supply where as Camp Lejeune was reported to be 460 ppm. To make a point it was 10 times higher at the USDB. In addition to the water supply we were exposed to Asbestos. It was everywhere in the Headquarters building and at the Disciplinary Barracks. Ceiling tiles were asbestos, floor tiles were asbestos, and all the pipe insulation was asbestos. There has been significant research and a refresh on current consideration is now mandated and I personally applaud this effort. title: Comment from Charles Burt on VA-2026-VACO-0001-0031
printtext:
The Honorable Douglas A. Collins
Secretary
U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs
810 Vermont Ave., NW
Washington, DC 20420
Submitted electronically via www.regulations.gov
Subject: Public Comment on Neurodegenerative Disease Review – Docket VA–2026–VACO–0001

Dear Secretary Collins:
My name is Charles A. Burt, Jr, and I am a United States military veteran who served from 1989-2013 in the Army. I am submitting this comment in response to the Department of Veterans Affairs’ notice regarding its review of neurodegenerative diseases and military environmental exposures.
I have been diagnosed with Parkinson’s disease. During my military service, I was exposed to oil well fire fallout, pesticides on my uniform and skin, burn pits, jet fuel, and numerous solvents. At the time, I was not aware of the potential long-term neurological risks associated with these exposures.

Parkinson’s disease has significantly affected my life in the following ways: I am not able to work outside the home for gainful employment due to varying symptoms such as tremors, fatigue, digestive irregularities, and cognitive changes. This has made me reliant on public benefits such as Social Security Disability and VA Compensation, which I would prefer not to collect when instead I could be working in gainful employment. My financial stability is dependent on continued government funding for the remainder of my life (I am only 55 years old), and I am restricted to the funds available through Congressional funding of these programs, which is not guaranteed year over year.

In addition, my plans for life after retiring from the military have been completely reconfigured due to Parkinsons disease. Every year my tremors and other symptoms become progressively worse and harder for me and my wife to live with, even with excellent treatment from my VA providers. Some days are worse than others, but baseline challenges that I face every day include not being able to cook for myself 5 out of 7 days per week, needing several days to recover from fatigue after activity, and taking more than 25 pills per day to control tremors and treat other service-connected disabilities.

I respectfully urge VA to thoroughly evaluate the strong scientific evidence linking military environmental exposures to Parkinson’s disease and to consider establishing or expanding presumptive service connection where supported by the evidence.
Veterans should not bear an unreasonable burden of proof when scientific literature and historical claims data indicate associations. Establishing presumptions would ensure timely access to earned benefits and health care.

I appreciate VA’s commitment under the PACT Act to reviewing emerging evidence and providing transparency through this public comment and listening session process.

Thank you for your consideration and for your continued service to veterans.
Respectfully,
Charles A. Burt, Jr
Lakewood, WA
charlesburt.artist@gmail.com

title: Comment from Brian Sawyer on VA-2026-VACO-0001-0167
printtext:
Subject: Support for Expanding Eligibility Criteria for SAH/SHA Grants to Better Address Service-Connected Mobility Impairments

Dear Department of Veterans Affairs, I am writing in response to the Agency Information Collection Activity notice regarding VA Form 26-4555 for Specially Adapted Housing (SAH) and Special Home Adaptation (SHA) grants. I strongly support the VA’s ongoing efforts to administer these critical programs and appreciate the opportunity to provide public comment. The SAH and SHA grants are essential tools that enable severely disabled Veterans to live independently and with dignity in their homes. By funding necessary adaptations—such as ramps, widened doorways, accessible bathrooms, and modified kitchens—these grants directly reduce barriers, prevent secondary injuries, and lower long-term healthcare costs for the VA and taxpayers. I commend the VA for regularly updating grant amounts to reflect construction costs.

However, the current statutory and regulatory eligibility criteria are overly narrow and do not fully capture the range of service-connected disabilities that significantly impair mobility and safe home navigation. Qualifying conditions are largely limited to loss or loss of use of multiple limbs, specific blindness thresholds, certain severe burns, and limited post-9/11 single lower extremity cases. Many Veterans with other severe, service-connected mobility impairments—such as progressive neuromuscular conditions, complex spinal or hip disorders, or other functional mobility limitations (e.g., FSHD or similar conditions causing profound weakness, balance issues, fatigue, and reliance on assistive devices)—are currently excluded despite facing equivalent daily challenges.

In my own case, I have a service-connected condition (FHSD) that has greatly impacted my mobility. While I do not have anatomical loss of limbs or qualifying burns, the functional limitations—difficulty with ambulation, transfers, stair navigation, and performing activities of daily living—create the same critical need for home adaptations as those who currently qualify. Many fellow Veterans in similar situations must choose between unsafe living conditions, institutional care, or out-of-pocket expenses that deplete their resources. I respectfully request that the VA consider advocating for or supporting modest legislative or regulatory expansions to the eligibility criteria. This could include adding a functional mobility category, such as: Service-connected disabilities resulting in the loss of use of lower extremities or overall mobility equivalent to the existing standards (e.g., requiring wheelchair, crutches, or other assistive devices for safe locomotion, or severe limitations in balance, strength, or endurance due to neuromuscular, orthopedic, or neurological conditions).

Such an expansion would align the program more closely with the intent of promoting independence for all severely disabled Veterans, not just those with specific injury types. It would also reflect advances in medical understanding of functional impairment and disability. Any changes should maintain rigorous medical documentation requirements (e.g., physician statements on functional limitations, VA disability ratings, and evidence of need) to ensure fiscal responsibility and target those with the greatest need.

Thank you for considering this important update to better serve Veterans. Expanding access modestly would have a profound, positive impact on quality of life while remaining true to the program’s mission. I am happy to provide additional details about my situation or connect with VA staff if helpful.

Sincerely,
Brian Sawyer
California

title: Comment from LifeLink of Florida on VA-2026-VACO-0001-0225
printtext:
Re: Patient Medical Records-VA (Docket No. VA-2026-VACO-0001, 91 FR 40662)

LifeLink of Florida appreciates the opportunity to provide comment on the Department of Veterans Affairs’ modified system of records notice for Patient Medical Records-VA.

LifeLink of Florida is an organ procurement organization, and we support strong privacy protections for Veterans and their beneficiaries. We also recognize the critical importance of timely, medically appropriate information-sharing with federally designated organ procurement organizations (OPOs) for the purpose of determining suitability for organ, eye, and tissue donation when a patient is at or near death.

We are concerned that Routine Use 45 appears to reintroduce limiting language stating that information disclosed to an OPO may not reveal medical treatment related to drug abuse, alcoholism or alcohol abuse, sickle cell anemia, HIV, or the names and addresses of Veterans and their beneficiaries. This language may create confusion for VA facilities and OPOs and could unintentionally restrict information that is necessary to evaluate suitability, protect recipient safety, and facilitate donation consistent with applicable law and regulation.

This limitation also appears inconsistent with VA’s prior 2009 explanation that Routine Use 46 was amended to delete similar exclusionary language after Congress authorized disclosure of information protected by 38 U.S.C. §§ 5701 and 7332 to OPOs for the purpose of determining suitability when death is imminent.

“Routine use forty-six (46) is amended to delete the language excluding medical treatment information related to drug or alcohol abuse, infection with the human immunodeficiency virus, or sickle cell anemia, and the names and home addresses of veterans and their dependents from the routine use. Congress enacted legislation to allow for the disclosure of information protected by 38 U.S.C. 5701 and 7332 to organ procurement organizations for the purpose of determining suitability of patients' organs or tissues for organ donation when death is imminent. This routine use allows VHA to honor the wishes of veterans to be organ donors.”
- 74 FR 60040 (FR Doc. E9-27786). Note: Current ‘Routine Use 45’ was ‘Routine Use 46’ at the time of this amendment.

LifeLink of Florida respectfully requests that VA revise Routine Use 45 to remove the exclusionary language or clarify that it does not limit disclosures authorized under 38 U.S.C. §§ 5701 and 7332 and 38 CFR §§ 1.485a and 1.514b for organ, eye, and tissue donor suitability determination. This is important because barriers to accessing medically relevant information can result in missed opportunities for donation and transplantation.

LifeLink of Florida welcomes further discussion and appreciates VA’s consideration of these comments.

title: Comment from The Veteran Benefit Desk on VA-2026-VACO-0001-0241
printtext:
The Veteran Benefit Desk is an independent publication founded by a veteran. We document how VA benefits work in practice, track VA form versions, and publish research built from FOIA records. We are commenting on VA Form 28-10286, Request for Retroactive Induction for a Period Previously Completed Under Chapter 33 (OMB Control No. 2900-0933), and attach a comment with nine recommendations.

The heart of it: the form is three pages, but the work is on page three. Depending on what the veteran requests, supporting documentation can include transcripts, a degree audit, tuition and fee records, scholarship documentation, course syllabi, book and supply receipts, and VA Form 28-1905m, all due within 60 days, sometimes for education completed years earlier. The 20 minute burden estimate should account for gathering those records or be revised, and VA should show the basis for the estimate of 144,601 respondents per year. Give veterans an eligibility checklist in everyday words before the paperwork starts, and use payment records VA already holds (kicker, STEM, Chapter 33 usage) instead of asking veterans to recreate them. Tell veterans what to do when a required record no longer exists. Reword Item 17 so a withdrawal cannot happen by accident. Give veterans an estimated reconciliation of any kicker or STEM debt before the transaction becomes final, since a claimant cannot know when the Regional Processing Office will process the request or what the debt will be at that moment. Ask whether the veteran wants VA to review a tuition, book, or housing difference instead of requiring the veteran to understand the calculation first. And add a worked example for the Chapter 33 to Chapter 31 entitlement conversion.

The full comment with sources is attached.

title: Comment from Daniel Tarlitz on VA-2026-VACO-0001-0031
printtext:
The Honorable Douglas A. Collins
Secretary
U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs
810 Vermont Ave., NW
Washington, DC 20420

Submitted electronically via www.regulations.gov

Subject: Public Comment on Neurodegenerative Disease Review – Docket VA–2026–VACO–0001

Dear Secretary Collins:

My name is Daniel M. Tarlitz, and I am a United States military veteran who served in the Army from 2003 - 2007. I am submitting this comment in response to the Department of Veterans Affairs’ notice regarding its review of neurodegenerative diseases and military environmental exposures.

I have been diagnosed with Parkinson’s disease. During my military service, I was exposed daily to Burn Pits, contaminated untreated water, jet fuel, and solvents as well as other environmental toxins while deployed in Iraq. At the time, I was not aware of the potential long-term neurological risks associated with these exposures.

Parkinson’s disease has significantly affected my life in the following ways:
I have tremors and rigidity on my left side. I have limited use of my left hand, arm, and leg. I have lost dexterity in my left hand and walking is becoming more difficult. I have severe fatigue (mental and physical), muscle pain, and joint pain. Everyday activities are becoming more challenging. I have always worked with my hands. I have recently had to leave my occupation as an automotive technician due to safety concerns and difficulty performing physical tasks. I am 44 years old. I now have to find another occupation that I am physically able to perform and that I can sustain while my symptoms progressively worsen.

I respectfully urge VA to thoroughly evaluate the strong scientific evidence linking military environmental exposures to Parkinson’s disease and to consider establishing or expanding presumptive service connection where supported by the evidence.

Veterans should not bear an unreasonable burden of proof when scientific literature and historical claims data indicate associations. Establishing presumptions would ensure timely access to earned benefits and health care.

I appreciate VA’s commitment under the PACT Act to reviewing emerging evidence and providing transparency through this public comment and listening session process.

Thank you for your consideration and for your continued service to veterans.

Respectfully,
Daniel M. Tarlitz
West Palm Beach, FL
DM.Tarlitz@yahoo.com

title: Comment from William  DeAugustinis on VA-2026-VACO-0001-0031
printtext:
I applaud the VA for commissioning the NASEM review of scientific literature on military environmental exposures and neurodegenerative diseases. However, I believe the study framework overlooks a significant population of affected veterans.
I am a Navy veteran who served on active duty from 1970 to 1977 and am now totally disabled with Inclusion Body Myositis (IBM), a progressive, incurable neurodegenerative disease. The VA has recognized my condition as 100% service-connected due to toxic exposures during my service, but only after more than a decade of appeals and the need for legal representation. During that time, my quality of life steadily declined.
NASEM’s study of military exposures is a very important step for veterans with IBM, as the study is required to ultimately have IBM approved as a presumptive disease under Title 38, § 3.318. IBM results in nearly identical symptoms as ALS, which is already presumptive, but IBM takes longer to result in total disability.
IBM is included in the NASEM study, yet the committee is limited to veterans who served in the Gulf War era and later, placing the average age of that cohort at about 55 or younger. This is problematic, as IBM typically manifests between ages 60–70, with an average diagnosis at 65. As a result, the study excludes the population most affected by IBM—primarily Vietnam-era veterans. Within our national Veterans with Myositis support group, we have no members with IBM from the Gulf War era or later; the vast majority are Vietnam-era veterans. NASEM will also find a much deeper level of experience with IBM with Vietnam-era veterans.
The study should also consider disease prevalence. VHA records indicate an IBM prevalence of approximately 189 per million among veterans, compared to about 12 per million in the general population. This disparity exceeds that which led ALS to be designated a presumptive service-connected condition.
NASEM’s upcoming May 20–21 listening session prioritizes Gulf War–era and later veterans, making it unlikely that participants will include individuals already diagnosed with IBM. The committee would benefit greatly from hearing directly from veterans with IBM who have active or completed disability claims, particularly given the difficulties of the appeals process and the lack of a VBA diagnostic code for IBM.
Respectfully,
W. C. DeAugustinis, CDR-USNR (Ret.)

title: Comment from Makita Thatcher on VA-2026-VACO-0001-0203
printtext:
VA OIG Hotline Privacy Act System
Privacy Act of 1974; System of Records
Inspector General Hotline / Complaint Center Records, 66VA53
Docket No. VA-2025-VACO-0001
91 FR 36230

06/16/2026

To the Department of Veterans Affairs:

I submit this comment on the modified system of records notice for the VA Office of Inspector General Hotline / Complaint Center Records, 66VA53.

The statutory hook is the Inspector General Act and the Privacy Act. The Inspector General framework exists to detect and prevent fraud, waste, abuse, mismanagement, abuse of authority, and dangers to public health and safety. The Privacy Act exists to give structure, limits, notice, and accountability to agency systems that maintain records about individuals.

The administrative choke point is the complaint record system. A hotline is not merely an inbox. It is the place where allegations become records, records become referrals, referrals become investigations or closures, and later oversight depends on whether the original material can be retrieved, understood, protected, and lawfully reviewed.

The human consequence is trust. Veterans, beneficiaries, employees, contractors, witnesses, and private citizens may hesitate to report wrongdoing if they cannot understand how their information will be stored, shared, searched, retained, corrected where appropriate, or protected from retaliation. A complaint system that is opaque may still receive allegations, but it may weaken confidence in whether the record will survive and whether the complainant will be protected.

The structural question is this: can VA OIG preserve investigative confidentiality while also giving the public enough clarity to trust that complaints will not disappear into an unreviewable chamber?

I urge VA OIG to clarify how complainant confidentiality is protected when complaints are referred outside the OIG; how anonymous complainants and witnesses are protected; how complainants may receive status or closure information where possible; and how uploaded documents, scanned evidence, correspondence, and reports remain linked to the relevant case record. The notice states that some uploaded materials cannot be searched or retrieved through a general database search. That limitation deserves careful attention because oversight depends not only on whether records exist, but whether they can be found.

I also urge VA OIG to publish aggregate, non-identifying data on complaint categories, referrals, dispositions, and processing timelines.

The principle is that an Inspector General hotline must protect investigations, but it must also preserve trust. A public accountability system should be confidential where necessary, but never structurally forgetful.

Respectfully submitted,
Makita Thatcher
Georgia resident

title: Comment from Leann Ledford on VA-2026-VACO-0001-0041
printtext:
RE: OMB Control No. 2900-0021 | FR Doc. 2026-03000 | VALERI System and Title Requirements for Conveyance of Real Property

I submit this comment as the spouse/caregiver of a disabled Marine veteran, since our family has been directly impacted by the VALERI information collection. I am the spouse of a disabled Marine veteran with a VA-guaranteed loan (Loan No. 0136811965), a 2022 Elizabeth Dole Foundation Caregiver Fellow, an MSW graduate student, and a Washington State Certified Victim Advocate who works in social work and community programs. Our case is the subject of an active VA OIG investigation (Ref. No. 2026-16691) and a CFPB complaint (No. 260407-31030512). I address each of VA's four questions in turn.

1. NECESSITY AND PRACTICAL UTILITY

The VALERI collection (38 CFR 36.4817) is necessary — but only functions if servicers submit events to the system. Freedom Mortgage Corporation never submitted our loan to VALERI at any stage of loss mitigation. A VA loan technician confirmed on a recorded call that there had been no VALERI activity on our loan since 2023. Because no events were submitted, no automated compliance checks triggered. VA foreclosed while our loss mitigation application was pending — also confirmed on a recorded call.

OMB records show VA has submitted this collection as "extension without change" in every cycle since 2020, despite the COVID forbearance crisis, VASP's creation and cancellation, and H.R. 1815's enactment in July 2025. None of these developments prompted substantive revision. That gap directly affected our family.

This failure is not isolated. Freedom Mortgage has accumulated $130.3 million in federal penalties across 18 enforcement actions and is a CFPB-designated "repeat offender." The violations in our case — rate cap, loss mitigation failure, dual tracking, false credit reporting — reflect patterns already established in prior findings against this servicer. On July 28, 2025, at a VA loan technician's direction, I submitted a written violation report to VA. VA transmitted it to Freedom Mortgage, which never responded. VA has not addressed the report since — despite direct follow-up after the February 2026 foreclosure notification and subsequent complaints to VA OIG, congressional offices, CFPB, and the Washington State Attorney General. The collection's practical utility is undermined when VA receives a documented violation report, transmits it to the servicer, and takes no further oversight action when the servicer does not respond.

2. ACCURACY OF BURDEN ESTIMATE

VA estimates 16,509 respondents. This figure likely undercounts affected borrowers: families whose servicers never submit to VALERI are not captured as respondents because they never appear in the system. We were subject to VALERI's oversight framework but invisible within it due to servicer non-compliance. Any burden estimate based solely on submitted events will systematically exclude the borrowers most harmed by servicer non-reporting.

3. QUALITY, UTILITY, AND CLARITY OF INFORMATION COLLECTED

Two documented gaps in our case directly undermine the collection's utility.

First, Freedom Mortgage offered a loan modification at 7.25% on a 2.25% VA-guaranteed loan — 400 basis points above the maximum permitted under VA's M26-4 Manual, Chapter 5. A VA loan technician reviewed this offer on July 24, 2025 and did not flag the rate cap violation. VALERI should collect modification terms at submission and apply automated rate cap validation before any offer reaches a borrower.

Second, the system collected no data on our loan during the period loss mitigation was supposedly being evaluated. Zero-event loans in active default were not flagged as anomalous. VA should treat the absence of servicer reporting — not just inaccurate reporting — as a compliance trigger requiring audit.

4. MINIMIZING BURDEN ON RESPONDENTS

When servicers fail to report, burden shifts to borrowers, who must navigate a system with no record of their case. The absence of VALERI reporting in our case meant no recourse through normal VA oversight channels.

To minimize burden on borrowers while improving integrity: (a) require automated servicer confirmation of VALERI submission at each loss mitigation stage, with a system hold on foreclosure referral until confirmed; and (b) implement regular audits of zero-event loans in default to identify non-reporting before foreclosure proceeds.

CONCLUSION

The VALERI collection serves a critical oversight function but cannot detect what servicers do not report, and has not been substantively revised since 2016. I urge VA to address non-reporting as a compliance category, implement automated rate cap enforcement under 38 CFR 36.4817, and audit zero-event loans in active default.

Leann Ledford
2022 Elizabeth Dole Foundation Caregiver Fellow
MSW Graduate Student | WA Certified Victim Advocate

title: Comment from Gregory  Willis  on VA-2026-VACO-0001-0224
printtext:
I appreciate the Department of Veterans Affairs’ efforts to modernize and maintain the Centralized Accounts Receivable System/Centralized Accounts Receivable Online System (CARS/CAROLS). Because this system contains sensitive financial information and is used in the collection of debts arising from VA benefit programs, it is essential that the system protect veterans’ rights while ensuring accurate administration.

I respectfully recommend that the final System of Records Notice include the following safeguards:

1. Accuracy Before Collection

The VA should verify the accuracy of all debts before initiating collection activity. Veterans should receive a clear explanation of how a debt was calculated, the legal basis for the debt, and the evidence supporting the determination.

2. Timely Notice and Opportunity to Respond

Individuals should receive prompt written notice before collection actions begin and be provided a meaningful opportunity to dispute the debt, submit additional evidence, request a waiver when authorized by law, or establish an appropriate repayment plan.

3. Strong Privacy and Cybersecurity Protections

Because the system contains personally identifiable and financial information, the VA should continue implementing strong cybersecurity safeguards, regular audits, encryption, and strict access controls to minimize the risk of unauthorized disclosure.

4. Transparency Regarding Record Sharing

The System of Records Notice should clearly identify every category of agency or organization with which records may be shared, the legal authority for each routine use, and the safeguards that apply to those disclosures.

5. Veteran Access and Correction Rights

Veterans should have a straightforward process to review their records, obtain copies, request corrections of inaccurate information, and receive timely responses to those requests.

6. Periodic Review of Outstanding Debts

The VA should periodically review accounts to ensure debts remain legally valid, accurately calculated, and collectible, while correcting administrative errors as quickly as possible.

The VA has an important responsibility to protect taxpayer resources while honoring its commitment to those who have served. A debt collection system that emphasizes accuracy, transparency, due process, and strong privacy protections will improve public confidence and help ensure fair treatment of veterans.

Thank you for the opportunity to provide these comments.

Respectfully,

Gregory Willis

title: Comment from Steven Singleton
printtext:
Opening a dedicated comment window on the environmental assessment before any substantive rule is proposed gives the public an early opportunity to flag environmental concerns, which is a sound practice worth preserving as this petition moves forward.

The notice's principal shortcoming is that it does not disclose the substance of what CAP 5C0339 actually proposes. It states that the petition would add heavy metal limits and secondary names for carrot oil, but the notice includes no numeric limits and no proposed names. A member of the public reading only the Federal Register text cannot evaluate whether the proposed heavy metal limits are appropriately protective, because the limits themselves are not stated. FDA should include the specific proposed limits and names in the notice, or in an easily accessible summary alongside the docket, so that the comment period is meaningful to readers who do not separately visit the Dockets Management Staff office.

A second gap is that the notice does not summarize the environmental assessment's findings regarding acetone as a solvent in carrot oil manufacture, including whether the assessment addresses residual solvent levels in the finished color additive reaching food products. Acetone residue is a food-safety-adjacent question distinct from the environmental-impact question the current comment period is limited to; FDA should clarify whether safety data on residual acetone levels will be part of the record reviewed before any proposed rule, and if so, when that data will be made public.

Finally, FDA reserves authority to "consider other changes to the regulation, as appropriate, during the course of our review," without stating what triggers or bounds such additional changes. Some indication of the criteria FDA would use to add scope beyond the petition as filed would help commenters anticipate what a resulting proposed rule might cover.

These points concern the notice's transparency and scope, not the petition's merits, which cannot be evaluated without the missing detail.

Americans for Scientific Integrity submits this supplemental comment to bring FDA’s attention to a recently accepted peer-reviewed study that further strengthens the biological plausibility underlying AFSI’s pending citizen petition regarding pediatric acetaminophen use.
The attached study, Sex-dependent effects of early-life paracetamol exposure on behavior and monoamines in the rat central nervous system (Górawski et al., Chemico-Biological Interactions, accepted January 2026), evaluates prenatal and early postnatal acetaminophen exposure in rodents and reports sex-dependent behavioral and neurochemical effects, with male and female offspring exhibiting different patterns of impact across behavioral domains and brain regions
Importantly, the findings do not reflect nonspecific or random neurotoxicity. Rather, the presence of systematic, sex-dependent differences suggests a biologically mediated effect consistent with known differences in neurodevelopment, hormone signaling, metabolism, and neurotransmitter systems between males and females. This pattern strengthens biological plausibility by arguing against chance injury and in favor of a drug-related developmental mechanism.
These sex-dependent findings align with observations in humans, where neurodevelopmental conditions such as autism spectrum disorder and ADHD are known to differ by sex in prevalence, presentation, and developmental trajectory. As such, this study adds relevant and timely preclinical evidence supporting AFSI’s request that FDA evaluate the need for precautionary labeling regarding pediatric acetaminophen use.
ASFI respectfully requests that FDA include this newly published study in its review and analysis of AFSI’s petition.

Please consider the attached comment in support of the precautionary case for pediatric acetaminophen warnings.

The comment addresses a broader safety concern: acetaminophen safety has historically been evaluated primarily through the lens of hepatic toxicity, but a growing body of evidence raises concern for possible non-hepatic effects, including reproductive and fertility-related endpoints, asthma/allergy associations, developing lung injury signals, and neurologic/dementia-related associations.

The relevance to pediatric use is that acetaminophen exposure during vulnerable developmental windows should not be assumed safe merely because liver toxicity is absent. If acetaminophen can affect other organ systems through oxidative stress, glutathione depletion, endocrine disruption, immune signaling, mitochondrial effects, or other non-hepatic mechanisms, then liver-only safety assumptions are inadequate for assessing risk in infants and young children.

This evidence does not require the FDA to conclude definitive causation. It supports the narrower and more appropriate precautionary conclusion that parents and clinicians should receive clearer warning language and risk communication regarding potential developmental and systemic risks associated with pediatric acetaminophen use.

title: Comment from Anonymous
printtext:
I am a board certified anesthesiologist practicing in the United States. I am submitting this comment in strong support of the Americans for Scientific Integrity citizen petition requesting that FDA add a pediatric warning to acetaminophen products.

From a pharmacology and drug safety perspective, what concerns me most is not a subtle scientific nuance. It is the simple fact that acetaminophen was effectively grandfathered into widespread pediatric use on the basis of safety testing that focused almost entirely on acute liver injury. We validated dosing for hepatotoxicity. We did not meaningfully evaluate this drug for long term effects on the developing brain or on other organ systems in early life.

To my knowledge, the first animal studies that looked specifically at neurodevelopment in the context of early life acetaminophen exposure appeared only about a decade ago. Those data, summarized in the Americans for Scientific Integrity petition, are deeply concerning. They show behavioral and neurochemical changes after early life exposure that are consistent with injury to the developing nervous system. At the same time, human epidemiologic studies now repeatedly associate prenatal and early childhood acetaminophen exposure with increased risk of autism spectrum disorder, ADHD, and related neurodevelopmental outcomes. None of these signals existed when acetaminophen was informally “grandfathered” into pediatric practice. They exist now.

If we apply first principles and imagine that acetaminophen were a completely new drug being brought to FDA today, with the same preclinical neurodevelopmental findings and the same pattern of observational human data described in the petition, I do not believe it would clear even the early regulatory hurdles for pediatric use. In fact, I doubt the agency would allow clinical trials in infants or pregnant women to proceed in the face of these signals. Exposing a large number of children in a controlled trial to further characterize the risk would almost certainly be considered unethical, precisely because we already have evidence of possible harm.

That logic leads to an uncomfortable but inescapable conclusion. We are in a situation where the totality of the existing data is troubling enough that we probably could not ethically design the very studies that would be required to approve this drug for pediatric use if we were starting from scratch. Yet at the same time, more than 90 percent of children in early childhood receive acetaminophen, often repeatedly, sometimes in the exact age window where the petition argues susceptibility is highest. A drug that would struggle to obtain approval for pediatric trials under current standards is being used casually by nearly every family in the country, without any warning to parents that neurodevelopmental safety has never been adequately established.

The FDA cannot undo the regulatory and cultural decisions of the past. However, it can acknowledge where the evidence has moved and take corrective steps to protect children going forward. The fact that it is difficult to accept that a familiar, trusted over the counter drug might play a role in the autism epidemic does not change the ethical analysis. Our regulatory decisions should follow the evidence and the precautionary principle, not our discomfort.

In my judgment, based on the evidence compiled in the Americans for Scientific Integrity petition, acetaminophen could not be introduced today as a new pediatric analgesic and antipyretic without extensive additional safety work in neurodevelopmental models and careful limitation of any pediatric clinical trials. It is hard to imagine that such trials would even be approved given what we already know. If it is not ethical to expose children in a randomized trial under present knowledge, it is difficult to justify continuing unlabelled mass exposure in routine clinical practice.

For these reasons, I urge the agency to grant the petition’s request for a clear pediatric warning. At a minimum, parents and clinicians should be informed that:

Historical safety testing of acetaminophen focused primarily on acute liver toxicity, not neurodevelopment.

Neurodevelopmental safety in pregnancy and early childhood has never been robustly established.

Multiple animal and human studies now raise serious concerns, even though causation has not been definitively proven.

The FDA cannot change the past decisions that allowed acetaminophen to become embedded in pediatric care. It can, however, change the future by ensuring that parents are told the truth about the limitations of the safety data and about the concerning signals that now exist. Failing to provide at least a warning, given what we know today, would in my view be inconsistent with the agency’s duty to protect the public, especially infants and young children in the most vulnerable period of brain development.
