title: Comment from Anonymous
printtext:
Please consider the attached materials in support of the precautionary case for pediatric acetaminophen warnings and informed consent.

Document 1 presents a Bayesian weight-of-evidence analysis of the evidence discussed in the citizen petition. The purpose of this analysis is to evaluate the cumulative strength of evidence across multiple independent lines of inquiry rather than relying on any single study design in isolation. The overall pattern of evidence, including epidemiology, animal models, mechanistic data, biomarker studies, and related disease associations, supports concern regarding neurodevelopmental risk in susceptible children.

Document 2 discusses the biomarker-based evidence on prenatal acetaminophen exposure and why these studies should be given substantial weight when interpreting the larger body of prenatal epidemiology. Biomarker-based designs help reduce problems associated with maternal recall bias and exposure misclassification that may affect retrospective survey-based studies. These findings strengthen the argument that observed associations in prenatal acetaminophen research may reflect genuine biological effects rather than statistical artifact alone.

The final document addresses the overlap between autism and asthma and their potential connection to acetaminophen exposure. This line of evidence is relevant because it suggests the possibility of shared underlying mechanisms involving oxidative stress, glutathione depletion, immune dysregulation, mitochondrial dysfunction, and inflammatory signaling. Importantly, it also supports the broader concern that acetaminophen-related effects may extend beyond traditional liver toxicity models and involve systemic developmental and immunologic pathways.

Taken together, these materials further support the need for precautionary pediatric warnings and more complete risk communication to parents and clinicians regarding potential developmental and systemic risks associated with acetaminophen exposure during vulnerable periods of childhood development.

title: Comment from Anonymous
printtext:
Please see the attached supplemental comment and supporting references regarding the limitations of sibling-control analyses in prenatal neurodevelopment research.

Recent literature suggests that sibling comparison designs may attenuate or obscure true associations in certain contexts involving developmental exposures, particularly where exposure misclassification, carryover effects, shared environmental susceptibilities, epigenetic mechanisms, or bias amplification may be present. These concerns are directly relevant to the interpretation of prenatal acetaminophen studies, where several large maternal recall studies employing sibling-control methodologies have been treated as disproportionately determinative in evaluating risk.

Importantly, the recently published JAMA study by Ahlqvist et al. (2024) on prenatal acetaminophen exposure and neurodevelopmental outcomes demonstrated substantial attenuation of associations in sibling analyses despite strong associations in population-level analyses, while contemporaneous methodological literature has cautioned that sibling-control methods may themselves introduce important bias under certain conditions. Additional large-scale prenatal neurodevelopment studies, including Madley-Dowd et al. (2024), similarly emphasize that sibling comparisons should be interpreted as one methodological tool among many, rather than as definitive evidence against causality.

Accordingly, these materials are submitted in support of the Americans for Scientific Integrity citizen petition requesting pediatric precautionary labeling for acetaminophen. At minimum, the evolving methodological literature suggests that null sibling-control findings should not be treated as dispositive when evaluating the overall weight of evidence regarding potential neurodevelopmental risk.

title: Comment from Americans for Scientific Integrity
printtext: Petitioner respectfully submits for inclusion in the administrative record the following newly published study: Herrington et al. (2026), “Two-Hit Exposure to Lipopolysaccharide and Acetaminophen Alters Larval Zebrafish (Danio rerio) Swim Behavior.”  This experimental study is notable because it directly models a “two-hit” framework in which early-life inflammation is followed by acetaminophen exposure, a sequence that closely mirrors real-world pediatric use, where acetaminophen is most commonly administered during fever, infection, or other inflammatory states. The authors report that acetaminophen exposure altered neurobehavioral outcomes in developing zebrafish and, importantly, that combined exposure to inflammation and acetaminophen produced interaction effects on behavior that were not fully explained by either exposure alone, including changes in activity and lateralized movement patterns. While the findings are modest, derived from an animal model, and do not establish causation in humans, the study is highly relevant from a regulatory perspective because it addresses a key limitation of the existing literature: most prior studies evaluate acetaminophen in isolation rather than in the biologically realistic context in which it is actually used. The authors themselves emphasize that this context is critical, noting that inflammation and illness are independently associated with neurodevelopmental risk and may interact with drug exposure. Accordingly, this study provides additional mechanistic and experimental support for the plausibility of a context-dependent risk model, in which acetaminophen exposure during periods of immune activation may have different developmental effects than exposure in a non-inflamed state. Petitioner does not contend that this study is dispositive on its own, but rather that it strengthens the overall evidentiary record by demonstrating that inflammatory context is not merely a confounder but may be an integral component of risk. For this reason, the study is directly relevant to the requested pediatric warning and should be included in the FDA’s evaluation of whether current labeling adequately reflects real-world conditions of use and potential susceptibility in early childhood.

title: Comment from Anonymous
printtext:
This comment is submitted in support of the request for a precautionary neurodevelopmental warning regarding acetaminophen use in infants and young children, including acetaminophen exposure beginning on the first day of life.
Attached is a PDF copy of Tylenol and Autism: Evidence, Scientific Blunders, and Medicine Gone Wrong by William Parker, PhD. The book is highly relevant because it collects and organizes evidence concerning acetaminophen exposure during early brain development, including neonatal exposure, immature infant metabolism, oxidative stress, susceptibility, laboratory animal evidence, human epidemiologic evidence, and the absence of adequate long-term neurodevelopmental safety testing for pediatric use.
This comment is not intended to ask FDA to rely on the book itself as dispositive evidence. Rather, the attached volume serves as a source guide, index, and synthesis of the underlying scientific literature, with citations to original studies provided in the notes section beginning on page 225.
Several sections are particularly relevant. Chapter 5, beginning on page 81, addresses the timing of acetaminophen-associated neurodevelopmental risk and explains why the period immediately after birth and the first years of life may be especially important. Pediatric acetaminophen exposure can begin in the hospital, during the immediate postnatal period, when drug metabolism, detoxification capacity, and brain vulnerability may differ materially from older children and adults.
Pages 85-90 are especially relevant to immature neonatal metabolism. Parker discusses evidence that newborns and young infants may not metabolize acetaminophen in the same way as older children and adults, and that the ability to process acetaminophen safely may change substantially during early life. This is central because long-standing assumptions about pediatric acetaminophen safety have often been based on liver injury endpoints, not long-term neurodevelopmental outcomes.
Pages 91-95 discuss case histories and the Schultz findings concerning regression into autism following early-childhood acetaminophen exposure. These sections address pediatric exposure after birth, including repeated dosing during illness, vaccination-related fever or pain, and other common childhood circumstances in which acetaminophen may be administered.
Chapter 6, beginning on page 97, summarizes laboratory animal evidence relevant to developmental neurotoxicity, including multiple studies reporting persistent behavioral, cognitive, social, auditory, or neurodevelopmental effects following early-life acetaminophen exposure. Pages 139-142 are especially important because they discuss recent work concerning N-acetyl-p-benzoquinone imine (NAPQI), the toxic metabolite of acetaminophen, and preliminary evidence of acetaminophen-related adduct formation in neonatal brain tissue. This evidence is directly relevant to biological plausibility and to whether the developing brain has been adequately protected by current pediatric labeling.
Chapter 7, beginning on page 113, addresses additional evidence bearing on pediatric safety, including the history of assumptions that acetaminophen was safe for babies and children, the weakness of the evidence base supporting that assumption, and the difference between evidence of safety and the absence of adequate neurodevelopmental safety testing.
Appendix B, pages 189-194, provides concise evidence summary tables organizing pharmacologic, epidemiologic, laboratory animal, and other lines of evidence. These tables may be useful to FDA as a roadmap for reviewing the underlying literature cited throughout the book.
The central regulatory issue is not whether every mechanism has been fully resolved, but whether current labeling adequately communicates the uncertainty and potential neurodevelopmental risk during the most vulnerable periods of pediatric brain development.
For these reasons, the attached book should be included in the administrative record and considered as a source guide and synthesis relevant to the requested pediatric neurodevelopmental warning for acetaminophen use in infants and young children.

title: Comment from Anonymous
printtext:
I respectfully submit the attached documentary history in support of the citizen petition filed by Americans for Scientific Integrity.

Although much of the documentary record concerns prenatal exposure, it documents a broader developmental neurotoxicity question that has remained under active evaluation by Johnson & Johnson, Janssen, Kenvue, FDA, NCTR, and CDER for nearly two decades. That history provides important context for the developmental neurotoxicity concerns presented in the pediatric petition because prenatal exposure represents only one portion of the broader developmental exposure period addressed by the petitioner.

During an FDA Science Advisory Board presentation in April 2023, John Talpos, Ph.D., Director of FDA's Division of Neurotoxicology at NCTR, stated: "Acetaminophen has a reputation for being safe during pregnancy. The reality is this has never been demonstrated." The attached chronology follows the development of this issue from the manufacturer's first documented safety-signal evaluation in 2008 through FDA's continuing developmental neurotoxicity research program in 2026. I respectfully request that this documentary history be included in the administrative record and considered together with the scientific evidence already submitted in support of the petition.

title: Comment from Anonymous
printtext:
I am submitting the attached 2026 study by Aslan et al., Plasma Metabolic Features Associated with Developmental Regression in Autism Spectrum Disorder: A Pilot Untargeted Metabolomics Study, because its findings may be relevant to the mechanistic questions raised in this petition.
The investigators compared children with regressive autism, children with non-regressive autism, and typically developing controls. Among the most notable findings, the feature putatively identified as prostaglandin E3 (PGE3) was reduced 7.13-fold in the regressive autism group compared with controls, versus only 1.58-fold in the non-regressive group. The study also identified marked differences involving DHEA-S, sialylated glycoconjugates, glycoprotein metabolism, and sphingolipid/myelin pathways. Several of these biochemical systems intersect pathways relevant to acetaminophen biology. Acetaminophen directly affects cyclooxygenase/prostaglandin signaling, while acetaminophen disposition in infants and young children depends substantially on sulfation, making the findings involving prostaglandin metabolism and the sulfated neurosteroid DHEA-S particularly worthy of further investigation.
This study did not measure acetaminophen exposure and therefore does not establish that acetaminophen caused these metabolic abnormalities. Its relevance is that it identifies significant biochemical differences associated specifically with developmental regression, including abnormalities in pathways that overlap with known acetaminophen pharmacology. In evaluating the totality of evidence concerning acetaminophen exposure during early neurodevelopment, FDA should consider these findings alongside the experimental, mechanistic, pharmacologic, and epidemiologic evidence already submitted to the record.

title: Comment from City of Lubbock - Citibus
printtext:
Dear Sir or Madam:

I am writing in strong support of a temporary Buy America waiver request for the low floor, zero emission minibus called the e-JEST. Sixteen transit systems from five states submitted the non-availability and public interest waiver request and over 150 transit systems from across the country have publicly weighed in with support. It’s critical this waiver is approved to ensure transit systems across the country can continue to provide timely, reliable, and quality service in the face of a growing crisis in the small bus marketplace.

The cutaway marketplace is experiencing significant challenges, including long delivery times and significant cost increases. Making matters worse, El Dorado National-California (ENC) will be exiting the cutaway market by winding down its manufacturing by the end of the year. The consolidation in the small bus marketplace is going to have serious and profound consequences on daily operations which invariably will lead to service disruptions and increasing safety issues.

The e-JEST is a purpose-built all-electric minibus with a 12–15-year useful life and can be delivered in three to six months. Functionally, the e-JEST is a good fit for the transit trend line of increasing zero emission vehicles in rural areas, on-demand, paratransit operations and urban circulators.

Providing a temporary waiver for the e-JEST, and other buses like it, will incentivize future domestic manufacturing in the United States and create hundreds of American jobs. If granted a temporary waiver, Karsan Automotive - the manufacturer of the e-JEST - and Damera Bus - the North American dealer - have committed to meet the 70% domestic content and final assembly requirements of Buy America within two years. They are in the process of sourcing domestic content in a phased-in approach and siting domestic supply and manufacturing facilities within the United States, including establishing a parts facility in Iowa and California.

Thus, we feel it is appropriate and within the spirit of Buy America to provide a temporary waiver to incentivize domestic manufacturing, production, and use of these needed vehicles to American transit systems. Incorporating these vehicles into U.S. fleets will allow our transit systems to meet important climate objectives, improve competition, alleviate the strain on the supply chain and provide the service capabilities needed by our transit riding public.

As such, we strongly support approval of the temporary, general non-availability and public interest waiver for a low entrance, zero emission minibus.

Thank you for your consideration of this important request.

title: Comment from RADAR
printtext:
Dear Sir or Madam:



I am writing in strong support of a temporary Buy America waiver request for the low floor, zero emission minibus called the e-JEST. Sixteen transit systems from five states submitted the non-availability and public interest waiver request and over 150 transit systems from across the country have publicly weighed in with support. It’s critical this waiver is approved to ensure transit systems across the country can continue to provide timely, reliable, and quality service in the face of a growing crisis in the small bus marketplace.



The cutaway marketplace is experiencing significant challenges, including long delivery times and significant cost increases. Making matters worse, El Dorado National-California (ENC) will be exiting the cutaway market by winding down its manufacturing by the end of the year. The consolidation in the small bus marketplace is going to have serious and profound consequences on daily operations which invariably will lead to service disruptions and increasing safety issues.



The e-JEST is a purpose-built all-electric minibus with a 12–15-year useful life and can be delivered in three to six months. Functionally, the e-JEST is a good fit for the transit trend line of increasing zero emission vehicles in rural areas, on-demand, paratransit operations and urban circulators.



Providing a temporary waiver for the e-JEST, and other buses like it, will incentivize future domestic manufacturing in the United States and create hundreds of American jobs. If granted a temporary waiver, Karsan Automotive - the manufacturer of the e-JEST - and Damera Bus - the North American dealer - have committed to meet the 70% domestic content and final assembly requirements of Buy America within two years. They are in the process of sourcing domestic content in a phased-in approach and siting domestic supply and manufacturing facilities within the United States, including establishing a parts facility in Iowa and California.



Thus, we feel it is appropriate and within the spirit of Buy America to provide a temporary waiver to incentivize domestic manufacturing, production, and use of these needed vehicles to American transit systems. Incorporating these vehicles into U.S. fleets will allow our transit systems to meet important climate objectives, improve competition, alleviate the strain on the supply chain and provide the service capabilities needed by our transit riding public.



As such, we strongly support approval of the temporary, general non-availability and public interest waiver for a low entrance, zero emission minibus.



Thank you for your consideration of this important request.

title: Comment from CapMetro
printtext:
December 26, 2024

US Department of Transportation
Federal Transit Administration
Docket No. FTA-2024-0018

Dear Sir or Madam:

On behalf of CapMetro, we are writing in strong support of a temporary Buy America waiver request for the low floor, zero emission minibus called the e-JEST. Sixteen transit systems from five states submitted the non-availability and public interest waiver request and over 150 transit systems from across the country have publicly weighed in with support. It’s critical this waiver is approved to ensure transit systems across the country can continue to provide timely, reliable, and quality service in the face of a growing crisis in the small bus marketplace.

As we have seen with the passenger bus industry, the continued supply chain issues, lack of qualified suppliers able to meet the Buy America requirements, and lack of overall competition in the marketplace continues to contribute to lengthy delays in vehicle procurement and acquisition, not to mention maintenance issues for part supplies and technical assistance. Having a new temporary waiver enabled provider enter the market, albeit in the adjacent cutaway marketplace, provides a pathway and progress to build upon for the strength of the overall industry.

 The cutaway marketplace is experiencing significant challenges, including long delivery times and significant cost increases. Making matters worse, El Dorado National-California (ENC) will be exiting the cutaway market by winding down its manufacturing by the end of the year. The consolidation in the small bus marketplace is going to have serious and profound consequences on daily operations which invariably will lead to service disruptions and increasing safety issues.

 The e-JEST is a purpose-built all-electric minibus with a 12–15-year useful life and can be delivered in three to six months. Functionally, the e-JEST is a good fit for the transit trend line of increasing zero emission vehicles in on-demand, paratransit operations and urban circulators.

 Providing a temporary waiver for the e-JEST, and other buses like it, will incentivize future domestic manufacturing in the United States and create hundreds of American jobs. If granted a temporary waiver, Karsan Automotive - the manufacturer of the e-JEST - and Damera Bus - the North American dealer - have committed to meet the 70% domestic content and final assembly requirements of Buy America within two years. They are in the process of sourcing domestic content in a phased-in approach and siting domestic supply and manufacturing facilities within the United States, including establishing a parts facility in Iowa and California.

As the industry knows, the construction and assembly of a vehicle generates far more positive economic impact as interstate commerce supports growing and thriving concerns. Enabling the e-JEST and similar vehicles to be ramped up for production in the United States, with this waiver, provides time for the product to mature in the industry, for the industry to build the demand necessary to support healthy ongoing operations, and enables an increase in economic competitiveness with reinvestment of tax funds to help lift communities.  

CapMetro feels it is appropriate and within the spirit of Buy America to provide a temporary waiver to incentivize domestic manufacturing, production, and use of these needed vehicles to American transit systems. Incorporating these vehicles into U.S. fleets will allow transit systems to improve competition, alleviate the strain on the supply chain and provide the service capabilities needed by our transit riding public. The ability to introduce a zero-emission cutaway minibus is an added benefit as we look to these vehicles to provide more trips requiring idling for alighting and disembarking of passengers than the traditional 40- and 60-foot vehicles.

 As such, we strongly support approval of the temporary, general non-availability and public interest waiver for a low entrance, zero emission minibus.

 Thank you for your consideration of this important request.

title: Comment from Anonymous

Dear Sir or Madam,

As a supplier of components in the USA in the bus industry I have personally seen from the inside the added cost, and efforts that all USA bus manufactures go through to meet the requirements of current regulations pertaining to Buy America and other compliance matters to ensure that vehicles are safe for the American public. Especially when creating new bus solutions in America. It adds years to the supply chain cycle and design timeframe. I would vote against any waiver in this small bus segment as there are great solutions that are better currently available. Support the growth of these manufactures who are providing resources and jobs in America and meet Buy America currently.
Covid was very hard on supply chain, but that phase has now passed. All the reputable bus manufacturers now have ample supply on the ground and can meet current demand. If anything, supply has now shifted to where there is enough supply and current delays seem to be from regulations and red tape rather than a supply issue.
I agree that agencies need to find good solutions for this category of minibus. However, there are several very close in design available now that are build with American jobs, provide tax basis to local communities and meet the current requirements. One key element to consider is that the current list of bus manufacturers has USA service centers, parts distribution, and networks to ensure that the vehicles can be serviced, maintained and supported as needed. This EV Low floor has nearly identical specs, but better in range, speed lower weight etc. They produce an EV and gas variant low floor MiniBus. They are pushing the development of new products. Driverge E-Transit- https://www.driverge.com/vehicles/ford/ford-e-transit/
Proven OEM Electric solution with more range and OEM service centers nationwide.

Proven OEM Electric solution with more range and OEM service centers nationwide.

Braun Ability Ram ProMaster ADA lowered Floor Van- https://www.braunability.com/us/en/commercial/mobility-products/wheelchair-vans/promaster-full-size-ada-van.html
Proven gas powered low floor van with long standing reputation and staple in American jobs and compliance. Known as an industry leader in the small van segment.

title: Comment from Yamhill County Transit
printtext:
Please please please broaden it beyond a waiver for small electric buses to all cutaways and especially low-floor ramp access cutaway vehicles in gas, diesel, and CNG. The bus manufacturing world has changed so much and with Forest River being almost the only vendor available, rural transit agencies have little to no options. I believe it is a civil rights issue, and I am committed to having low floor ramp access mid-size buses because it creates equality for those using wheelchairs and walker who ride our buses. Sure.... the available mid-size buses have Wheelchair LIFTS but I lived with someone who used a scooter for 30 years and I know the humiliation and the degrading feeling of riding up in the wheelchair lift while everyone is waiting and watching until the chair is loaded and secured. A vehicle with a ramp allows the person in the chair to board like anyone else. These buses are impossible to find or cost a fortune and BUY AMERICA is part of the problem since I am sure FOREST RIVER can't make any money when building custom modified vehicles. There are many requirements that need change, but I support 100% the waiver for BUY AMERICA But I prefer it be for electric and all small and midsize buses for rural transit agencies.

title: Comment from Iowa Public Transit Association
printtext:
Dear Sir or Madam,

On behalf of Iowa Public Transit System, and our 35 public transit systems, I am writing to express our strong support for the Proposed Buy America Waiver for Battery Electric Minibuses. As part of Iowa’s Public Transit System, we recognize the critical importance of this waiver in advancing sustainable transportation solutions while addressing the unique challenges faced by public transit providers across the state and the nation.

This waiver will provide Iowa’s transit agencies with the flexibility needed to procure state-of-the-art battery electric minibuses that are currently unavailable domestically. It will also ensure that our transit systems can continue to deliver reliable service to rural and urban communities, many of which rely heavily on these vehicles for mobility and access to essential services.

Additionally, this waiver aligns with the broader goals of the Federal Transit Administration’s mission to support public transportation systems that are economically and environmentally sustainable. By granting this waiver, the FTA can help accelerate the transition to clean energy technologies while fostering the development of a robust domestic manufacturing base for battery electric vehicles in the future.

title: Comment from NCDOT - Integrated Mobility Division
printtext:
NCDOT-Integrated Mobility Division is in support of a temporary Buy America waiver for the low floor e-JEST minibus. As we explore potential alternative fuel solutions in NC with zero-emission options, it would be helpful to have this product offering available to any systems who are interested in exploring the zero-emission minibus marketplace.

We would also like FTA to consider temporary waivers for demand response-type vehicles in the zero emission marketplace. As the domestic content percentage for Buy America compliance is now at 70%, several manufacturers are no longer under consideration in the transit vehicle space. Especially during a time where supply chain issues are still having a ripple effect into deliverables for these vehicle types, we believe allowing a temporary waiver would offer other vehicle manufacturers the opportunity to become compliant with the domestic content percentage if given a window to source domestically. As there is now less competition in the marketplace, prices for vehicles have gone up dramatically since pre-COVID and delivery timeframes are significantly longer.

It is in the spirit of Buy America to incentivize domestic manufacturing and we feel that a temporary waiver extending to other vehicle types may help that effort. As we want to help spur the transition to zero emission vehicles in NC, a waiver may help not only the demand response vehicle marketplace but also fixed route and microtransit space as well.

title: Comment from MPower Mobility, Inc
printtext:
January 5, 2025

Ms. Veronica Vanterpool
Acting Administrator
Federal Transit Administration
U.S. Department of Transportation
1200 New Jersey Avenue, SE
Washington, DC 20590

Subject: Proposed Buy America Waiver - Docket number FTA-2024-0018-0001

Dear Ms. Vanterpool:
I am writing to oppose the proposed Buy America waiver for the Karsan e-Jest battery-electric minibus, as detailed in docket number FTA-2024-0018-0001. The waiver request overlooks several domestically produced alternatives that surpass the Karsan e-Jest in both performance and compliance with Buy America standards.
Available U.S.-Produced Alternatives:
1.Optimal-EV S1 Low Floor and Sunset Vans RP159EV:
oBoth vehicles have demonstrated superior performance, with the S1 Low Floor already tested at the FTA’s Altoona facility and the RP159EV pending a final report.
oAt 150 and 104 miles respectively compared to 75 miles, the RP159EV and the S1 Low Floor offer significantly more range per charge than the Karsan e-Jest.
oWith top speeds over 65 mph, both the RP159EV and the S1 Low Floor can easily be driven on the freeway, while the Karsan e-Jest, with a top speed of only just over 46 mph really cannot.
2.30' Class Vehicles:
oThe Axess EVO-BE by El Dorado and the New Flyer/Arboc Equess Charge offer larger, more robust options in the 30' vehicle class. Additionally, both the Axess and Equess Charge offer range per charge performance that is significantly better than the Karsan e-Jest.
oContrary to a recent comment suggesting otherwise, El Dorado's California plant is under new ownership and has resumed operations, further bolstering domestic manufacturing capacity.
3.Ford E-Transit Commercial Vans:
oThere is a significant inventory of unsold Ford E-Transits available through upfitters such as Forest River and Sunset Vans. These vehicles provide better range and top speeds than the Karsan e-Jest, offering additional options for smaller, accessible vehicles that meet performance needs without compromising on accessibility.
Economic and Strategic Considerations:
Granting a waiver to the Karsan e-Jest would undermine domestic manufacturing efforts and contravene the objectives of the Buy America provisions. Supporting foreign-made vehicles when superior U.S.-made alternatives exist not only weakens the domestic economy but also risks reliance on foreign suppliers for critical transportation infrastructure.
Conclusion:
In light of the above points, I strongly urge the FTA to reject the waiver request for the Karsan e-Jest. Embracing domestically manufactured alternatives will ensure better performance, compliance with Buy America standards, and the continued growth of the U.S. manufacturing sector.
Thank you for your attention to this matter.
Sincerely,

Stanton D. Saucier, PE

President
MPower Mobility, Inc.

title: Comment from American Public Transportation Association
printtext:
Full Letter is attached.

Ms. Veronica Vanterpool
Deputy Administrator
Federal Transit Administration
Washington, DC 20590

Re: Notice of Proposed Buy America Waiver for Battery Electric Minibuses and Request for Comment (Docket No. FTA-2024-0018)

Dear Deputy Administrator Vanterpool:

The American Public Transportation Association (APTA) represents a $79 billion industry that directly employs 430,000 people and supports millions of private-sector jobs. Our members include more than 340 US public transit agencies, many of which provide public transportation services using vans and minivans.

We greatly appreciate the opportunity to respond to the Federal Transit Administration’s (FTA) Notice of Proposed Buy America Waiver for Battery Electric Minibuses and Request for Comment (Docket No. FTA–2024-0018), published in the Federal Register at 89 FR 104285 on December 20, 2024.

APTA strongly supports Buy America and applauds the Administration’s continued efforts to ensure the use of American-made materials in FTA-funded projects. These Buy America requirements are critical to U.S. job creation, timely project delivery, quality, and building U.S. manufacturing capacity.

To help achieve these Buy America goals, APTA strongly supports the phased three-year general non-availability waiver of Buy America requirements proposed by FTA for battery electric minibuses used in public transportation.
 
On November 18, 2024, FTA issued a five-year partial, time-limited general unavailability waiver of Buy America for vans and minivans because FTA was unable to identify any manufacturer of non-Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA)-accessible vans and minivans that fully complies with Buy America. APTA had urged and fully supported that waiver. The proposed waiver for battery electric minivans used in public transportation is appropriate and important for the same reason: the unavailability of Buy America-compliant electric vehicles. Approximately 150 letters have been submitted to FTA in support of the waiver. Granting the waiver will enable public transportation agencies to procure electric minivans, providing safe and climate-friendly transportation to thousands of transit riders.

APTA members deploy minivans for on-demand, paratransit, and carpool services. The use of electric minivans helps transit agencies meet state zero-emission and climate mandates and supports important community efforts to provide non-polluting transit vehicles. The use of larger zero-emission buses to serve on-demand and paratransit needs typically is neither economical nor operationally feasible. Electric minivans are sized to serve these smaller, highly specialized markets in an environmentally friendly manner. Unfortunately, as FTA has concluded, there simply are no electric minibuses available in the United States that meet FTA’s domestic content or final assembly requirements under Buy America.

APTA was very fortunate to participate with FTA and the members of the Administration at the White House Clean Bus Manufacturing Roundtable held in February 2024. Through the APTA Bus Manufacturing Task Force, we have worked together with bus manufacturers, suppliers, and public transit agencies to build a more competitive, financially stable bus manufacturing capacity in this country. These efforts are critical as the nation’s transit agencies transition to zero-emission bus technologies. Unfortunately, more work is required to ensure that all types of zero-emission buses—from heavy duty buses to minivans—can be manufactured in the U.S. in compliance with Buy America.

The proposed phased waiver will provide a two- to three-year cushion for building U.S. capacity to manufacture electric minivans, while preserving the ability of transit agencies to meet their immediate needs for such minivans. Moreover, the procurement of minivans now will help demonstrate to manufacturers and suppliers that there is a strong and long-term market in the United States for U.S.-manufactured and US-assembled buses and bus components. APTA, of course, strongly encourages foreign minivan manufacturers to incorporate American-made and compliant parts and components that are readily available and would not adversely impact delivery requirements.

Thank you for your consideration and support for public transportation in the United States.

Sincerely,

Paul P. Skoutelas
President and CEO

title: Comment from Everett Transit
printtext:
January 3, 2025
U.S. Department of Transportation
Docket. No. FTA-2024-0018-0001

Everett Transit strongly supports the proposed Buy America waiver on electric minibuses. Everett Transit has made significant progress electrifying its fleet and expects nearly 70% of its fixed-route fleet to be electric by the end of CY 2025. However, Everett Transit has been unable to progress in electrifying its demand response paratransit fleet due to the lack of availability of Buy America compliant electric minibuses. This waiver will enable Everett Transit to make progress in electrifying the paratransit fleet which will result in emission reductions for the climate.

In addition, Everett Transit recommends the waiver be put in place for five years rather than the three years proposed in the Federal Register. Long lead times for vehicles will limit transit agencies’ ability to make use of the waiver if the waiver is only good for three years. This will also give vehicle manufacturers more time to establish production of electric minibuses in the United States, ensuring that agencies can procure electric minibuses while production is still being established. Extending the waiver will also ensure that the resulting environmental benefits of electric minibuses are realized continuously until Buy America compliant vehicles are made available.

Thank you for your consideration.

title: Comment from Rochester Genesee Regional Transportation Authority
printtext:
DRAFT FEDERAL REGISTER SUBMISSION
In Support of DOT/FTA Docket No. FTA-2024-0018
Federal Register Published Document: 2026-16812 (91 FR 53478)

Dear Colleagues,

The Rochester Genesee Regional Transportation Authority (RGRTA) in Rochester, NY, writes today in strong support of the FTA's temporary and targeted Buy America waiver (FTA Docket No. FTA-2024-0018) submitted to the Federal Transit Administration (FTA).

Following the initial waiver request submitted from sixteen transit systems across five states, we are pleased to see this waiver move to final consideration. Timely approval of this waiver will help ensure these transit systems and others across the country can continue to provide timely, reliable, and quality service in the face of a growing crisis in the small bus marketplace.

The cutaway marketplace is experiencing significant challenges, including long delivery times and significant cost increases. Further, consolidation in the small bus marketplace will continue to to have serious and profound consequences on daily operations which invariably will lead to service disruptions and increasing safety issues.

The e-JEST and JEST vehicles are purpose-built minibuses with a 12-15 year useful life that can be delivered in as little as three to six months. Functionally, these products are a good fit for the transit need to increase traditional propulsion and zero-emission vehicles in rural areas, on-demand and paratransit operations.

Providing a temporary waiver for a buses like these will incentivize future domestic manufacturing in the United States and create hundreds of American jobs. If granted a temporary waiver, Karsan Automotive - the manufacturer of the JEST and e-JEST - and Damera Bus - the North American dealer - have committed to meet the 70% domestic content and final assembly requirements of Buy America within two years. For example, the e-JEST already has 30% American content and will be incorporating battery packs made by One Battery in Michigan, which will immediately increase domestic content to over 50% and invest in the U.S. battery marketplace.

Thus, we feel it is appropriate and within the spirit of Buy America to provide a temporary waiver to incentivize domestic manufacturing, production, and use of these needed vehicles to American transit systems. Incorporating these vehicles into U.S. fleets will allow our transit systems to meet important climate objectives, improve competition, alleviate the strain on the supply chain and provide the service capabilities needed by our transit riding public. As such, we respectfully request a limited duration, general non-availability and public interest waiver for low entrance, 20-foot, zero-emission minibuses.

Thank you for your time and consideration.

Sincerely,
Miguel Velázquez, CEO

As a California employer, we’ve put in the hard work and capital to ensure our products fully comply with the Buy America Act. Please protect the real progress we’ve made together under Buy America and reject Waiver Docket No. FTA-2024-0018. Keeping these standards high ensures continued investment in American manufacturing and better transit solutions for the riders who depend on them.

title: Comment from Steve Bolin
printtext:
Subject: Comment on FTA Proposed Buy America Waiver for Electric Minibuses

Greetings. Hoekstra Transportation is a 4th generation, family-owned Michigan small business operating since 1928 and is currently one of the largest small and medium duty bus dealers in the USA. We have over 30 years of FTA funded contract experience and represent some of the best bus and van manufacturers in the world, including electric mini-buses.

We are responding to requested comments on the Federal Transit Administration’s (FTA) proposed general non-availability waiver of Buy America requirements for electric minibuses, which was recently published for public input. Hoekstra Transportation strongly opposes this proposed waiver and urges the FTA to review its implications.

Under the Buy America statute, federally funded rolling stock projects must meet stringent domestic content and assembly requirements, ensuring that U.S.-manufactured vehicles are prioritized.
As a dealer for Optimal Low-Floor EV, a Michigan based company, the S1 low-floor electric shuttle is fully compliant with these standards, and this proposed waiver would not only undermine these established principles but also negatively impact our business and the broader domestic manufacturing sector.

The proposed waiver allows exceptions for electric minibuses that meet certain specifications and cites the non-availability of compliant vehicles. This is simply not the case. Optimal EV supplies two different products that meet the Buy America criteria with the Electric Low-Floor Transit product also being Altoona tested, as required by the FTA. The S1 would compete directly with the product line(s) asking for the waiver.

We believe the waiver could have several detrimental effects, including:

1. Erosion of Market Share for Compliant Manufacturers:
Optimal EV, a Buy America-compliant manufacturer, has invested significantly in developing vehicles that meet these standards. The proposed waiver would enable non-compliant vehicles to enter the market, creating unfair competition and undermining the investments made by U.S. manufacturers.

2. Disincentivizing Domestic Manufacturing:
Allowing non-compliant vehicles would reduce the urgency for manufacturers to establish domestic supply chains and final assembly facilities, directly countering FTA’s stated goals of fostering onshoring and building domestic manufacturing capacity.

3. Job Losses in the U.S. Manufacturing Sector:
By granting waivers for non-compliant vehicles, the waiver could redirect procurement funds to foreign manufacturers, potentially leading to job losses in U.S.-based operations and assembly facilities.

4. Market Saturation by Non-Compliant Imports:
The waiver’s broad scope and its application to any eligible FTA funding recipient risk saturating the market with non-compliant imports, limiting opportunities for compliant manufacturers to grow and innovate.

We believe that granting this waiver would set a concerning precedent, weakening the Buy America statute’s intent, and adversely affecting U.S. manufacturers and workers.

Thank you for the opportunity to voice our concerns and for your attention to our strong opposition.

title: Comment from Anonymous
printtext:
While I recognize the urgency of addressing supply constraints, I would like to raise several critical considerations about the scope and potential impacts of this Buy America waiver for battery electric minibuses.

1. The proposed waiver lacks any explicit limitation on the number of units that may be procured under its terms. Given the basis of the waiver is the lengthy timelines to receive Buy America-compliant vehicles, it is essential for the Federal Transit Administration (FTA) to determine what quantity of production would normalize these timelines. Establishing a cap on the number of units procured under the waiver would ensure that domestic suppliers are not unfairly undercut by prolonged or excessive reliance on non-compliant alternatives.

2. The proposed three-year duration is meant to foster domestic manufacturing; however, there is no assurance that this period will yield the intended results. Instead, it is possible that the influx of vehicles produced using cheap offshore labor could shutter existing domestic manufacturing capacity. This would leave the market dependent on foreign suppliers, potentially necessitating a longer-term or even permanent waiver, which would be counterproductive to the goals of Buy America.

3. The waiver provides no binding assurances that foreign suppliers will establish manufacturing facilities in the United States to create a level playing field. Without firm commitments or clear penalties for failing to establish domestic operations, the waiver could fail to achieve its stated purpose of encouraging onshoring. I urge the FTA to impose conditions that require foreign suppliers to establish U.S.-based production facilities within the waiver period to qualify for future contracts.

4. Given China’s designation as a non-market economy and the concerns about anti-competitive practices, I strongly recommend that the waiver explicitly prohibit the import of minibuses manufactured in China or manufactured in the U.S. by a foreign entity of concern, or affiliate. Allowing these vehicles to enter the U.S. market could undermine the domestic industry further by leveraging state-subsidized production that operates outside fair market norms. This would be inconsistent with the intent of Buy America to foster a robust and sustainable domestic manufacturing base.

While the proposed waiver addresses a legitimate supply chain concern, it must be carefully structured to balance immediate needs with long-term domestic manufacturing goals. Thank you for your consideration of these comments. I hope the FTA will take these issues into account to strengthen the waiver’s alignment with the broader goals of Buy America – protecting domestic industry, economic interests, and national security.

title: Comment from Portage Area Regional Transportation Authority (PARTA)
printtext:
Dear Sir or Madam:

I am writing in strong support of a temporary Buy America waiver request for the low floor, zero emission minibus called the e-JEST. Sixteen transit systems from five states submitted the non-availability and public interest waiver request and over 150 transit systems from across the country have publicly weighed in with support. It’s critical this waiver is approved to ensure transit systems across the country can continue to provide timely, reliable, and quality service in the face of a growing crisis in the small bus marketplace.

The cutaway marketplace is experiencing significant challenges, including long delivery times and significant cost increases. Making matters worse, El Dorado National-California (ENC) will be exiting the cutaway market by winding down its manufacturing by the end of the year. The consolidation in the small bus marketplace is going to have serious and profound consequences on daily operations which invariably will lead to service disruptions and increasing safety issues.

The e-JEST is a purpose-built all-electric minibus with a 12–15-year useful life and can be delivered in three to six months. Functionally, the e-JEST is a good fit for the transit trend line of increasing zero emission vehicles in rural areas, on-demand, paratransit operations and urban circulators.

Providing a temporary waiver for the e-JEST, and other buses like it, will incentivize future domestic manufacturing in the United States and create hundreds of American jobs. If granted a temporary waiver, Karsan Automotive - the manufacturer of the e-JEST - and Damera Bus - the North American dealer - have committed to meet the 70% domestic content and final assembly requirements of Buy America within two years. They are in the process of sourcing domestic content in a phased-in approach and siting domestic supply and manufacturing facilities within the United States, including establishing a parts facility in Iowa and California.

Thus, we feel it is appropriate and within the spirit of Buy America to provide a temporary waiver to incentivize domestic manufacturing, production, and use of these needed vehicles to American transit systems. Incorporating these vehicles into U.S. fleets will allow our transit systems to meet important climate objectives, improve competition, alleviate the strain on the supply chain and provide the service capabilities needed by our transit riding public.

As such, we strongly support approval of the temporary, general non-availability and public interest waiver for a low entrance, zero emission minibus.

Thank you for your consideration of this important request.

title: Comment from Valley Regional Transit
printtext:
Valley Regional Transit (VRT) is the regional public transportation authority for Ada and Canyon counties in Idaho. VRT serves two individual urbanized areas: one large urban area encompassing Boise, Meridian and the surrounding area with an urbanized population of 449,776, and one small urban area encompassing Nampa, Caldwell and the surrounding area with an urbanized population of 193,935 as reported from the last census. VRT’s full urbanized population is 643,711, and the service area (two-county region) population is approximately 822,890.

VRT relies on federal funding for a portion of all rolling stock and is therefore obligated to meet Buy America standards for all purchases. VRT has a strategic goal of reducing our carbon footprint through the use of electric and low-emission vehicles. We are currently working to set a target for achieving that goal for all our rolling stock.

VRT’s transit fleet (full-size) is currently a mix of Battery Electric Buses (BEB) and Compressed Natural Gas (CNG) buses. These buses are designed for transit use with a low floor entry design and a longer useful life than body-on-chassis vehicles. The transit fleet is used for high volume fixed route service.

VRT has a paratransit fleet of body-on-chassis vehicles and large transit vans. Some of these have been converted to CNG propulsion, while others are gasoline powered. We have not been able to find smaller battery electric vehicles that meet current standards. Additionally, none of our paratransit fleet has low-floor entry and the useful life of the vehicles is a shorter span than our transit fleet. Our paratransit fleet is used on lower volume fixed routes as well as various demand response services including paratransit and microtransit services.

VRT desires to transition the entire fleet, both transit and paratransit, to low and no emission vehicles to achieve our energy goals. In order to meet that target, we are interested in procuring zero emission battery electric minibuses that also meet our other goals of low floor entry and longer useful life. We are confident that battery electric unibody low floor vehicles will improve the energy efficiency, accessibility, comfort and rider experience on our lower volume routes and VRT’s many demand response services.

VRT researched vehicles available for procurement that meet FTA's domestic content or final assembly requirements for Buy America eligibility and have been unable to find a domestic manufacturer of electric minibuses who meet our criteria. VRT is one of the agencies that signed on to support the non-availability request for waiver for electric minibuses.

We ask FTA to finalize and grant a three-year non-availability waiver of FTA's Buy America rolling stock requirements for any vehicle with all of the following characteristics.
•Powered by a battery electric propulsion system
•Has, or is capable of having, low-floor entry
•Is of unibody or monocoque construction
•Has a gross vehicle weight rating or weight of less than 11,794 kg (26,001 lbs)
•Is designed to transport fewer than 16 seated passengers including the driver
•Is not required to report to the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration under the American Automobile Labelling Act

VRT is confident that such a waiver will encourage potential market entrants to build the requisite domestic supply chains and establish a final assembly facility in the United States, and we hope it will spur domestic manufacturers to compete in this market. VRT understands that that the waiver would phase out over time and end three years after it is finalized.

Please grant the waiver as proposed.

Sincerely,

Elaine Clegg
CEO Valley Regional Transit
eclegg@ridevrt.org
valleyregionaltransit.org

(F) 208.846.8564

title: Comment from Lynn Gessler
printtext:
Docket No. FDA-2015-D-4750-0439
Food and Drug Administration
5630 Fishers Lane, Room 1061
Rockville, MD 20852

Re: FDA’s Reclassification of Desiccated Thyroid Extract (DTE) as a Biologic

To Whom It May Concern:

I am writing with deep concern about the FDA’s recent decision to reclassify desiccated thyroid extract (DTE) as a biologic. For more than 100 years, DTE has been a lifeline for patients like me who do not do well on synthetic thyroid medicines. The decision puts that lifeline at risk.

For many of us, DTE isn’t just another treatment option, it’s the only treatment that makes daily life possible. Without it, we face fatigue, weight gain, brain fog, depression, and countless other symptoms that make even basic tasks difficult. I have seen how quickly quality of life deteriorates when DTE is taken away, and I am not alone.

This reclassification just doesn’t make sense for patients. It creates unnecessary barriers and opens the door for a single company to control the product, driving up costs and shutting out the compounding pharmacies that have provided access to this medicine for years. The result will be fewer choices, higher prices, and patients left with no effective alternatives.

What makes this especially painful is that this change wasn’t made because of new science or safety concerns. It seems to be happening because of pressure from a large drug company with financial interest. Patients like me are left wondering why our voices don’t matter more than corporate profits.

I urge the FDA to reconsider this harmful action. Please keep DTE regulated the same way it has been for decades, protect patient choice and access, and put patients first by ensuring DTE remains available at compounding pharmacies for when other treatments fail.

For hundreds and thousands of Americans, this is not an abstract policy change. It’s about whether we can live full, healthy lives. I ask you to stand with patients and preserve access to DTE.

Respectfully,

printtext:
Docket No. FDA-2015-D-4750-0439
Food and Drug Administration
5630 Fishers Lane, Room 1061
Rockville, MD 20852

Re: FDA’s Reclassification of Desiccated Thyroid Extract (DTE) as a Biologic

To Whom It May Concern:

I am writing with deep concern about the FDA’s recent decision to reclassify desiccated thyroid extract (DTE) as a biologic. For more than 100 years, DTE has been a lifeline for patients like me who do not do well on synthetic thyroid medicines. The decision puts that lifeline at risk.

For many of us, DTE isn’t just another treatment option, it’s the only treatment that makes daily life possible. Without it, we face fatigue, weight gain, brain fog, depression, and countless other symptoms that make even basic tasks difficult. I have seen how quickly quality of life deteriorates when DTE is taken away, and I am not alone.

This reclassification just doesn’t make sense for patients. It creates unnecessary barriers and opens the door for a single company to control the product, driving up costs and shutting out the compounding pharmacies that have provided access to this medicine for years. The result will be fewer choices, higher prices, and patients left with no effective alternatives.

What makes this especially painful is that this change wasn’t made because of new science or safety concerns. It seems to be happening because of pressure from a large drug company with financial interest. Patients like me are left wondering why our voices don’t matter more than corporate profits.

I urge the FDA to reconsider this harmful action. Please keep DTE regulated the same way it has been for decades, protect patient choice and access, and put patients first by ensuring DTE remains available at compounding pharmacies for when other treatments fail.

For hundreds and thousands of Americans, this is not an abstract policy change. It’s about whether we can live full, healthy lives. I ask you to stand with patients and preserve access to DTE.

Respectfully,

5630 Fishers Lane, Room 1061

Re: FDA’s Reclassification of Desiccated Thyroid Extract (DTE) as a Biologic

To Whom It May Concern:

As a prescriber who has cared for patients with thyroid disease for many years, I am writing to express my strong concern about the FDA’s decision to reclassify desiccated thyroid extract (DTE) as a biologic.

For some patients, synthetic levothyroxine or combination therapy simply does not restore thyroid balance or quality of life. In those cases, DTE is not just one option among many—it is often the only therapy that provides meaningful relief from debilitating symptoms such as fatigue, cognitive impairment, and depression. When patients are denied access to DTE, they are left with no effective alternative.

This reclassification threatens to eliminate an essential therapy by restricting its availability to a single manufacturer and cutting compounding pharmacies out of the supply chain. That outcome will reduce patient choice, drive up costs, and undermine the physician’s ability to exercise clinical judgment in tailoring care to the individual.

What makes this action especially troubling is that it appears to rest not on new scientific evidence or safety concerns, but rather on a change in regulatory posture that is inconsistent with FDA’s own long-standing treatment of DTE. The process was unusual, lacking the transparency and public engagement that a decision of this magnitude demands.

I urge FDA to reconsider. DTE has been prescribed safely for more than a century. It should continue to be regulated as a drug, not a biologic, and remain available through compounding pharmacies so that physicians can prescribe it when clinically appropriate. My patients’ well-being depends on it.

Respectfully,

I am writing with deep concern about the FDA’s recent decision to reclassify desiccated thyroid extract (DTE) as a biologic. For more than 100 years, DTE has been a lifeline for patients like me who do not do well on synthetic thyroid medicines. The decision puts that lifeline at risk.

For many of us, DTE isn’t just another treatment option, it’s the only treatment that makes daily life possible. Without it, we face fatigue, weight gain, brain fog, depression, and countless other symptoms that make even basic tasks difficult. I have seen how quickly quality of life deteriorates when DTE is taken away, and I am not alone.

This reclassification just doesn’t make sense for patients. It creates unnecessary barriers and opens the door for a single company to control the product, driving up costs and shutting out the compounding pharmacies that have provided access to this medicine for years. The result will be fewer choices, higher prices, and patients left with no effective alternatives.

What makes this especially painful is that this change wasn’t made because of new science or safety concerns. It seems to be happening because of pressure from a large drug company with financial interest. Patients like me are left wondering why our voices don’t matter more than corporate profits.

I urge the FDA to reconsider this harmful action. Please keep DTE regulated the same way it has been for decades, protect patient choice and access, and put patients first by ensuring DTE remains available at compounding pharmacies for when other treatments fail.

For hundreds and thousands of Americans, this is not an abstract policy change. It’s about whether we can live full, healthy lives. I ask you to stand with patients and preserve access to DTE.

Respectfully,

title: Comment from Karen McGuggart
printtext:
I strongly urge the FAA to require that all commercial aircraft carry epinephrine auto-injectors for both adults and children as part of their onboard emergency medical equipment.

Severe allergic reactions can occur without warning, even in individuals with no known history of allergies. Anaphylaxis is a rapidly progressing, life-threatening emergency, and the only first-line treatment is prompt administration of epinephrine. Every minute of delay increases the risk of respiratory failure, cardiac arrest, and death.

While many aircraft carry basic emergency medical kits, these kits often do not include epinephrine auto-injectors that can be administered quickly and safely. Flight attendants and fellow passengers should have access to easy-to-use epinephrine auto-injectors that can be administered while coordinating with any medical professionals who may be onboard and preparing for an emergency landing if necessary.

Food allergies continue to rise in both children and adults. Millions of Americans live with life-threatening allergies, and many travel by air. Having FAA-required epinephrine auto-injectors onboard every commercial flight provides a critical safety net that has the potential to save lives.

Thank you for considering my comment.

Heather Clamp

title: Comment from Mindy Valle
printtext:
I strongly support modernizing emergency medical kits (EMKs) aboard commercial aircraft, but I urge the FAA to ensure that increased flexibility for air carriers does not result in reduced minimum standards for lifesaving medications and equipment.

As both a registered nurse and the parent of a young child with multiple severe food allergies, including allergies capable of causing anaphylaxis, I am acutely aware of how quickly a medical emergency can become life-threatening. An aircraft at cruising altitude is a uniquely vulnerable environment. Passengers cannot simply call 911 or be transported to an emergency department, and diversion to the nearest airport can take significant time. The medical resources available onboard during those critical minutes matter.

Any performance-based standard should therefore establish clear, enforceable minimum requirements for time-sensitive emergencies, particularly anaphylaxis. Commercial aircraft should carry an adequate supply of epinephrine in forms and doses appropriate for both adults and children. The availability of epinephrine should not depend upon whether an individual passenger happens to have brought an autoinjector, whether that device is accessible, or whether a medically trained passenger happens to be onboard.

I also urge the FAA to consider pediatric patients specifically when establishing minimum EMK capabilities. Children are not simply smaller adults. Medication concentrations, dosing, equipment sizes, and treatment needs can differ significantly. A kit may technically contain a medication while still being functionally inadequate if it cannot be safely administered to a child.

In addition, flexibility in kit contents should be paired with strong requirements for inspection, replacement of expired medications, accessibility during an emergency, standardized organization and labeling, and meaningful crew training. Flight crews should be able to rapidly identify and access emergency medications, and medical professionals who volunteer to assist should not lose critical time trying to determine what medications or equipment are actually available.

I encourage the FAA to adopt a performance-based approach only if it establishes a strong national safety floor. Airlines may be permitted to exceed or adapt beyond that standard, but essential lifesaving capabilities should not vary significantly depending on which carrier a passenger happens to fly.

For passengers with serious medical conditions and for parents of children at risk of anaphylaxis, adequate onboard emergency medical resources are not a convenience. At 35,000 feet, they may represent the only immediate medical treatment available. I urge the FAA to prioritize passenger safety by requiring EMKs that are adequately stocked, pediatric-capable, readily accessible, consistently maintained, and equipped to treat anaphylaxis and other foreseeable life-threatening emergencies.

Expecting flight crew or passengers to manually measure and draw doses into a syringe during extreme turbulence and high-stress panic is unsafe and unrealistic. Pre-measured auto-injectors or nasal sprays allow anyone to act instantly.

As a frequent traveler and someone who lives with a severe allergy, I know that exposure can sometimes be unexpected and difficult to control in public environments. I also have family members with multiple food and environmental allergies, reinforcing how unpredictable allergic reactions can be.

Importantly, a passenger does not need to have a known allergy to experience anaphylaxis. Allergies can develop at any point in a person's life, and a first severe reaction may occur without warning. Having epinephrine readily available on every aircraft provides an essential safety measure for passengers and gives flight crews an important tool during a medical emergency.

I urge the FAA to require epinephrine on all commercial aircraft. It is a relatively simple safety measure that could save lives when seconds matter.

title: Comment from Fernando Campos
printtext:
Recommendation – Add Return-to-Service Activity on Transport-Category Aircraft as a Qualifying Recent-Experience Activity

I recommend that the FAA expand the proposed recent-experience requirements to recognize qualifying return-to-service (RTS) activity involving transport-category aircraft.

Specifically, I recommend that completion of at least six qualifying RTS events on transport-category aircraft within the preceding twelve calendar months be accepted as an additional means of satisfying the Inspection Rating recent-experience requirement.

The current activity-based pathways do not fully reflect the maintenance environment in which many experienced A&P mechanics and IA holders work. In particular, mechanics supporting complex transport-category aircraft may exercise substantial technical, regulatory, inspection, records-review, and airworthiness responsibilities without routinely performing annual inspections or personally executing major repairs or major alterations in a manner that qualifies under the existing activity pathways.

A return-to-service event involving a transport-category aircraft may require a mechanic to evaluate completed maintenance, review applicable technical data, assess maintenance records and required documentation, verify completion of inspection requirements, evaluate open discrepancies, confirm compliance with applicable Airworthiness Directives and other airworthiness requirements, and determine whether the aircraft is eligible for approval for return to service.

These responsibilities directly exercise many of the same competencies that the Inspection Rating is intended to preserve, including regulatory knowledge, technical-data application, records review, inspection judgment, and airworthiness decision making.

Accordingly, I recommend that the FAA add a sixth qualifying recent-experience pathway based on documented RTS activity involving transport-category aircraft. Specifically, completion of at least six qualifying RTS events within the preceding twelve calendar months should satisfy the recent-experience requirement.

To ensure that the activity represents meaningful exercise of inspection and airworthiness responsibilities, the FAA could define a qualifying RTS event as one in which the Inspection Rating holder personally exercises return-to-service authority following a substantive maintenance event on a transport-category aircraft and makes the required maintenance record entry or otherwise assumes documented responsibility for the return-to-service determination.

This additional pathway would better recognize the actual work performed by experienced mechanics in corporate, business aviation, air carrier, and other complex aircraft maintenance environments while maintaining an objective, documentable, and safety-relevant recent-experience standard.

title: Comment from Tracy Ryan
printtext:
Re: Docket No. FAA–2026–6671

I strongly support the FAA's proposal to replace the current Inspection Authorization (IA) with a permanent Inspection Rating. Eliminating the recurring renewal process while retaining appropriate qualification requirements is a welcome modernization that reduces unnecessary administrative burden while maintaining aviation safety.

I respectfully request that the FAA expand the transition provisions to include mechanics whose Inspection Authorization expired before the effective date of the final rule.

Under the proposal, an individual who holds a valid Inspection Authorization on the effective date would transition directly to the new Inspection Rating. However, an equally qualified mechanic whose Inspection Authorization expired before that date would still be required to begin the process anew by submitting FAA Form 8610-1, obtaining authorization from the FAA, and successfully completing another Inspection Authorization knowledge test and oral evaluation.

This creates an arbitrary distinction based solely on the expiration date of an Inspection Authorization rather than on the mechanic's qualifications, competence, or continued involvement in aircraft maintenance.

For example, two mechanics could have identical backgrounds, identical experience, and identical employment histories. One mechanic whose IA remains valid on the effective date would automatically receive the new Inspection Rating. The other mechanic, whose IA expired only a short time earlier—even by a single day—would be required to repeat the entire application and examination process. The difference between these two individuals is not one of knowledge, skill, or safety, but simply the date on which the authorization expired.

An individual who previously earned an Inspection Authorization has already demonstrated the qualifications, knowledge, and experience required by the FAA. Many former IA holders continue to work full-time as certificated mechanics after their authorization expires. Although they are no longer authorized to perform IA-specific functions such as annual inspections or major repair and alteration approvals, they continue to maintain and develop the technical knowledge and maintenance skills that originally qualified them to hold an Inspection Authorization.

I encourage the FAA to establish a pathway that allows former IA holders whose authorization expired before the effective date of the final rule to obtain the new Inspection Rating without repeating the initial application and examination process, provided they can demonstrate that they have remained actively engaged in aircraft maintenance as certificated mechanics since their IA expired.

This approach would be fully consistent with the FAA's stated objective of reducing unnecessary administrative burden while maintaining safety. It would recognize qualifications that have already been demonstrated, avoid requiring experienced aviation maintenance professionals to repeat examinations they have previously passed, and eliminate an arbitrary distinction based solely on the effective date of the rule rather than on any meaningful difference in competency or safety.

Providing this transition pathway would also increase the number of experienced mechanics available to perform inspection functions. At a time when the aviation industry continues to face challenges in recruiting and retaining qualified maintenance personnel, enabling former IA holders who have remained active in aircraft maintenance to regain inspection privileges without unnecessary administrative barriers would strengthen the aviation maintenance workforce while preserving the FAA's high standards for safety. This outcome would benefit aircraft owners, repair stations, and the general aviation community by expanding the pool of experienced inspection-qualified mechanics without reducing qualification standards.

Thank you for considering this recommendation.

title: Comment from Shaune Maycock
printtext:
I am an FAA-certificated Airframe and Powerplant mechanic who has held an Inspection Authorization (IA) for 17 years and has owned and operated an aircraft maintenance facility for the past 20 years. During that time, I have performed hundreds of annual inspections, major repairs, and major alterations on a wide variety of general aviation aircraft.

Overall, I support replacing the current Inspection Authorization with an Inspection Rating. The proposal reduces unnecessary administrative burden while maintaining the high standards expected of mechanics exercising inspection privileges.

My support is based on the understanding that this change will not result in additional testing or certification requirements for mechanics to demonstrate proficiency on specific aircraft types, makes, or models. Current regulations already require mechanics to determine whether they possess the knowledge, experience, and current technical data necessary to perform maintenance or inspections on a particular aircraft. That principle has served the industry well and should remain unchanged.

I encourage the FAA to consider one additional aspect that directly affects aviation safety.

A complete annual inspection is physically demanding. It often requires climbing ladders, crawling beneath instrument panels, accessing wing roots, landing gear compartments, tail cones, and other confined areas. If a mechanic cannot physically access these areas, it becomes difficult to ensure every required inspection item has been completed.

During my 17 years as an IA, I have attended FAA-sponsored IA seminars. I have tremendous respect for the experienced mechanics recognized for decades of service. However, I have also observed some individuals whose physical limitations raised legitimate questions about whether they could still perform every aspect of a complete annual inspection.

My concern is not age. Many mechanics remain highly capable well beyond traditional retirement age, while others develop physical limitations much earlier. My concern is whether an individual exercising the privileges of an Inspection Rating remains physically capable of performing the duties required by the regulations.

I encourage the FAA to consider implementing a process for periodically observing the physical ability of Inspection Rating holders to perform those duties. One possible approach would be an observation by an Aviation Safety Inspector at the local FSDO, or another FAA-approved evaluation process. The purpose would not be to re-test technical knowledge, but simply to determine whether the mechanic can physically perform the inspection tasks associated with the privileges of the Inspection Rating. Any additional evaluation should be based on demonstrated functional ability rather than age alone.

Finally, I would like to raise a broader concern regarding mechanic certification and recent experience requirements. While this proposal focuses on Inspection Rating holders, I believe the FAA should also place greater emphasis on enforcing the recent experience requirements that already apply to certificated Airframe and Powerplant mechanics.
As the owner of an aircraft maintenance facility for 20 years, I have interviewed applicants who held valid A&P certificates but had spent little or no time actively working in aircraft maintenance. Some obtained their certificate primarily to maintain their own aircraft. There is nothing improper about that; however, they are still required to meet the recent experience requirements before exercising the privileges of their certificate.

In my experience, the issue is not a lack of regulation but a lack of enforcement. Mechanics who actively work in the industry every day are expected to remain current, while others who perform only occasional maintenance may continue exercising certificate privileges despite not meeting the recency requirements. Consistent enforcement of the existing regulations would promote a more uniform professional standard and further enhance aviation safety.

I appreciate the FAA's efforts to modernize the Inspection Authorization process while maintaining safety. I believe this proposal is a positive step forward and encourage the FAA to continue improving safety without creating unnecessary burdens for certificated mechanics.
