I do support the FAA making the IA certificate a permanent certificate like an Airframe or Powerplant rating. However, I don't believe it is in the best interest of the National Aerospace System (NAS) to change the IA in this way. The proposed rule, in my opinion, takes more of a reactive approach to IA surveillance since there is no longer a review of IA paperwork every odd year in March. The reason I believe this to be a reactive approach is because Aviation Safety Inspectors (ASI) do not regularly, if at all, audit mechanics. So the only time an ASI would audit an IA under this proposed rule making would more than likely be after an accident has occurred or a complaint received on that individual.

What may be a good middle ground between the FAA's goal in saving money and maintaining the integrity of the NAS could be implementing a system similar to the flight reviews that certificated pilots must adhere to. The FAA could still issue permanent cards while also implementing a "maintenance review" wherein an IA holder would contact an ASI 24 calendar months after their IA issue date to have that ASI determine if the IA holder has met the renewal requirements of their IA.

Lastly, I believe implementing a basic medical certificate for IA holders would be in the best interest of the NAS. There are many aircraft (nearly every single helicopter) that require some sort of climbing, whether on the aircraft itself or on a ladder, to inspect critical flight components. However, there are still plenty of aircraft that require no climbing, so thus, limitations could be implemented on the medical certificate that could state: "restricted to low wing aircraft", "unable to perform inspection on rotorcraft", "limited to inspection of aircraft that do not require climbing", etc.

As a current IA holder, I would love to have a permanent card and put an end to filing renewal applications every odd year, however, not in the way this current proposed rule making proposes.

title: Comment from Fernando Campos
printtext:
I support the FAA’s proposal to convert the Inspection Authorization (IA) into a permanent Inspection Rating (IR) and replace the current biennial renewal process with appropriate recent-experience requirements. This represents a logical modernization of mechanic certification and has the potential to reduce unnecessary administrative burden without diminishing the qualifications or responsibilities associated with inspection privileges.

However, I recommend that the FAA further clarify the proposed rolling twelve-calendar-month recent-experience requirements, provide nationally consistent guidance regarding the meaning of “actively engaged,” reconsider whether the fixed-base-of-operations requirement remains appropriate in today’s digital and mobile maintenance environment, and clearly define acceptable documentation for demonstrating recent experience.

I also recommend that the FAA reconsider whether the proposed Inspection Rating Airman Certification Standards (ACS) framework is the most appropriate testing model for the IR. While I support clear, standardized, and legally enforceable testing standards, the FAA should demonstrate why integrating task-specific risk-management elements into the Inspection Rating standard is necessary and how those elements will be objectively evaluated. The FAA should consider whether a more focused PTS-style standard would better evaluate the technical, regulatory, records, inspection, and airworthiness competencies central to IR privileges.

Finally, I recommend careful review of the optional oral-examination pathways for maintaining or restoring recent experience. A lapse in recent experience should not, by itself, be treated as evidence that an otherwise qualified mechanic is no longer competent to hold the rating. Any oral examination process should be objective, nationally consistent, narrowly tailored to current inspection knowledge, and governed by clear standards regarding scope, scoring, retesting, and potential consequences.

title: Comment from JOHN MCDERMOTT
printtext:
I am writing as a current Inspection Authorization (IA) holder to comment on the proposed conversion of the IA to a permanent Inspection Rating (IR) with a rolling recent-experience requirement. I support eliminating the biennial March renewal process and the “start-over” consequence of an expired IA. A non-expiring rating with a 12-month recent-experience requirement is a practical modernization that reduces administrative burden while preserving safety.
Proficiency and Recent Experience; The five activity options from § 65.93(a) remain appropriate. The strongest safety path is actual exercise of the privileges—performing annual inspections or major repairs/alterations requiring IA/IR approval. Progressive inspections are also valuable when applicable.
The 8-hour refresher course and FAA oral test should remain available as alternatives. The final rule and guidance should:
Emphasize hands-on exercise of privileges as the preferred method of maintaining proficiency.
Explicitly confirm that courses and seminars listed on the FAA Safety Team (FAASTeam) website (FAASafety.gov), including those that also qualify for AMT Awards Program credit, continue to satisfy the 8-hour refresher option.
Provide clear examples of acceptable documentation for each of the five options.
Confirm that records need only be retained for the preceding 24 months and produced upon request, with no new mandatory reporting outside of surveillance or investigation.
Clarify that completion of an acceptable 8-hour course or oral test restores privileges for the next 12 months without re-application or a written exam.
The proposed 24-month transition window plus grace period is reasonable, provided the process to obtain a replacement mechanic certificate showing the Inspection Rating is simple, online, and free of charge.
Recommendation; Adopt the permanent Inspection Rating and rolling 12-month recent-experience structure essentially as proposed. Strengthen the guidance to prioritize actual exercise of inspection privileges, retain the established FAASTeam/AMT Awards pathway for refresher credit, and provide clear, low-burden documentation methods. This maintains safety, reduces unnecessary administrative work, and gives IA/IR holders a practical path to remain current.
Thank you for the opportunity to comment.

title: Comment from Steve Keesey
printtext:
Purpose: Comment on Proposed IR Rule, docket number FAA-2026-6671
After reviewing this proposed IR rule and noting the statement “FAA’s process for issuing and renewing IAs in this manner has remained largely unchanged since the early 1960s” highlights the need to take the opportunity now to change the current regulatory IA renewal options of 65.93(a)(1)-(5). The two current activity options I am addressing are the four (4) annual inspection requirement, or eight (8) major repair and/or alteration requirement for renewal activity. It is common knowledge for AMTs and the FAA that a person conducting various IA privilege activities is less likely to be a risk in the NAS than a person strictly sitting thru an 8-hour seminar, especially when seminars often contain material that have no relevance to an IA’s responsibilities and more to do with a vender’s opportunity to present their products for sale. This includes the FAA “Approved” courses for IA renewal that have nothing to do with the education of an IA. Examples of this are specialized manufactures maintenance courses on aircraft an IA holds no responsibility for inspections on, but rather only requires an A&P to conduct the inspections and approval for return to service.
Due to the items discussed above and experience as an IA for 30 years, I am recommending a change to Part 65.93(a)(1) and (a)(2) to change to a combination of items listed in (1) and (2) of the regulation for the purpose of renewal. My recommendation, although I am sure there are others, is to give major repairs and/or alterations the equiveillance of one annual inspection, or any other combinations as seem adequate. This would also remove the finical burden for the need to take off work to attend an 8-hour seminar, which can require travel and a hotel stay to attend, or loose productive time completing an online course when the IA has completed a combination of the activities but is short on either inspections or repairs to be elidable for renewal on either. IA’s have always been puzzled by this oversight of the renewal requirements originally provided. This proposed IR rule is the right time to correct the renewal issue thereby removing the time and financial burdens placed on the IA because of these current requirements.
As with the FAA benefits listed for the purpose of this change to a rating, the FAA should apply its own standards to the IA that would increase active IA/IR efficiency, save critical hours for safety-focused tasks maintaining the aircraft fleet, and remove cost and lost time burdens linked to complying with the existing regulation’s current 8-hour renewal requirement when a combination of activities have been met.

title: Comment from Anonymous
printtext:
I am an A&P mechanic with Inspection Authorization, and I support efforts to modernize and simplify the current IA renewal process. That said, I have some concerns about replacing the biennial renewal process with a permanent Inspection Rating while relying mostly on individual mechanics to track and document their own recent-experience requirements.

Under the current system, the biennial renewal provides a regular compliance checkpoint. An IA has to periodically show that they’ve completed the required activity or training to keep exercising IA privileges. Even though the underlying requirements are already annual, the renewal process provides an outside check that those requirements have actually been met.

Under the proposed system, the Inspection Rating would stay permanently on the mechanic certificate, and the mechanic would be responsible for deciding whether they’re current and keeping the supporting records. My concern is that without a periodic verification process, some mechanics could unintentionally lose currency and continue exercising inspection privileges, while others might simply fail to comply because there’s no routine FAA review.

This could lead to mechanics holding an Inspection Rating and signing off annual inspections, major repairs, or major alterations without actually meeting the recent-experience requirements. In many cases, that noncompliance might not be discovered until an FAA inspection, enforcement action, accident, or other investigation.

I think the permanent Inspection Rating is a reasonable idea, but I recommend keeping some form of periodic compliance verification. For example, every two years, an Inspection Rating holder could electronically certify that they’ve met the recent-experience requirements and keep the supporting documentation available for FAA review. This could cut down on much of the administrative burden of the current IA renewal process while still providing an important compliance checkpoint.

I respectfully ask the FAA to consider whether eliminating routine verification of Inspection Rating currency could lead to more inadvertent or intentional noncompliance, and what mechanism would replace the existing biennial renewal process for identifying mechanics who haven’t maintained the required recent experience.

He goes to work in a bookstore, and for years applies unsuccessfully for a pilot job. After some years, he is asked by his neighbor to teach his daughter to fly. Having maintained his CFI by taking the online courses, he agrees to teaching the young lady to fly. So, a BFR and 3 take offs and landings and he is now in the right seat. title: Comment from Michael Moore
printtext:
I agree that putting the IR on the certificate eliminates an additional cert, but I oppose the proposed replacement of the Inspection Authorization with a permanent Inspection Rating that relies principally upon self-maintained records of recent experience. This will not go well and this is my short answer.

Inspection Authorization privileges are granted based upon two essential qualifications: a thorough working knowledge of the applicable regulations and maintenance standards, and substantial relevant experience within the aviation-maintenance industry. The written examination may adequately establish an applicant’s knowledge at original issuance, but an examination taken once cannot establish professional currency indefinitely. Only continued relevant experience, recurrent exposure to changing regulations and maintenance information, and meaningful oversight can establish that an individual remains qualified to exercise these privileges.

I also disagree with issuing or preserving inspection privileges as what are sometimes informally called “trophy certificates.” By that term, I mean credentials sought or retained primarily for status by individuals who are not genuinely and actively engaged in the work upon which the privileges are based. Active engagement is not an incidental qualification. It is an express basis for initial issuance under § 65.91 and continued renewal under § 65.93. A person who wants the credential but does not maintain meaningful participation in certificated-aircraft maintenance does not satisfy the purpose of these requirements.

Fraud, abuse, and falsification already occur within the aviation-maintenance system. This includes applicants misrepresenting their qualifications or experience and authorization holders documenting work, inspections, or approvals for which they were not properly qualified or which they did not properly perform. The existence of falsification regulations and FAA enforcement actions demonstrates that self-certification cannot always be accepted without verification. The FAA should examine and disclose its own enforcement data concerning fraudulent experience claims, falsified maintenance records, improper annual inspections, and unauthorized approvals before concluding that less frequent oversight will provide an equivalent level of safety.

A rule that eliminates scheduled renewal and substitutes self-maintained records risks allowing unqualified or inactive individuals to retain inspection privileges largely unchecked. It also makes enforcement primarily reactive: the FAA may discover noncompliance only after defective work, an improper approval for return to service, an enforcement investigation, or an accident has brought the individual’s records under scrutiny. Oversight is most valuable when it identifies a deficiency before that deficiency contributes to an unsafe condition.

This proposal would also largely erase the practical distinction between ordinary mechanic privileges and the substantially greater authority exercised by an IA. An IA does not merely perform maintenance. An IA independently determines whether an aircraft conforms to its approved configuration and is in a condition for safe operation following an annual inspection and may approve aircraft and related products for return to service following major repairs and major alterations. These are consequential airworthiness determinations and justify a higher continuing standard.

Other airman privileges are routinely conditioned upon continuing demonstrations of fitness or currency. Depending upon the operation and privileges exercised, pilots may be subject to medical qualification, recurrent training, flight reviews, recent-flight-experience requirements, proficiency checks, and drug-and-alcohol testing requirements. Although those requirements differ according to the operation, the underlying safety principle is consistent: holding a certificate or rating does not, by itself, establish continuing qualification to exercise every privilege indefinitely.

Inspection personnel should not be treated differently merely because the FAA seeks to reduce its administrative workload. Administrative efficiency is a legitimate objective, but it is not sufficient justification for removing the only routine external verification that an IA holder remains active, properly equipped, informed, and professionally current.

A better approach would retain periodic FAA renewal while modernizing the process. Renewal could be handled electronically through IACRA, supported by documented qualifying activity and mandatory recurrent training. The FAA could also conduct targeted or random audits of renewal activity, facilities, technical-data access, and inspection records. This would reduce administrative burden while preserving meaningful oversight and deterring inactive, unqualified, or dishonest applicants from obtaining or retaining inspection privileges.

title: Comment from Thomas Soerens
printtext:
Docket No.: FAA-2026-6671-0001
Mechanic Certification: Inspection Rating and Recent Experience Requirements

Regarding the NPRM to add an IR rating to the A&P Airman Certificate, I am opposed to the proposed regulatory changes. In my opinion – the NPRM is ‘working too hard for what little you want to accomplish.’ The primary ‘little’ you want to accomplish is to remove the FAA ASI’s responsibility to review and process the Application Form 8610-1 (Application) and Form 8610-5 (IA card) bi-annually. I have been an IA since 1975. I have completed a lot of renewal forms.

14 CFR 65.91(a) states: An application for an inspection authorization is made on a form and in a manner prescribed by the Administrator.

The form and manner for the past 70 years, the Inspection Authorization Renewal has been a paper application and card for the IA authorization.

The term ‘Form and Manner’ indicates FAA Guidance is the process, meaning no NPRM is necessary to make changes. Eliminating the FSDO ASI review of Form 8610-1 and the issue of the bi-annual renewal letter can be accomplished in the IACRA System without having ASI ‘hands on.’ The only element currently missing in IACRA is the issuing of the renewal authorization letter.

Possibly 90% of IA renewal is already in place. This electronic system could be upgraded to include the renewal letter function. The Volpe Center in Cambridge, Ma or whomever has the IACRA contract could assist in this upgrade – and any added ‘feature’ deemed necessary by the FSDO (i.e. Form and Manner Guidance – no NPRM needed).

I am a DAR-T. Annually, in DMS (Designee Management System) I electronically answer a list of questions, digitally sign the application stating the information is true and correct and SUBMIT the application. DMS processes my request at that submission, and if all my answers are correct – it generates my renewal letter with the submission date, the new expiration date of my designation, and the Letter of Authority, signed by my FSDO’s Front Line Manager. The ASI (Managing Specialist) does not review or issue any part of that designation renewal.

IACRA could be developed to function in the same capacity for Inspection Authorization renewal, and no ASI would be involved in the renewal process. IACRA has link to NVIS in the event the FSDO/IFO decides to review an application – if the ASI determines that IA may require dedicated oversight.

Currently IACRA makes a determination if you have the correct minimum number of Annual Inspections, Progressive Inspections, or Major Repairs/Alteration for renewal. IACRA also has the requirement for listing the approved training course name and number and uploading that document and/or an Activity Report. IACRA allows only one renewal method per application (ex. Sufficient annual inspections or training, but not both) before the system moves to the next phase.

Within the 94 pages of the NPRM – there was no discussion of safety concerns with the current IA Regulations and renewal process – other than the review of IA paperwork is ‘work’ for the ASI. For 70 years the current regulations have existed. The NPRM (III Background, B. Need for Rulemaking Action, Paragraph 1, .pdf page 13) states there has been no substantive review of the IA rules for almost 3 decades. The ‘system must have been working effectively for not requiring a review for that long of period. The NPRM paragraph (second sentence) also states in part: ‘Since that time, FAA and industry have enjoyed advances in technology and processes, - - - “

If the NPRM ‘believes’ that text – then use and enhance the existing IACRA system as the advance in technology and processes. Please do not change the Regulations just for the sake of change. The NPRM, in my opinion, opens too many doors for the FAA to lose accountably of an IA’s currency, which could result in illegal entries for return to service.

Additionally, for an IA @$56.45/hr to attend an 8-hour training session is $56.45 x 8hr = $451.60. Added costs for lost revenue of the base of operations when the IA attends that training (lead shop floor technician is ½ of the shop rate) which is $112 x 8hr = $896.00, has a cost of $1348.00 per year, ($2696.00 per 2-years). This cost does not change for an IA in this NPRM. Training is still required.

The NPRM figure of $14.11 to complete the renewal form every 2 years – is really an insignificant cost (.5% of the training cost) per IA.

Thank you for your consideration of my comments. Please read the IACRA User Guide for IA Renewal as an element of your evaluation.

title: Comment from CAE
printtext:
To Whom It May Concern:
I appreciate the opportunity to comment on the FAA's Notice of Proposed Rulemaking regarding the replacement of the Inspection Authorization (IA) with an Inspection Rating and the transition to rolling recent-experience requirements.
I support the FAA's proposal to streamline the maintenance of inspection privileges and align the Inspection Rating with other mechanic ratings. Reducing administrative burden while maintaining safety and competency standards represents a positive modernization of the certification framework. [ACTION NEE...Deadlines | Outlook], [IA Renewal...iderartion | Outlook]
As the FAA considers the future structure of inspection-rating qualifications and recent-experience requirements, I respectfully encourage consideration of maintenance human factors and inspection-supervision competencies as activities that directly support the safe exercise of inspection privileges.
The holder of an Inspection Authorization, and under the proposed rule an Inspection Rating, is authorized not only to perform inspections but also to supervise progressive inspections. The supervisory component of this privilege is significant. Effective inspection supervision requires communication of inspection requirements, coordination of maintenance personnel, evaluation of discrepancies, oversight of corrective actions, review of documentation, and communication of airworthiness-related decisions. These activities directly affect inspection quality, regulatory compliance, and aviation safety. [RE: IA ren...training - | Outlook], [RE: IA ren...rotection | Outlook]
The aviation maintenance community has long recognized that human factors are among the most significant contributors to maintenance errors. Communication failures, ineffective supervision, poor coordination, documentation deficiencies, and decision-making errors can directly influence airworthiness outcomes. As a result, training that addresses these subjects should not necessarily be viewed as general professional development but rather as maintenance-safety competencies that support the effective performance of inspection responsibilities.
I encourage the FAA to consider recognizing instruction related to:

Maintenance human factors;
Inspection-team communication;
Maintenance documentation and record accuracy;
Supervisory oversight of inspection activities;
Error prevention and error-management strategies;
Airworthiness decision-making;
Risk management in maintenance environments; and
Inspection-related safety culture.

Such training directly supports the competencies required to exercise inspection privileges safely and effectively. These topics strengthen the ability of inspection-rating holders to prevent maintenance errors, ensure regulatory compliance, improve documentation quality, and supervise inspection activities in accordance with FAA standards.
As the FAA moves toward a recent-experience-based model, I believe consideration should be given to recognizing certain human-factors and inspection-supervision training activities as qualifying means of maintaining inspection competency, provided the curriculum is directly linked to aircraft maintenance, inspection practices, airworthiness determinations, and regulatory compliance.
I commend the FAA for pursuing a modernization effort that reduces administrative burden while maintaining safety oversight. Thank you for the opportunity to provide comments for consideration.
Respectfully,

title: Comment from Helicopter Maintenance Magazine
printtext:
Subject: Comments on NPRM FAA-2026-6671 – Mechanic Certification: Inspection Rating and Recent Experience Requirements
I support the FAA's objective of reducing unnecessary administrative workload associated with Inspection Authorization renewals. Redirecting Aviation Safety Inspector resources from processing renewal applications toward meaningful surveillance and safety oversight is a worthwhile goal.
However, I respectfully recommend that the FAA modify the proposal to include a mechanism for periodic independent verification of a mechanic's recent-experience qualifications.
Under the proposed rule, Inspection Rating holders would maintain qualification records independently without any routine validation by the FAA. This represents a significant change from the current IA renewal process, where an FAA inspector periodically verifies that renewal requirements have been satisfied.
Although the proposal appropriately maintains recent-experience requirements, it appears to rely almost exclusively on self-determination of currency until an FAA inspection, investigation, or enforcement action occurs.
I recommend the FAA consider implementing a simple electronic validation process, perhaps every two years, allowing Inspection Rating holders to upload documentation through an online FAA portal. Such a process could be largely automated, would eliminate the administrative burden associated with current paper renewals, and would preserve an important element of independent oversight.
This modification would satisfy the FAA's stated objective of reducing paperwork while maintaining confidence that mechanics exercising Inspection Rating privileges continue to meet qualification requirements.
Thank you for the opportunity to comment.
Mike (RotorDoc) Broderick, Contributing Writer for Helicopter Maintenance Magazine

title: Comment from Joshua Rauch
printtext:
I support the FAA’s proposal to replace the current Inspection Authorization (IA) with an Inspection Rating (IR) and to transition from a periodic renewal process to a recent-experience-based system.

The proposed Inspection Rating more accurately reflects how experienced maintenance professionals remain engaged in aircraft maintenance and airworthiness oversight throughout their careers. I believe this approach will reduce administrative burden while maintaining or improving aviation safety.

I recommend that the FAA explicitly clarify in the final rule that qualifying recent experience may include maintenance, inspection, supervisory, quality assurance, and technical oversight duties performed under a Part 145 Repair Station certificate.

Many experienced mechanics holding inspection privileges serve in positions such as inspectors, avionics specialists, quality assurance personnel, maintenance supervisors, shop managers, directors of maintenance, and technical leaders. These individuals routinely exercise maintenance judgment, oversee maintenance activities, evaluate airworthiness, review maintenance records, supervise corrective actions, and ensure regulatory compliance, even when they do not personally perform a significant number of annual inspections or approve major repairs and alterations each year.

Without explicit recognition of these duties, the final rule could unintentionally discourage experienced maintenance professionals from accepting supervisory or specialized technical positions while still remaining actively engaged in aircraft maintenance.

I recommend the FAA clarify that employment and maintenance-related duties performed under a certificated Part 145 Repair Station, including supervisory and inspection-related responsibilities, constitute qualifying recent experience for the purpose of maintaining Inspection Rating currency.

Such clarification would better reflect the structure of modern maintenance organizations while preserving the intent of ensuring that Inspection Rating holders remain actively involved in aviation maintenance and airworthiness activities.

Thank you for the opportunity to comment.

Respectfully,

title: Comment from MARK BINGAMON
printtext:
To Whom It May Concern,

I support the FAA's proposal to replace the Inspection Authorization with an Inspection Rating and to streamline the process for maintaining inspection privileges. The proposed shift toward recent-experience requirements appears to reduce administrative burden while maintaining safety oversight.

I submit this comment as an aviation professional who has managed aircraft maintenance and refurbishment projects for many years. While I am not an A&P mechanic or Inspection Authorization holder, I have worked closely with maintenance teams, inspectors, planners, and customers in large maintenance environments.

During my career, I have observed that some of the most costly maintenance and inspection issues did not result from a lack of technical skill. Instead, they resulted from human factors such as communication, coordination, documentation review, and decision-making.

For example, I witnessed multiple situations where communication breakdowns between departments resulted in required parts not being ordered. The maintenance requirements were known, but the information was not effectively communicated. As a result, aircraft deliveries were delayed while waiting for parts to arrive.

In another project, maintenance personnel began disassembling portions of an aircraft to accomplish a service bulletin. Only after significant labor had been expended was it discovered that the service bulletin was not applicable due to a previously installed aircraft modification. The technical work itself was performed correctly, but a more thorough review of aircraft records and configuration information beforehand could have prevented unnecessary labor, parts procurement, and restocking costs.

These experiences reinforced my belief that maintenance human factors including communication, documentation review, coordination, supervision, and decision-making have a direct impact on inspection effectiveness, maintenance quality, regulatory compliance, and aviation safety.

As the FAA develops the framework for Inspection Ratings and recent-experience requirements, I encourage consideration of maintenance human factors, inspection supervision, documentation quality, and airworthiness decision-making as competencies that directly support the safe exercise of inspection privileges. These topics are not simply professional-development subjects, they are practical tools that help prevent maintenance errors and improve inspection outcomes.

Thank you for considering these comments.
Respectfully,
Concerned Aviator

title: Comment from Brian Johnson
printtext:
I am a certificated Airframe and Powerplant mechanic with a current Inspection Authorization and 36 years of aviation maintenance experience. I am writing in strong support of the FAA's proposal to replace the Inspection Authorization with an Inspection Rating on the mechanic certificate.

The current biennial renewal system creates administrative burden without meaningfully measuring competency or currency. Replacing it with a permanent rating — consistent with how Airframe and Powerplant ratings already work — is a logical, overdue improvement. The shift to rolling recent experience requirements also makes far more sense than an arbitrary renewal deadline tied to odd-numbered years.

I support this rule. I ask for one amendment before it is finalized.

The recent experience activities proposed under § 65.93(a) do not include aviation maintenance supervisory and management roles. This is a significant gap. Many of the most experienced IA holders in the industry have moved into roles as Directors of Maintenance, Quality Assurance Managers, and Maintenance Supervisors. These professionals oversee inspection programs, manage A&P teams, ensure regulatory compliance, and maintain airworthiness daily. They are unquestionably "actively engaged" in aviation maintenance — yet nothing in the proposed rule explicitly recognizes their experience as qualifying.

Excluding supervisory and management roles risks sidelining the most experienced segment of our workforce at a time when the aviation industry is already facing a serious experience and staffing shortage. It would be counterproductive to a rule that is otherwise designed to reduce burden and retain qualified professionals.

I urge the FAA to explicitly include aviation maintenance supervisory and management roles as qualifying recent experience activities under § 65.93(a). This single addition would make an already strong proposal significantly better.

Thank you for the opportunity to comment.

title: Comment from Kertzman, Andrew
printtext:
In the 2016 final rule economic analysis, OSHA estimated an annualized cost of the final rule would total $305 million (81 FR 82847). OSHA estimated that retrofitting fixed ladders between 24 feet and 30 feet in height with ladder safety and personal fall arrest systems would total $8.5 million in aggregate costs, for the approximately 109,200 fixed ladders OSHA stated would be affected.

OSHA's estimation of the number of affected ladders, and associated costs are divorced from reality. OSHA published "Impacts Exhibit V-1: Estimated Annualized Costs and Benefits of the Final Rule" Explicitly states in the last row the "More stringent Alternative - Mandated Combination of Cages, Wells, Landing Platforms, and Ladder Safety Systems" has "Modestly Higher Benefits (...)" for "Significantly Higher Costs (Possibly over $1 Billion). There is no difference in policy or effect between what OSHA promulgated, and OSHA's "more stringent alternative" described in the preamble (The more stringent alternative would require that employers provide cages, wells, landing platforms, and ladder safety devices for all fixed ladders; the cost of this alternative would be highly significant, while the incremental benefits would be modest relative to the preferred alternative.) OSHA promulgated a "more stringent alternative" policy, while disingenuously claiming "preferred alternative" costs in it's economic analysis.

Many of the sources below are cited in the final rule.
Commercial Buildings Energy Consumption Survey
Dept of Defense, Base Structure Report
US Census Bureau, American Housing Survey
US Energy Information Admin, Manufacturing Energy Consumption Survey

Numbers of buildings in the US are provided below from these sources.
~800,000 warehouse/storage buildings,
~400,000 religious buildings,
~400,000 education buildings,
~400,000 food service buildings,
~1,700,000 two story or greater commercial buildings,
~30,000,000 two story or greater residential buildings

OSHA conservatively estimates of the more than ~34 million two story or greater buildings in the US, around 0.3% are affected. Both the quantity of affected ladders in the US, as well as the associated costs of the rule are off by no less than two orders of magnitude.

OSHA heavily sourced all of their numbers and costs from the Eastern Research Group "Technical and Analytical Support and Docket Review for OSHA's Preliminary Analysis of Costs, Benefits, and Economic Impacts for OSHA's Proposed Standard for Walking and Working Surfaces.", but the numbers are +20-30 years old and don't account for growth/inflation.

Many supported scaffolding systems (not even identified in OSHA's 2016 economic analysis) use fixed external ladders, and are used not just in construction sites, but also building and equipment maintenance activities in fixed industry establishments covered by the rule. If these are assembled onsite, the associated ladders would be "built/assembled" after the 2016 final rule, requiring anchorages/SRLs, etc.

OSHA's identified economic feasibility burdens fundamentally relies on fixed ladders having a 20 year lifespan, when in truth if maintained in good condition and regularly inspected have a potentially indefinite lifespan. If a fixed ladder with cage was installed indoors in a warehouse the year before OSHA's 2016 rule was promulgated, and then only used 20 or 40 times, and was still in pristine condition; OSHA would burden that employer with the cost of disposing of the ladder and replacing it something engineered to support a ladder safety system.

Lastly, and most importantly; nearly all of the costs of compliance with the final rule are tied to this particular element, and the preamble to the 2016 final rule doesn't even attempt to represent how many lost work days or fatalities are specifically tied to falls from fixed ladders with cages. In 2020, only 5 deaths and ~5% of ladder fall injuries and illnesses are associated with fixed ladders compared to portable ones. As close as makes no difference to all ladder risks are associated with the portable ones; and OSHA requires zero fall protection on portable ladders whatsoever. The reason OSHA doesn't provide fixed ladder specific injury/illness numbers is BLS data mostly isn't/wasn't that granular. In OSHA's 2016 final rule fixed ladder risks and costs are comingled with portable ones, likely in an effort to lend justification to the fixed ladder requirements which are untenable on their own. As a result, all of the portable ladder injuries/illnesses will occur unimpeded, while all of the economic burden gets shifted to facilities with fixed ladders.

title: Anonymous Public Comment
printtext: Nearly a decade ago, a close family member of mine was working in construction when he fell off of an unsecured roof, and severely injured his shoulder while trying to catch himself on the way down. A lifelong manual laborer, he has been unable to find solid work years afterwards, and is still struggling with the effects of this injury today. Even within the status quo, professions that are reliant on ladders rank among the most dangerous, with OSHA listing “Roofers” and “Helpers in Construction Trades” as the second and fourth most dangerous jobs in the United States respectively, and furthers that the leading cause of fatalities for both is falls. In 2021 for example, falls accounted for 37% of construction site fatalities. As such, it seems incredibly inadvisable to not just maintain the status quo, but to take action to specifically remove safety measures, which is exactly what this rule change would do. There’s a reason this regulation was put in place to begin with: ladder cages are simply not safe enough. They do nothing to break or even slow a fall should one occur, and simply direct you downwards to your death instead of outwards toward your death. Furthermore, beyond the obvious lack of a safety system, this rule change would actually encourage workplaces to continue using increasingly unsafe, aging ladders. According to Ladders UK Direct, the upper end of a lifespan for a commercial ladder is about 20 years. This rule was first implemented in 2016, which is 20 years before the 2036 deadline. Under this rule change, if employers replace a ladder that is currently in place, they will still need to equip the new one with a personal fall arrest system. In other words, once employers are approaching the 2036 deadline, they will almost certainly be required to implement a personal fall arrest system regardless of the deadline. Therefore, since there is no longer a blanket deadline, employers will be incentivized to use potentially unsafe, past-lifespan ladders to avoid these requirements. OSHA is seeking comment on both the currently proposed deadline removal, and the potential repeal or revision of the requirement at large. Both of these changes would be egregiously bad ideas, and I would further say that given the poor safety conditions of these workplaces in the status quo, more safety regulations are needed, not less. The entire purpose of OSHA, the Occupational Safety and Health Administration, is to ensure good safety and health practices are being followed in the workplace. Changing this regulation will lead to nothing but unnecessary hazard, injury, and even death in the workplace. I urge you not to finalize this change.

title: Comment from Henn, Daniel
printtext:
Regarding the petition submitted by the American Fuel & Petrochemical Manufacturers (AFPM), American Chemistry Council (ACC), and the American Petroleum Institute (API), which seeks to dilute the requirements established in 29 CFR §1910.28(b)(9): I oppose this petition and reject the propositions asserted therein.
To begin, the negotiation of fixed ladders which are unprotected by ladder safety systems or personal fall arrest systems is a pervasive hazard for the American worker. The sheer verticality of these ladders requires the worker to negotiate them at an unnatural angle requiring physical effort to not only climb the ladder, but to remain adhered to the ladder as well.
BLS data published over the last ten years illustrates that 40% of all fatal fall occurs in fall distances of 15 feet or less, and in this respect, the regulation is generous in that it only targets ladders of 24 feet or greater. Furthermore, it is important to note that this same data suggests that one out of six fatal falls is ladder related. I concede that this data is heavily contaminated by incidents involving portable ladders as well, but when we consider that the ten-year trend of fatal occupational falls shows that the number of SIF incidents for workers at height is increasing or remaining stable; occupational fatalities overall are decreasing over time. It is clear to those of us engaged in mitigating fall hazards that not enough is being done to protect workers at height. The increasing median days away from work for those involved in non-fatal fall incidents helps to emphasize this point as well.
I would also add that the financial impact of complying with the rule was wildly inflated in the petition, estimated to be approximately $54,000 per ladder, on average. Many of these hazards could easily be remediated with commercially accessible solutions on a self-performing basis at a cost of $1,000 - $3,000 per ladder. Even with the full burden of third-party qualified person involvement, procurement, engineering, installation, certification, etc. – the $54,000 per ladder figure is exaggerated by a factor of three to five times what it would cost for a more financially burdensome, outsourced approach.
Cages and wells are not functionally effective preventative measures and cannot prevent or effectively arrest a fall in a predictable or repeatable fashion. Such an assertion ignores the many developments in fall protection methods and technologies that have been developed to effectively mitigate hazards such as these since Subpart M was implemented back in 1994. It ignores 32 years of progress and evolution in the field of occupational height safety in favor of archaic methods that do little if anything to protect the people doing the work that makes the existence of the AFPM, ACC and API possible.

title: Comment from Wing, Josh; Valcourt Group
printtext:
(1) Introduction
I work in the commercial real estate industry, supporting building owners and operators across a large portfolio comprising thousands of workers. My role involves assisting with OSHA compliance, as well as overseeing fall protection system installations, inspections, and repairs. Through this experience, I regularly evaluate fixed ladder systems and advise on regulatory requirements, giving me direct, practical insight into how these standards are interpreted and applied in the field.
________________________________________
(2) Background
This comment pertains specifically to 29 CFR §1910.28(b)(9), which addresses fall protection requirements for fixed ladders that extend more than 24 feet above a lower level. The regulation outlines when ladder safety systems or personal fall arrest systems are required and clarifies the phase-out of cages and wells as compliant fall protection for new installations.
________________________________________
(3) Analysis
In practice, there is widespread misunderstanding within the commercial real estate market regarding the applicability of this regulation. Many building owners incorrectly believe that fixed ladders under 24 feet in height require ladder fall protection systems or cages. This misinterpretation leads to unnecessary installations and added costs without corresponding safety benefits.
Based on our portfolio of serviced buildings, which includes thousands of fixed ladders, only approximately 10%–20% meet the threshold requiring ladder safety systems under §1910.28(b)(9). The remaining ladders fall below the 24-foot trigger and do not require such systems under current OSHA standards.
This confusion appears to stem not from deficiencies in the regulation itself, but from a lack of clear understanding and consistent interpretation in the field. As a result, building owners are often overcorrecting, implementing systems that exceed regulatory requirements. This can divert resources away from higher-risk safety improvements and create inefficiencies in compliance planning.
Importantly, the regulation as written appropriately targets higher-risk scenarios—namely, longer ladder climbs such as those found on water towers and similar structures—where fall protection systems provide meaningful risk reduction. Applying these requirements to shorter ladders does not proportionally enhance worker safety and may dilute focus on more critical hazards.
________________________________________
(4) Recommendations
I recommend maintaining the current structure and thresholds outlined in §1910.28(b)(9), as they effectively balance safety and practicality. However, I strongly encourage OSHA to provide additional clarification and outreach to address common misinterpretations in the market. Specifically:
•Issue clearer guidance or interpretive materials emphasizing that the 24-foot threshold is the trigger for fall protection requirements on fixed ladders.
•Reinforce that cages are not required for ladders under 24 feet and are no longer considered compliant fall protection for new ladders exceeding that height.
•Consider publishing practical examples or industry-specific FAQs to help building owners and compliance professionals better understand when systems are—and are not—required.
________________________________________
(5) Conclusion
The current regulation under §1910.28(b)(9) is well-structured and appropriately focused on higher-risk ladder applications. In my experience, the primary issue is not the rule itself, but widespread misinterpretation leading to unnecessary compliance measures. Maintaining the existing regulation while improving clarity through guidance and education will better support building owners, reduce unnecessary costs, and ensure that safety resources are directed where they are most effective.

title: Anonymous Public Comment
printtext:
I strongly believe the regulation should remain in force exactly as written because the rule was created to protect workers. These workers routinely climb towers, monopoles, rooftops, and other elevated structures in high-risk environments, and having this rule in place continues to protect their health and safety. OSHA’s final Walking-Working Surfaces rule was published on November 18, 2016, and the expected service life of a fixed ladder system is 15-20 years, depending on environmental factors. This rule established a 20-year phase-in period for these ladders which would end in 2036, which aligns with the expected timeline of the natural lifecycle of these ladder systems.

Any fixed ladder installed immediately before the 2016 rulemaking would be at or near the end of its useful life by the 2036 deadline. At a minimum, those systems would reasonably be expected to require substantial inspection, corrosion mitigation, structural repair, or full replacement to remain safe for continued use. This makes the existing implementation schedule both technically reasonable and economically predictable for employers.

Falls remain the leading cause of death in construction, consistently accounting for the largest share of fatal occupational injuries year after year. OSHA continues to identify falls as one of the “Fatal Four” causes of construction deaths, underscoring that preventing falls from height remains one of the most effective ways to save lives on the job. Choosing to help save people's lives and prevent further injury should be the priority of OSHA.

For these reasons, I believe the current rule language and compliance deadline should stand unchanged.

title: Comment from Phillips, Jesse
printtext:
Regarding the proposed removal of the November 18, 2036 deadline for fixed ladder replacement, I support the vacating of this obligation. The costs are excessive and the incidents are too infrequent to compel this replacement.

If (or when) there are injuries, due to companies failing to replace or augment their fixed ladder systems, the civil judiciary should determine whether and to what degree the company is liable.

It is reasonable to allow employers to assume the risk for their own operations.

The obvious best practice is to have fall arrest or ladder safety systems in place; however, allowing extant ladder equipment to serve through the end of the useful life of the equipment will facilitate flexibility and preclude burdensome and onerous obligations on the part of employers.

The government compelling an action by an independent and private company is counter to the nature of this country. Many such cases. That said, I agree that it is in the best interest of employers and employees to willingly replace or upgrade systems to reflect industry best practices and would prefer to see that occur.

Thank you for your attention to this matter.

title: Comment from Schatz, Gabriel
printtext:
In their own words, OSHA’s main goal is to “provide safe and healthful working conditions for American workers,” and in order to continue to do so effectively, I firmly stand behind the notion of maintaining the established regulation deadline.
The original rule that was established in Walking-Working Surfaces (2016) enacted this deadline because OSHA knew that cages and wells were not enough to prevent deaths and injuries from falls. Rightfully so, considering that according to the CDC, in 2020 alone, there were almost twenty-three thousand workplace injuries involving ladders and over 160 deaths. With fall arrest or other safety systems in place, we significantly improve workplace conditions and protect workers from injury if a fall does inevitably occur.
Working on repair sites and around individuals who have twenty-plus years of experience, I have seen firsthand and heard countless stories about the dangers associated with a reluctance to comply with workplace safety. Rules like this are in place not to maliciously increase the financial burden of those who must meet compliance, but to maintain the safety of the American workers who have no other avenue of protection. OSHA has already established that worker safety is reliant on full compliance with this rule, and the deadline that is at risk of being eradicated embodies the procedural implication of this rule, not some optionality that implies a trivial basis of the argument.
If we allow the removal of this deadline, we are critically weakening any future prospects of complete compliance with the rule. The deadline should continue to be maintained as it effectively ensures a firm point of completion, not to mention the fact that it works to combat against the vagueness that “end-of-life replacement” presents with indefinite deferment. Without it, this vagueness opens up avenues that can prove to be harmful to workers who are left at the mercy of employers who have deferred this obligation of safety to their next most convenient moment.
This is not only a failure in regard to safety and operations, but a failure to the people and families whose lives have been lost or forever changed due to avoidable workplace deaths. OSHA has even stated that the current cages do not prevent falls; in fact, they can actually increase the severity of the injuries sustained during falls. Going even further, falls are cited as one of the leading causes of workplace-related deaths by OSHA, with fixed ladders being at the center of most incidents. The unavoidable truth is that this deadline can help enforce a rule that is projected to save almost thirty lives a year and thousands of injuries. It is the only action to take; alternatively, the removal of this deadline will undoubtedly undermine OSHA’s own safety projections, something that seems to actively work against its mission of safety.
Essentially, this action can be boiled down to a core cost-driven justification of action rather than a safety-driven administrative improvement. If the goal really is to simply provide increased flexibility and reduce the compliance burden, then establish a new deadline or create a broader scope of compliance. Simply removing the deadline is not the answer.
The original rule was crafted as a thoughtful response to persistent workplace fatalities; finding something that could stop the falls instead of redirecting them was a game-changer. However, this move to abolish the deadline tarnishes the original intent of the rule. Employers were never told nor expected to retrofit their ladders overnight; they were simply told to provide their workers with safer equipment that could help save lives. But now, as the compliance window shrinks with every passing day, the deadline is being questioned. Not because it was an action that was rushed or enacted without enough time to reflect, but because employers must soon begin taking action to better the conditions for their workers. The deadline eliminates this problem, while employers flirt with a delayed compliance loophole, and undoubtedly continue to use the old infrastructure well beyond the originally intended replacement date, the deadline presents a firm avenue to safety.
This move is nothing more than a corporate incentive push disguised as a break for employers who don’t need one. With no deadline, employers aren’t burdened with a fixed retrofit deadline, and in turn are not required to spend any money. Safety becomes a game of cost-benefit, where repairs are preferable to safer replacements, and upgrades are deferred indefinitely. OSHA enforcement becomes a metric of unpredictable case benefit, and it all happens at the expense of the worker. Workers are the ones stuck dealing with old, unsafe equipment and unreliable safety equipment improvements. The risk is now constant for workers, while the cost obligation becomes flexible for employers, and the cycle continues.

title: Comment from Jonas, Carsten
printtext:
I strongly support this proposed rule. Removing standards that address hazards covered by building and fire codes helps avoid confusion and inadvertent violations that can easily occur when the codes are inconsistent with OSHA standards.

Many OSHA standards were enacted decades ago. Building and fire codes have significantly evolved since then, often at a much faster pace than OSHA standards. Additionally, the pace at which states and local jurisdictions adopt new editions of building and fire codes varies significantly throughout the US.

When two sets of prescriptive regulations (OSHA standards, and building and fire codes) both address the same hazard, this can easily lead to confusion and inadvertent violations.

I believe it would be advisable for OSHA to review its other standards as well to identify standards that address hazards covered by building and fire codes, and to repeal those standards (thus using the General Duty Clause to address those hazards) or replace their prescriptive requirements with performance-based objectives, which can easily be used in connection with any version of a building or fire code without hindering innovation.

Some people might be concerned about what this would mean for the few (mainly rural) jurisdictions that have not adopted building or fire codes and are in a state without statewide code adoption. However, even if the codes are not adopted into law in a jurisdiction, they can still be used as a benchmark to assess the safety of a workplace in relation to hazards covered by the codes.

In conclusion: this proposed rule is an excellent starting point to fostering a cooperative relationship between OSHA standards and building and fire codes. I strongly encourage OSHA to not only move forward with this proposed rule but also work to repeal or modernize its other standards that are duplicative of building and fire codes.

title: Comment from Physicians for Human Rights
printtext:
Dear Commissioner Makary, 

On behalf of Physicians for Human Rights (PHR), we submit this comment in full support of citizen petitions FDA-2025-P-0377-0001; FDA-2025-P-1576-0001; FDA-2025-P-2162-0001 that, among other measures, request the FDA to refrain from imposing additional restrictions on mifepristone. Recently, PHR and over 370 health care workers and 1974 allies wrote to you voicing their concerns on the recently announced FDA review of mifepristone.1 This comment consolidates these submissions and echoes support for the safety of mifepristone and its continued approval by the FDA. 

 

The FDA’s initial approval of mifepristone, also known by the brand name Mifeprex and RU486, in 2000 was predicated on years of rigorous, evidence-based research demonstrating the overwhelming safety and efficacy of mifepristone in use. It is recognized by the World Health Organization as a core medication on the Model List of Essential Medicines due to its safety, efficacy, and importance to health systems worldwide.2 In addition to its use in combination with misoprostol to assist abortion, mifepristone has been approved for the treatment of Cushing syndrome under the brand name Korlym since 2012. It is also under investigational use in the United States and other countries for the treatment of mental health and neurological conditions such as depression, dementia, post-traumatic stress disorder, Gulf War syndrome, delirium, suicide, psychosis, catatonia, and cognitive deterioration; cancers – particularly breast cancer; endometriosis; and uterine fibroids. Prior, post-approval updates to mifepristone access and REMS scheduling have similarly echoed the consensus of the existing literature, which demonstrates, based on concrete data and thousands of patients' experiences, that delivery of mifepristone is overwhelmingly safe and integral to the health of thousands of Americans.  

 

PHR has conducted extensive research on the impacts of abortion bans on US patients and clinicians, including specifically assessing the effects of depressed access to Mifeprex. These findings, most recently published in the brief “Cascading Harms: How Abortion Bans Lead to Discriminatory Care Across Medical Specialties,”3 demonstrated the negative repercussions of mifepristone restrictions on reproductive and non-reproductive clinicians. More than 100 peer-reviewed clinical studies have been conducted on mifepristone to assess its long-term safety, all of which showed the drug to be safe and effective.4

 

As PHR5 and other coalitions of experts and reproductive health scientists6 have expressed, the methodology and conclusions of the Ethics and Public Policy Center (EPPC) report which the present review of mifepristone is based fails to meet the high evidentiary, transparency, and methodological standards required of objective, empirical research.7 In contrast to the non-transparent data, unsubstantiated conclusions, and skewed methodological framing of the EPPC, the FDA’s prescribing information cites the findings of 10 clinical trials with more than 30,000 patients which show that serious adverse effects occur in fewer than 0.5% of patients.8 Similar reviews and studies have found comparable rates in both in-person and telehealth delivery of mifepristone.9 

 

Periodic reviews of medication are a meaningful and valuable tool to ensure patient safety, but they must be grounded in established medical evidence and scientific rigor. Rejecting medical precedent and injecting partisan politics into this process not only foments disinformation and undermines public trust in American health care authorities but also directly harms patients who depend on mifepristone for safe, effective care. 

 

PHR and its medical partners echo the requests included in the four petitions referenced above to reject additional restrictions on access to mifepristone for reproductive and non-reproductive use in the United States. As experts and health care providers, we urge the FDA to support evidence-based standards and align its regulatory standards with established patient-centered care. 

 

Sincerely, 
Physicians for Human Rights

FemInEM's mission is to address disparities in outcomes for patients by equipping medical professionals with the tools, knowledge, and resources they need to deliver effective and time-sensitive care.

FemInEM respectfully urges FDA to (1) remove the Mifepristone Shared System REMS, including all of its ETASU; or (2) in the alternative, at a minimum, refrain from taking any action that would further reduce patient access to mifepristone and/or increase the burdens associated with prescribing or dispensing mifepristone.

The scientific and medical evidence overwhelmingly demonstrates that mifepristone is safe and effective, including when prescribed via telehealth and dispensed through pharmacies and by mail. Emergency department visit data does not support any characterization of mifepristone as unsafe; rather, it reflects the reality that Americans use emergency departments for a wide array of non-urgent healthcare needs due to systemic barriers to accessing other care.

Maintaining or increasing restrictions on mifepristone will deny patients safe methods of accessing care and impose far-reaching effects on emergency departments' ability to provide necessary healthcare, particularly in rural and underserved communities. The evidence is clear that mifepristone is safe, effective, and critical to the practice of emergency medicine.

Please see attached PDF for full comment.

title: Comment from Sriha Srinivasan
printtext:
As a medical student, a young woman, and a future physician committed to providing reproductive health and abortion care, I strongly support the Citizen Petition urging the FDA to remove the remaining REMS restrictions on mifepristone.

My medical education has taught me that clinical care should be guided by evidence. Mifepristone has been used in the United States for decades, and its well-established safety record does not justify subjecting it to restrictions that create additional barriers for patients, pharmacies, and clinicians. Requirements that providers register with manufacturers, pharmacies undergo special certification, and patients sign a medication-specific agreement do not make abortion care meaningfully safer. They make it harder to provide and harder to access.

As a future abortion provider, I am particularly concerned about what these requirements mean for the next generation of physicians. Every additional hurdle between a qualified clinician and their patient has consequences, particularly for patients who already face geographic, financial, logistical, or social barriers to reproductive healthcare.

I also write as a young woman who could need this medication myself. There is something deeply consequential about learning how to care for patients while simultaneously watching evidence-based reproductive healthcare become more difficult for people my age to obtain. Patients seeking medication abortion deserve the same respect, autonomy, and evidence-based standards that we expect throughout medicine. They should not be singled out for exceptional requirements when the evidence does not support them.

The FDA has an obligation to regulate medications according to scientific evidence and demonstrated risk. Maintaining unnecessary restrictions on mifepristone when the evidence no longer warrants them undermines that principle and imposes real burdens on patients and healthcare professionals.

I urge the FDA to grant the petition and remove the remaining REMS requirements for mifepristone. As someone preparing to spend my career caring for patients, I want to practice in a healthcare system where medical decisions are governed by evidence, where clinicians can provide appropriate care without unnecessary barriers, and where patients are trusted to make decisions about their own bodies and futures.

I am writing in strong support of this petition to limit the exposure of refined carbohydrates used in industrial food processing. As someone deeply concerned about the health of our communities, I believe this represents one of the most important public health actions we can take.

What troubles me most is how parents today are unknowingly raising their children on products that bear little resemblance to what previous generations consumed. Many of us reach for the same brand names our parents trusted, assuming we're making safe choices for our families. But the formulations have changed dramatically—often without our awareness. Products that were once made with whole ingredients now contain excessive amounts of refined carbohydrates and processed sugars, sometimes hidden under technical names that even informed consumers struggle to identify.

This disconnect between perception and reality is causing profound harm. Parents believe they're providing their children with familiar, safe foods, when in fact they're inadvertently contributing to patterns of consumption that lead to obesity, type 2 diabetes, and cardiovascular disease. The betrayal of that trust—and the manipulation of our natural desire to feed our families well—is unconscionable.

The scientific evidence connecting refined carbohydrates to our current health crisis is overwhelming, yet families continue to be misled by marketing that exploits nostalgia and brand loyalty. Children are particularly vulnerable, both to aggressive advertising and to the metabolic consequences of these reformulated products. We are watching preventable chronic diseases appear in younger and younger populations, while parents remain in the dark about how drastically our food supply has changed.

I urge the agency to adopt this petition and implement meaningful limits on refined carbohydrates in industrial food processing. Families deserve transparency and protection. We need regulations that ensure the products on our shelves are worthy of the trust parents place in them when feeding their children.

title: Comment from Lindsay M
printtext:
Zorbium is an incredibly dangerous drug that I believe should be removed from the market.

Our cat would almost certainly have died after receiving Zorbium had we not intervened with supportive care, including subcutaneous fluids, anti-nausea medication, an appetite stimulant, and repeated doses of Narcan (naloxone). For nearly a week, he was unable to eat, drink, or sleep. Narcan (which only temporarily reverses the effects for approximately one to two hours) was the only thing that allowed him to eat, drink and sleep. We administered it multiple times over several days, and I truly believe it is the primary reason he survived.

Unfortunately, many other cats have not been as fortunate. I am a member of a support group where desperate cat owners come for help every day after their cats receive Zorbium. Reading story after story of severe reactions, and in some cases the loss of beloved pets is absolutely heartbreaking. While I cannot speak to the exact number of affected cats, there appear to be a substantial number of reports from owners who believe Zorbium contributed to serious illness or death.

In my opinion, this medication is simply too potent and too long-acting to be safe. Once it is applied, there is no practical way to stop its effects until the drug wears off, which can take four or more days. If a cat experiences a severe adverse reaction, there is little that can be done beyond supportive care. In contrast, our cat had previously received regular buprenorphine without any problems whatsoever.

Immediately after his procedure, I knew something was terribly wrong. The profound sedation was unlike anything we had ever experienced. It was as though our cat had become a completely different animal. We even began calling it “Zombium” because of the zombie-like state it left him in.

There is simply no need for a medication like this when traditional buprenorphine and other pain medicines are safer and provide effective pain control with a much shorter duration.

What is equally concerning is that our veterinarian did not ask for our consent before administering Zorbium. This is something we hear repeatedly from other cat owners seeking support. Pet owners deserve to be informed that this medication will remain active for several days and that there is no reliable way to reverse its effects if a serious adverse reaction occurs.

I urge you to carefully review the growing number of adverse event reports associated with Zorbium and to reevaluate whether its benefits truly outweigh its risks. No family should lose a beloved cat because of a medication that, in my opinion, poses unnecessary and unacceptable dangers when safer alternatives are available. Please consider removing Zorbium from the market to help prevent other families from experiencing the fear, heartbreak, and devastation that we, and so many others have endured.

The only information I was given was by a receptionist who laughingly told me that my cat was "gonna be loopy" when I picked her up and she said not to touch the back of her neck because it would be "sticky for awhile".
The veterinary clinic was Audubon Veterinary Clinic. Their address is 2120 West Northwest Blvd., Spokane, Washington 99205. Their phone number is (509) 328-7120. The vet that administered this poison is Dr. Olivia Young. As I discovered later, she had used Zorbium off-label three different ways. She administered it minutes before she was sent home. The instructions say it is to be used BEFORE surgery. The instructions also say that it was never tested on cats older than five. Mine, as I've stated, was seventeen. And the instructions clearly state that it's not to be used on cats with underlying medical issues--renal disease is the first one listed. And Dr. Young had been treating my cat for Stage 2 renal disease for several months.
She came home just as you'd expect from a cat that just had eleven teeth pulled. She used the litter box, meowed, drank water, and jumped on the couch. Within an hour her breathing was almost imperceptible. I couldn't feel her heartbeat. Her eyes were dilated to a point that no color was visible. She could no longer hold her head up. And wide awake. Unable to move. She didn't eat, drink water, or sleep for five days. She spent four and a half days at our pet emergency clinic and multiple doses of Narcan are clearly what saved her life. I will never forget what the vet at the emergency clinic told me when I brought her in: We don't have Zorbium on the premises. We deal with the effects of Zorbium all the time". That's a direct quote.
She never recovered. Zorbium put her into complete kidney failure. Prior to Zorbium she was diagnosed with Stage 2 kidney disease. She never reached that threshold again. After two months of intensive treatment she stayed at Stage 3. And she never ate right again. I guess it could be called anoexia. It was a nightmarish challenge.
She had a stroke May 26, 2025, and had to be euthanized. The stroke was 100% the result of the kidney disease that had advanced because of the Zorbium. My new vet said strokes are frequently linked to renal disease. In people, too.
Dr. Olivia Young couldn't have been sorrier. At least that's what she kept saying. She admitted the off-label use but kept saying "We do it all the time". She wasn't sorry enough to give me a credit on the first day of my cat's treatment when I took her back. That was an additional $500.00 before they gave up and sent us to the emergency clinic. I can't even begin to list the expenses of the following two months. Elanco, the company that makes this poison did reimburse me for about 1/5 of the expenses. This is apparently something they do on a regular basis.
Zorbium should never have been approved. Period. And should be taken off the market immediately. This nightmare should never have happened.

printtext:
As a student studying to be a Nuclear Engineer, I see this as a great first step towards bringing a Nuclear Renaissance. I am passionate about Nuclear Power, and I see it as the best way to meet future energy needs particularly with the AI Boom. I am clear with my biases, unlike other commenters. Who determines what is "reasonable?" Is it bureaucracy? Is it shareholders? Is it engineers? All of these groups may have different answers, and may adopt eachothers' answers depending on the context of the "radiation exposure event." The point is, whoever wrote this disgustingly sloppy regulation either had five minutes to clock out on a Friday, or they had no understanding of radiation exposure risk.

Many commenters will say something like "There is no evidence that low level radiation is safe." However, there is no evidence that low level radiation is HAZARDOUS either. Because there is no clear relationship, we must therefore determine the intersection between how safe and how practical a limit is. I agree that all deaths and diseases causes by radiation is a tragedy, but the SAME commenters that choke the Nuclear Power Industry to death are the SAME commenters that warn of "global warming" and brag about their electric car. Let me ask you, what powers your electric car? It is MOSTLY coal and natural gas plants. Where is your concern for the NOX gasses, SO2, particulate matter, and even Carbon-13? Now lets actually get technical and use numbers. For this example, we will be using a unit called rem (1 rem=1,000 mrem for my fellow Americans). Just using the data we have regarding low dose radiation exposure, we cannot find any kind of relationship between an increase in cancer rates and a radiation exposure below 10 rem. For context, we are naturally exposed to about 0.09-0.27 rem annually. The public around a Nuclear Plant is legally allowed to be exposed to another 0.1 rem/year. This means that in a (highly unethical) experiment, subjects could receive 100 times the legal limit of radiation, or 37 times the natural dose of radiation, or 25 times the natural dose for Denver, CO Residents, and there would STILL be no measurable difference in cancer rates. If someone needs to work for 10 minutes in an area with a 0.001 rem/hour exposure, but the radiation dose is expected to fall to 0.0005 rem/hour at some time tomorrow, then they are legally required to postpone the job so that the dose is "reasonably" low, even though there is no way to prove that the radiation difference would change anything. Again, this is all due to a SLOPPY standard.

There are PLENTY of young Americans who are just as enthusiastic about Nuclear as I am. It is literally my favorite n-word lmao. We want to be the generation that brings an power renaissance. We are excited about each new reactor design that is announced and approved. You gave us AI, the technology that changed the world. We are ready to give the world Nuclear. And if it is just me on this hill, then let me lead the charge and have my peers fall in behind me.

title: Comment on FR Doc # 2026-14208, NRC-2025-1140-0001, from Hiroto Kawakami
printtext:
Comments on the NRC's Proposed Modernization of Radiation Protection
In the current proposed rulemaking, the NRC proposes, as the first of its Major Provisions, to remove the ALARA requirements from 10 CFR Chapter I and replace them with a Graded Approach to Dose Management.
In the section entitled "Reconsideration of LNT and ALARA," the NRC states that it is not rejecting the Linear No-Threshold (LNT) model itself, but rather identifies problems with the way the LNT model has been implemented in practice. This position appears to be based on the recognition that, at present, there is no scientific consensus demonstrating the existence of a dose threshold below which stochastic effects can be stated with certainty never to occur.
Consequently, I find the proposed Graded Approach to Dose Management to be generally unconvincing. It appears to be an arbitrary revision intended primarily to preserve consistency with the current regulatory framework rather than to reflect advances in scientific understanding.
The NRC justifies its continued reliance on the LNT model by citing the fact that the INWORKS study and the Million Person Study currently being conducted by the NRC have not disproved the LNT hypothesis, that organizations such as the ICRP continue to endorse the LNT model, and that the National Cancer Institute (NCI), as referenced in SECY-12-0064 (2012), concluded that the LNT model cannot presently be rejected.
However, conventional statistical analyses used in cohort studies have important methodological limitations. Because these analyses are dominated by data from highly exposed individuals, increasing the amount of data alone will not invalidate the LNT model, nor will it allow the radiation risks associated with low-dose exposure to be evaluated appropriately. These statistical issues have recently been highlighted in the Journal of Radiological Protection (DOI: 10.1088/1361-6498/ae890f).
I therefore recommend that the NRC use data from the Million Person Study to perform an analysis similar to that presented in the above paper, in order to obtain a more accurate understanding of radiation risks in the low-dose region before finalizing the proposed revisions. I hope that the final rule will reflect both the results of cohort analyses based on this methodology and the latest findings in medical epidemiology, thereby leading to regulations that are scientifically sound and broadly acceptable to the public.
